synthesis.bigPicture: Robot control is the engineering of a chain of nested feedback loops, each running roughly 10x faster than the one above it and each trusting the layer below to have already made the world safe and well-behaved: a planner or policy thinks at 1-10 Hz, a trajectory controller interpolates at 100 Hz, a servo's own PID closes at ~1 kHz, and a PWM stage commutates at tens of kHz. Everything you build is a scheme for choosing one saturating integer per motor per millisecond without a human in the loop, and the whole architecture exists so that a slow, unbounded, possibly-wrong computation up top cannot produce a setpoint discontinuity down below. The discipline's real content is therefore boundary discipline: what data crosses each boundary, in what units, at what rate, and what the layer below does when the layer above stalls or lies. The process that builds it mirrors the architecture — you validate from the bottom up and from cheap to expensive, because a failure three layers up is indistinguishable from a failure one layer up if you never checked layer one.

stack.job: Decide what the robot should attempt next, own the e-stop, and reset the scene between trials.
stack.crossesDown: A goal pose, a named configuration, or an 'engage policy' flag.
stack.realtime: no — a human is the slowest and most reliable component
stack.typicalImplementation: A person with a hand on a latching mushroom switch; a launch argument; a trial-loop script.

stack.job: Search for a collision-free joint-space path from A to B, then time-parameterise it.
stack.crossesDown: control_msgs/FollowJointTrajectory goal — waypoints 0.1 s apart (TOTG resample_dt default), positions in rad.
stack.runsAt: 0.05-2 s per plan call; unbounded worst case
stack.realtime: no — sampling planners are probabilistically complete and non-deterministic, which is exactly why this cannot live inside a control period
stack.typicalImplementation: MoveIt 2 move_group, OMPL RRTConnect, AddTimeOptimalParameterization adapter; SRDF supplies the allowed-collision matrix.

stack.job: Map an observation window (images + proprioception) to a chunk of H future actions.
stack.crossesDown: An [H, action_dim] array — either absolute joint positions (ALOHA/LeRobot/ROBOTIS) or relative SE(3) EE deltas + absolute gripper width (UMI).
stack.crossesUp: Nothing. A policy is a pure function of the observation; it has no goal, no plan, no termination condition, and cannot report infeasibility.
stack.runsAt: 5-15 Hz typical; ACT 5 ms/call, SmolVLA ~100 ms, pi-0 ~210 ms on an RTX 4090
stack.realtime: no — latency is jittery and unbounded (CUDA sync, GC, page faults); chunking exists to absorb exactly this
stack.typicalImplementation: torch in a separate container/process; LeRobot policy classes; gRPC async-inference client if the GPU is off-robot.

stack.job: Keep a valid, smooth trajectory in the controller's queue at all times despite a source that produces commands 10-25x slower than the control loop.
stack.crossesDown: trajectory_msgs/JointTrajectory with positions (rad), velocities (rad/s) and time_from_start; published to the controller's topic interface, not its action, because each message must supersede the last with no handshake.
stack.crossesUp: sensor_msgs/JointState as the anchor pose; TF for the EE frame.
stack.runsAt: Replan 4-10 Hz (execute E<H steps then discard the tail)
stack.realtime: soft — a late chunk degrades smoothness rather than causing a discontinuity, because JTC keeps interpolating what it last received
stack.typicalImplementation: Your own rclpy node; MoveIt Servo (publish_period 0.01 s) is the vendor-supported equivalent for Cartesian jogging; joint_trajectory_executor for one-shot homing.

stack.job: Turn sparse waypoints into one dense position setpoint per joint per control tick by sampling a spline against the real clock.
stack.crossesDown: One double per joint (rad) written into the claimed command interface — no topics, no serialization.
stack.runsAt: Sampled at the controller_manager rate — 100 Hz here
stack.realtime: yes (soft RT) — it runs inside the control thread and must be allocation-free
stack.typicalImplementation: joint_trajectory_controller/JointTrajectoryController; positions-only input silently degrades to LINEAR interpolation (velocity step at every waypoint), and a final point with non-zero velocity rejects the whole message.

stack.job: Run the ordered read() -> update() -> write() heartbeat, and enforce that exactly one controller claims each command interface.
stack.crossesDown: Calls hardware read/write; hands controllers raw double* into shared state/command arrays.
stack.crossesUp: /controller_manager services (list/load/configure/switch_controller); claim conflicts surface as activation errors rather than races.
stack.runsAt: update_rate: 100 (verified in open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml); 400 Hz on the OMY arms in the same repo
stack.realtime: yes if you claim it — needs CAP_SYS_NICE + rtprio ulimit for SCHED_FIFO; the vendor container grants both and nothing uses them
stack.typicalImplementation: ros2_control_node, one OS process containing the hardware plugin and every active controller.

stack.job: Own the serial port, convert ticks<->radians, and push the full per-servo register configuration at every activation.
stack.crossesDown: One Sync Write of Goal Position (4 bytes x 6 servos) per cycle, plus a register-config burst at on_activate.
stack.crossesUp: One Sync Read of Present Position/Velocity into the state interface array; a return_type::ERROR stops every controller on that hardware.
stack.runsAt: Triggered per control cycle; with is_async="true" (verified, line 4) it runs on its own thread
stack.realtime: soft — async trades determinism for non-blocking; the price is that state you read is at least one cycle stale
stack.typicalImplementation: dynamixel_hardware_interface/DynamixelHardware, baud_rate 1000000, disable_torque_at_init true; the <gpio> blocks are the idempotent register push that fixes 'RAM resets on power cycle'.

stack.job: Carry bytes from the host to six servos on one 3-wire daisy chain, master-initiated, strictly turn-taking, CRC-16 framed.
stack.crossesUp: Status packets in ID order; a collision is not a retry, it is corrupted torque commands.
stack.runsAt: ~1.78 ms per read+write cycle (562 Hz ceiling on the wire) but 2-4 ms real round trip because USB Full-Speed schedules on 1 ms frames — 200-300 Hz is the honest ceiling
stack.realtime: no — this is where your latency budget is quietly spent and it appears in no architecture diagram
stack.typicalImplementation: OpenRB-150 or U2D2 enumerating as /dev/ttyACM0 (CDC-ACM) or /dev/ttyUSB0 (FTDI, where the default 16 ms latency_timer alone caps you near 60 Hz).

stack.job: Refuse to let the commanded setpoint step; build a trapezoidal or triangular velocity profile from present position to goal.
stack.crossesDown: An interpolated setpoint stream into the PID, plus desired velocity/acceleration for the feedforward terms.
stack.crossesUp: Nothing — it is invisible to the host and silently filters your command stream.
stack.runsAt: Regenerated on every Goal Position write; evaluated at the firmware loop rate
stack.realtime: yes, in firmware — this is the last line of mechanical defence and no host bug can disable it by accident
stack.typicalImplementation: DYNAMIXEL Drive Mode 4 (verified) = TIME-based, so Profile Velocity 50 / Acceleration 25 mean 50 ms total and 25 ms of accel — a pure triangular profile that acts as a ~50 ms low-pass filter on your 100 Hz commands.

stack.job: Close position and velocity loops on encoder error and emit a PWM duty.
stack.crossesDown: Signed PWM duty, clamped by PWM Limit.
stack.crossesUp: Present Position / Velocity / Current in the control table; Hardware Error Status.
stack.runsAt: ~1 kHz (working assumption; ROBOTIS does not publish the figure)
stack.realtime: yes — it is inside the actuator precisely because a 1 kHz loop across a shared 1 Mbps bus is arithmetically impossible
stack.typicalImplementation: Position P/I/D Gain 1000/0/1000 (verified). KPP = 1000/128 = 7.8125 PWM-units per pulse, PWM saturates at 885, so ~10 degrees of tracking error commands full motor power; I=0 means gravity droop is configured, not broken.

stack.job: Drive the H-bridge inverter at the commanded duty, turning a number into average winding voltage.
stack.runsAt: Carrier in the tens of kHz
stack.typicalImplementation: ARM Cortex-M + H-bridge inside each XL430/XL330 case. Everything above collapses into this one saturating integer.

nodeGraph.role: A Zenoh router on tcp/7447 that every node opens a client session to; it is the graph, and it is not a ROS node.
nodeGraph.publishes: none — it has no name in `ros2 node list`
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Not lifecycle-managed and not started by any launch file. rmw_zenoh disables UDP multicast scouting by default, so without it nodes start cleanly, log nothing, and `ros2 node list` is empty. Check `ss -ltnp | grep 7447` before debugging anything ROS-level.

nodeGraph.role: The single process that owns /dev/ttyACM0 and contains controller_manager, the DynamixelHardware plugin, and every loaded controller.
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Not itself a lifecycle node, but it drives the lifecycle of every hardware component and controller inside it. Services: /controller_manager/{list,load,configure,switch,unload}_controller, list_hardware_components, set_hardware_component_state.

nodeGraph.role: A controller that claims all state interfaces and no command interfaces; the bridge from zero-copy control memory into the ROS graph.
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Lifecycle-managed by controller_manager (unconfigured -> inactive -> active). If it is not active, /joint_states never exists, so /tf is empty, RViz shows a grey robot, MoveIt refuses to plan, and your policy node hangs forever with no error.

nodeGraph.role: joint_trajectory_controller/JointTrajectoryController — holds the active trajectory and interpolates it against the real clock every tick.
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Lifecycle-managed by controller_manager. Activation is what claims joint1..joint5 position command interfaces, which is why two controllers can be loaded but only one active.

nodeGraph.role: position_controllers/GripperActionController — exposes the gripper as a force-limited close/open so stalling on an object counts as success.
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Lifecycle-managed. Present only in the non-AI config; the omx_f_follower_ai config folds gripper_joint_1 into arm_controller so one policy 6-vector arrives as one atomic message.

nodeGraph.role: A transient process that waits for /controller_manager services, calls load -> configure -> one atomic switch_controller, then exits.
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Not lifecycle-managed; it is the thing that DRIVES the lifecycle. Its exit is launch's only 'controllers are active' event (OnProcessExit) — but it exits on failure too, so verify with `ros2 control list_controllers`, not the launch log.

nodeGraph.role: Parses the URDF into a KDL tree and turns the flat scalar list in /joint_states into a pose tree, so no other node ever has to parse the URDF.
nodeGraph.publishes: /tf (tf2_msgs/msg/TFMessage, RELIABLE depth 100), /tf_static (RELIABLE TRANSIENT_LOCAL, published once), /robot_description (std_msgs/msg/String, TRANSIENT_LOCAL depth 1)
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Not lifecycle-managed. Params: robot_description, frame_prefix, use_sim_time. A second robot needs BOTH a namespace (moves topics) and frame_prefix (moves TF frames) — neither implies the other.

nodeGraph.role: MoveIt's planning process: planning scene, OMPL search, time parameterisation. It is an action CLIENT of the controller, not a hardware driver.
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Not lifecycle-managed. Absent from omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py entirely — the imitation-learning path deliberately has no planner in the loop.

nodeGraph.role: Pure consumer; the only tool that shows the TF tree and the robot model in one frame, which catches a wrong joint sign in seconds.
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Not lifecycle-managed. It reads /robot_description with TRANSIENT_LOCAL, so starting it before robot_state_publisher leaves RobotModel empty with only small red text as the complaint.

nodeGraph.role: Owns the camera device and publishes frames plus intrinsics; for imitation learning this stream IS the observation, so its timestamps are load-bearing.
nodeGraph.publishes: /camera1/image_raw (sensor_msgs/msg/Image), /camera1/image_raw/compressed, /camera1/camera_info; RealSense adds depth, extrinsics and its own /tf_static optical frames
nodeGraph.lifecycle: realsense2_camera_node is lifecycle-capable; usb_cam is not. Image topics use BEST_EFFORT (SensorDataQoS), so a RELIABLE subscriber silently never connects.

nodeGraph.role: Publishes the measured hand-eye transform once, so recalibrating is a launch-argument change rather than a code change.
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Not lifecycle-managed. Once you stop recalibrating, promote it into the URDF as a fixed joint so robot_state_publisher owns it instead.

nodeGraph.role: A transient rclpy node that drives the arm to named configurations from YAML and exits — the canonical shape of an application node.
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Not lifecycle-managed; exits on completion so launch can sequence on it. Uses the ACTION, not the topic, because it needs result, feedback and preemption.

nodeGraph.role: Your node: reads state, runs inference, decodes the chunk, publishes a trajectory, replans on a timer.
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Not lifecycle-managed, and does not need to be. In this repo it occupies the leader arm's slot: omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py:144 remaps /arm_controller/joint_trajectory to /leader/joint_trajectory, so teleop and policy paths are interchangeable by construction.

nodeGraph.role: A second complete ros2_control_node plus RSP and three controllers, pushed into /leader, that lets a human backdrive an arm to generate demonstrations.
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Its controllers (gravity_compensation_controller on the effort interface, trigger_position_controller, joint_trajectory_command_broadcaster) are lifecycle-managed by its own /leader/controller_manager. The `/**:` wildcard at the top of every controller YAML is load-bearing — without it, parameters keyed on plain `controller_manager:` match nothing once namespaced.

nodeGraph.role: Wraps each link in an FCL capsule, runs FK on incoming joint states, and publishes a boolean veto the broadcaster checks before publishing.
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Not lifecycle-managed. It checks the LEADER's states so the bad command is never sent, not stopped mid-motion. It models nothing outside the URDF — no table, no fixture, no human — and is an interlock, not a safety system.

nodeGraph.role: Qt sliders that FAKE /joint_states so you can inspect a URDF with no robot present.
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Not lifecycle-managed, and mutually exclusive with live hardware — two publishers on /joint_states makes robot_state_publisher interleave them and the TF tree jitter between two poses.

nodeGraph.role: Subscribes whatever you name and writes MCAP with per-message receive timestamps; for imitation learning the bag is both flight recorder and dataset.
nodeGraph.lifecycle: Not lifecycle-managed. It records what it RECEIVES, so a best-effort image topic under load drops frames silently; and it replays TRANSIENT_LOCAL topics as VOLATILE unless you pass --qos-profile-overrides-path.

stages.title: Pin the substrate
stages.what: Write down which Ubuntu, which ROS distro, which JetPack/L4T, then choose a base image from those three answers rather than from a tutorial. Put every external repo in a .repos file pinned to a SHA, not a branch.
stages.proves: That every later failure is a change you made rather than a change apt made. Without it, bisection is contaminated forever and 'reproduce the March bug' is impossible in September.
stages.tools: lsb_release -a; echo $ROS_DISTRO; cat /etc/nv_tegra_release; FROM ros:jazzy-ros-base; vcs import src < robot.repos; vcs export --exact src > frozen.repos
stages.skippable: No. It costs an hour. ROS distro to Ubuntu is a hard 1:1 binding (Jazzy=Noble/py3.12, Humble=Jammy/py3.10) and a Jetson container built against the wrong L4T dies even when arch and Ubuntu both match.

stages.title: Host device and transport plumbing
stages.what: udev SYMLINK rule keyed on USB serial number plus ATTR{device/latency_timer}="1"; compose grants (devices, cap_add SYS_NICE, rtprio, network_mode host, ipc host, /dev/shm); RMW_IMPLEMENTATION and ROS_DOMAIN_ID identical in every shell; start rmw_zenohd.
stages.proves: That the device path and the transport are constants, so a discovery failure can no longer be mistaken for a logic failure. Fixes the default 16 ms FTDI latency_timer that alone caps you near 60 Hz, and the Docker bridge that does not forward DDS multicast.
stages.tools: udevadm control --reload; ss -ltnp | grep 7447; ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd; ros2 doctor --report
stages.skippable: No. This repo's own rule is broken — `KERNEL=="ttyACM*", DRIVERS=="ftdi_sio"` can never match, since ttyACM is cdc_acm — and four files disagree on the port (launch defaults ttyACM0/ttyACM2, xacro default ttyACM1). Fix both here or reboot roulette continues.

stages.title: Physical stop and bus-ownership rules
stages.what: Install a latching mushroom e-stop in series with the servo DC feed (not the USB line). Write down the single-owner rule for /dev/ttyACM0 and add a pre-flight command to it. Define the park/fold pose that is the only pose in which torque may be cycled.
stages.proves: That you can stop the arm when software is wedged, and that the class of bug where two processes interleave bytes on a half-duplex bus is now a procedure violation rather than a mystery. ISO 13850 permits only power removal as an e-stop; everything you can write in ROS is a stop request.
stages.tools: ~$15 NC mushroom switch; sudo fuser -v /dev/ttyACM0; lsof /dev/ttyACM0; docker ps
stages.skippable: No, and it must precede any energised motion. Note the honest trade: the arm has no brakes, so cutting power to an extended arm drops 335 g — which is why the park pose rule exists alongside it.

stages.title: Read the servos, then make one limits source authoritative
stages.what: With the ROS stack stopped, run a read-only probe over IDs 11-16 dumping Operating Mode, Drive Mode, Min/Max Position Limit, PID gains, Profile Velocity/Acceleration, Shutdown, Temperature Limit. Then generate the URDF <limit> tags and your Python limits from that one table.
stages.proves: The ID-to-joint mapping (positional in the xacro, stated nowhere in prose), the tick-to-radian conversion, and which of the disagreeing limit sources actually stops the motor. Nothing moves, so it is free.
stages.skippable: No. The URDF here rates every joint ±2π, effort 1000 Nm — placeholders against ~1.5 Nm real stall torque — while the servo registers clamp joint2 to ticks 830..3129. Three sources disagreeing is a structural defect, not a puzzle to solve once.

stages.title: Robot description plus the four-step validation ladder
stages.what: Write the URDF as xacro macros with prefix/port/sim/mock as arguments, then validate in ascending cost: xacro expands, check_urdf passes, urdf_to_graphiz matches the physical chain, and RSP + joint_state_publisher_gui + RViz shows correct axes and senses.
stages.proves: Syntax, then topology, then geometry, then sign — each a strictly stronger claim than the last, and each caught in seconds instead of as 'IK never converges' three weeks later. No hardware is touched.
stages.tools: xacro file.urdf.xacro port_name:=/dev/omx_follower > /tmp/r.urdf; check_urdf /tmp/r.urdf; ros2 launch open_manipulator_description omx_f.launch.py
stages.skippable: No. The URDF is the single input to four unrelated consumers (ros2_control, RSP, MoveIt, RViz), so one mistake in it produces four unrelated-looking errors.

stages.title: Collision geometry and the SRDF allowed-collision matrix
stages.what: Replace collision meshes with boxes/cylinders/capsules, then write the SRDF: planning groups, named poses, end effector, and the disable_collisions list for adjacent pairs.
stages.proves: That a planner can evaluate a state in microseconds and that links touching at their shared joint does not read as a collision. Without the ACM every configuration reports collision and the planner returns 'start state in collision' forever.
stages.skippable: Yes if you never run a planner — the imitation-learning path does not. Cost: you then have no geometric collision check anywhere in the runtime path, and a z-floor check in your own gate is carrying the whole load.

stages.title: Kinematics off-robot, with tests
stages.what: Choose analytic or numerical IK, write down the explicit 6-DOF-to-5-DOF projection policy, and test three ways: FK->IK->FK round trip compared in POSE space, workspace sampling for success rate and solve time, and branch continuity along a dense Cartesian path.
stages.proves: The maths is right independently of ROS, hardware, timing and transport — so when the arm later goes to the wrong place you have exactly one candidate explanation left.
stages.tools: pytest; KDL / TRAC-IK / pick_ik as the numerical alternatives; `position_only_ik: True` is MoveIt's blunt version of the projection
stages.skippable: The tests, no. The analytic derivation, yes — if you train a policy on absolute joint positions there is no FK, no IK, no frames and no branch flips at runtime, and the whole class of bug disappears.

stages.title: The whole node graph on mock hardware
stages.what: Flip one xacro argument so the plugin becomes mock_components/GenericSystem, which mirrors commands straight back to states, and run the complete launch file including your own nodes.
stages.proves: Controller activation, that YAML joint names match URDF joint names (the number-one 'controller failed to activate' cause), that your JointTrajectory is accepted and not rejected for a velocity or timestamp violation, that remaps are right, and that the TF tree closes. Roughly 70% of integration bugs, at zero risk.
stages.tools: ros2 launch open_manipulator_bringup omx_f.launch.py use_mock_hardware:=true start_rviz:=true
stages.skippable: No, and it is the single most commonly skipped stage. Mock hardware cannot fight over a port and cannot swing into a table, so every failure here is unambiguously software.

stages.title: Physics simulation
stages.what: Run the same controllers against gz_ros2_control (Gazebo Harmonic pairs with Jazzy) or MuJoCo, with use_sim_time:=true on every node.
stages.proves: Contact, gravity droop, and that planned paths do not sweep through the table.
stages.skippable: Yes for an imitation-learning capstone — your data comes from the physical arm, so sim's role shrinks to collision sanity checking. It cannot reproduce serial bus timing, servo PID response, stiction, backlash, thermal derating or camera exposure anyway, and with effort=1000 in the URDF it is simulating a robot that does not exist.

stages.title: First hardware session as a ladder
stages.what: Enumerate the device; read-only scan every ID; torque OFF and backdrive by hand watching positions change; write something harmless; torque ON one joint and command +2 degrees with a finger on the switch; then all joints, small amplitude.
stages.proves: Each rung one thing: the bus works, then the ID map and tick conversion simultaneously and for free, then the write path, then one closed loop, then six coexisting on one half-duplex line.
stages.skippable: You can compress it, but not reorder it. The principle is the discipline in one line: read before write, harmless write before motion, one joint before six, small before large.

stages.title: Hand the bus to ros2_control and verify bottom-up, then hold
stages.what: Swap in the real plugin with disable_torque_at_init true and the <gpio> register blocks. Then check in strict order: hardware component active, controllers active, /joint_states at ~100 Hz, tf2_echo changes when you backdrive. Finally command exactly the pose the arm is already in.
stages.proves: That one process owns the port and servo configuration is idempotent rather than remembered. The hold test then proves joint ordering, units, frames, remapping and the whole controller chain end-to-end — and the correct outcome is visibly 'nothing happens', at zero velocity.
stages.tools: ros2 control list_hardware_components; ros2 control list_controllers; ros2 topic hz /joint_states; ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo link0 end_effector_link
stages.skippable: No. If the arm twitches on the hold test, your joint ordering or frame convention is wrong and you have learned it at 0 rad/s instead of at full reach.

stages.title: Home through the action, then enable the limiters
stages.what: Run the homing node so a FollowJointTrajectory goal drives the arm to a known pose and reports arrival. Then fill real numbers into the URDF <limit> tags, add <safety_controller> soft limits, enable enforce_command_limits, add JTC constraints/goal_time/cmd_timeout, and set Bus Watchdog (addr 98) to ~100 ms.
stages.proves: That the command path reports completion (not just acceptance), and that a bad command is now clamped by the framework and a dead host is now caught by firmware. Homing comes first because gravity compensation and every learned policy assume a known starting configuration.
stages.tools: init_position:=true; ros2 control list_controllers; test the watchdog by physically pulling USB while the arm creeps in a safe pose
stages.skippable: The limiters are technically skippable and this is where most student projects stop. Cost: a position-mode DYNAMIXEL holds its last goal forever when your process dies, and JTC reports success while the arm sits stalled against an obstacle.

stages.title: Calibrate, in the forced order
stages.what: Joint zeros, then gravity/friction identification, then camera intrinsics, then hand-eye extrinsics.
stages.proves: The order is not preference. A constant joint offset propagates as a configuration-dependent tip error that never looks like an offset. And hand-eye solves AX=XB where the B terms are computed from the intrinsics, so bad intrinsics produce a confidently converged and completely wrong transform.
stages.tools: ros2 run camera_calibration cameracalibrator; easy_handeye2; gravity_compensation_controller torque_scaling_factors / kinetic_friction_scalars
stages.skippable: Gravity/friction only if you never teleoperate. Hand-eye only if your policy is image-to-joint with no Cartesian frame anywhere. Expect 1-3 mm with a rigid mount; a flexing 3D-printed bracket puts a floor under your accuracy that no amount of sampling removes.

stages.title: Teleoperate, measure time sync, then record
stages.what: Stand up leader-follower with the leader gravity-compensated, have a human do the task dozens of times, and BEFORE recording anything measure the camera-to-joint timestamp offset rather than assuming it is zero.
stages.proves: That the task is physically possible with this gripper and workspace; that the real-time path holds at task speed with a human able to stop it; and that the dataset does not contain a systematic lie. Teleop also DEFINES the action space — whatever the leader publishes is what the policy will be trained to emit.
stages.tools: ros2 launch open_manipulator_bringup omx_ai.launch.py; ros2 bag record -o ep_0001 /joint_states /leader/joint_trajectory /camera1/image_raw/compressed; ros2 bag info to check count == duration x rate
stages.skippable: No. A 50 ms constant camera offset on a 40 ms control step is more than one full action step of unrecoverable error baked into every episode, invisible in the data, and it manifests later as 'the model needs more data'.

stages.title: Policy node behind a safety gate, dummy model first
stages.what: Build the receding-horizon executor against a dummy policy with the real output signature, wrapped in a gate that checks per-step VELOCITY (not per-step angle), IK feasibility, workspace floor, NaN/inf, and /joint_states staleness. Reject and hold; never clamp.
stages.proves: That the deployment path is correct independently of model quality, so when the trained policy underperforms you know it is the policy. A planner that fails returns 'no solution'; a policy that fails returns a confident, well-formed, physically insane float vector with no in-band signal.
stages.tools: chunk_executor_node.py --dry-run and --hold; publish further ahead than you execute so JTC's mandatory zero-velocity tail stays beyond the replan point
stages.skippable: The dummy-policy step feels skippable and is not — it is the only way to separate a pipeline bug from a model bug. Clamping instead of rejecting is worse than no gate: a clamped action is a new action the policy never chose, executed in a state it has never seen.

stages.title: CI, cold-container reproduction, and a frozen snapshot
stages.what: Build from scratch on every push with rosdep check as a hard gate. Then `docker compose down && docker compose up -d` and repeat stages 2 through 12. Stamp every run with git SHAs, image digest, .repos export, and a servo control-table dump.
stages.proves: That no undocumented manual step exists. CI catches the undeclared dependency the day it appears rather than the day a new teammate clones; the cold restart catches the thing someone typed once into a shell.
stages.tools: rm -rf build install log && rosdep install --from-paths src --ignore-src -r -y && colcon build; rosdep check ... || exit 1; vcs export --exact src > frozen-$(date +%F).repos
stages.skippable: CI can be deferred on a capstone; the cold-container reproduction and the run stamp cannot, because RAM registers reset on power cycle and the servo's actual configuration is recoverable only if you dumped it.

isolationPractice: Pin the ROS distro in the FROM line, because distro-to-Ubuntu is a hard 1:1 binding (Jazzy=Noble+py3.12, Humble=Jammy+py3.10) and every ros-<distro>-* .deb is compiled against that release's libstdc++/Python/Boost. Prevents: the teammate on 22.04 who cannot apt-install a single package your robot uses.

On a Jetson, derive from an L4T base matching the flashed revision and run with the NVIDIA container runtime. Prevents: an image where the Ubuntu release and aarch64 arch both match and the CUDA userspace still does not, because JetPack version-locks kernel, driver, CUDA, cuDNN and TensorRT together at flash time. Record the JetPack version in the README the day you flash.

Pin every external source to a SHA in a .repos file, not a branch. Prevents: two teammates building identical Dockerfiles a week apart and getting different source trees. This repo pins realsense-ros to cbd8b848 and leaves five ROBOTIS repos on `git clone -b jazzy` — the asymmetry is the lesson.

Declare dependencies as <depend> tags and let rosdep derive the apt lines, then gate CI on `rosdep check ... || exit 1`. Prevents: the build that works on your machine forever and fails on the next clone, because you apt-installed until it compiled and never added the tag.

Source the underlay then the overlay, never the reverse. Sourcing prepends to AMENT_PREFIX_PATH so the last one wins — that is the entire mechanism that lets your workspace shadow a distro package with no uninstall step. Prevents: patching files under /opt/ros that the next apt upgrade silently reverts, and ABI crashes that look like memory corruption.

Treat --symlink-install as 'edits to existing files take effect', not 'no rebuild ever'. setup.py data_files globs are evaluated at build time, so ADDING a launch file or yaml does nothing until you rebuild. Prevents: hours spent believing a negative result about a file the install tree has never seen.

Keep build/, install/ and log/ out of git and never edit install/. With symlink-install half of it is symlinks into src/ and half is copies, and you cannot tell which by looking. `rm -rf build install log && colcon build` must always be a free, safe action.

Drop empty COLCON_IGNORE / AMENT_IGNORE markers in any directory inside src/ that is not a package. This repo does it for docker/. Prevents: colcon trying to build your dataset directory or vendored notebooks when the whole repo is bind-mounted into the workspace.

Put torch/lerobot/diffusers in a SEPARATE container from ROS, talking over topics with ipc: host and network_mode: host. Prevents: a pip install of numpy silently replacing the module rclpy was built against — Ubuntu 24.04 ships EXTERNALLY-MANAGED for exactly this reason, and this image disables it globally with break-system-packages plus --ignore-installed, which also suppresses the conflict warning.

Use network_mode: host and ipc: host, and know what each buys. Bridge networks do not forward the UDP multicast that classic DDS discovery needs, so `ros2 topic list` comes back empty with no error; and without a shared IPC namespace DDS silently falls back from shared memory to loopback UDP, which for 1280x720 at 30 Hz is real CPU and latency. Cost: ROS_DOMAIN_ID becomes machine-wide and LAN-visible (hardcoded 30 here), so a teammate's sim nodes can join your robot's graph.

Grant cap_add SYS_NICE plus rtprio/memlock ulimits if you want a real-time control thread. Without them controller_manager's SCHED_FIFO request fails SILENTLY and you get a 'realtime' loop at normal priority. Note this container grants them and nothing claims them — the s6 run script just execs ros2 launch with no chrt.

Prefer narrow `devices:` plus device_cgroup_rules over privileged + /dev:/dev. privileged always works, which is the problem: your compose file stops documenting your hardware dependency, nothing fails loudly when the arm is unplugged, and a bug in your node can write to /dev/sda.

Run as a UID-matched non-root user. This image is all root with your checkout bind-mounted at /root/ros2_ws/src, so on a Linux host every build artifact and log lands root-owned and your editor cannot save. Podman's rootless userns makes this disappear without the UID dance.

Use s6-overlay (or any real init) as PID 1 with down-signal SIGINT and a recorded PGID. Container PID 1 does not reap zombies or forward signals to a process group, so a bare `CMD ros2 launch` means docker stop kills the wrapper and leaves the ros2_control node holding your serial port as an orphan. But turn OFF `restart: always` for an arm — it re-energises a crashed robot with nobody present.

Tag images by digest, not by a moving tag. Compose reuses an existing local image with that tag and only builds when none exists, so a stale local robotis/open-manipulator:5.1.1 is used forever even after you change the Dockerfile. `docker compose build --no-cache` when you actually mean it.

Put local deviations in docker-compose.override.yml, not in the vendor's file. Trap already half-hit here: an explicit `-f docker-compose.yml` SUPPRESSES automatic override merging, so ./container.sh start does not apply your LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE fix while a bare `docker compose up -d` from docker/ does.

WHAT CONTAINERS DO NOT ISOLATE — devices. /dev/ttyACM0 inside and outside are the same character device, the same driver instance, the same single half-duplex bus. There is no serial namespace in Linux, and opening a tty twice is not an error: DynamixelSDK opens with O_RDWR|O_NOCTTY|O_NONBLOCK and does not set TIOCEXCL, so two writers both succeed and their bytes interleave. The symptom is never 'port busy' — it is intermittent CRC errors and phantom timeouts that vanish when you add a print.

WHAT CONTAINERS DO NOT ISOLATE — udev, the kernel, the GPU driver ABI, or the network when you use host mode. .rules files COPYed into the image sit at /etc/udev/rules.d and do nothing, because there is no udevd in the container; they must be installed on the HOST. Likewise the RViz-window-that-never-paints in this repo is Mesa half-loading a hardware driver whose vendor .so is outside the container — a GL path problem, not a ROS problem, fixed with LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1.
learnedPolicyDelta: The planner is gone. move_group does not appear in omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py at all — the policy IS the planner, and there is consequently no collision checking anywhere in the runtime path. Whatever MoveIt was giving you for free (reachability, self-collision, obstacle avoidance) you now owe yourself.

The intelligence moves offline. Training is a batch job on a workstation with no connection to the robot, so the feedback loop from 'the arm did something dumb' to 'the arm stops doing that' is hours long, not seconds. That latency in the engineering loop is the defining project-management fact of imitation learning.

A policy cannot report infeasibility. A planner returns 'no solution'; a policy returns a confident, well-formed float vector — an EE pose 40 cm inside the table, a 170-degree wrist flip in one 40 ms step — with no in-band signal that anything went wrong. Every sanity check ros2_control and MoveIt gave you must be rebuilt as an explicit gate.

A new architectural component appears: the rate-bridging chunk executor. Inference runs at 5-15 Hz, ros2_control at 100 Hz, and something must keep a valid trajectory in the queue at all times while discarding the tail that the next inference will supersede. It is a real control component with a hard deadline, and it is where essentially every imitation-learning bug lives.

The action/topic choice inverts. Homing uses the FollowJointTrajectory ACTION because it needs result, feedback and preemption. The policy uses the TOPIC, because each message must replace the active trajectory with no handshake and you have no use for a result callback you will cancel in 200 ms.

Two ROS 2 details become load-bearing: JointTrajectoryController falls back to LINEAR interpolation when points carry no velocity (a velocity step at every waypoint), and it REJECTS the entire message if the final point has non-zero velocity. The standard answer is to publish further ahead than you execute, so the mandatory zero-velocity tail always sits beyond the replan point and the arm lives in the smooth middle of the spline.

The action representation is chosen once and is expensive to reverse, because it invalidates the dataset. Absolute joint positions (ALOHA / LeRobot / ROBOTIS) need no kinematics at runtime and cannot transfer to another arm; relative SE(3) EE deltas (UMI) are hardware-agnostic and inherit every IK branch flip as a potential discontinuity. Rotation is parameterised as continuous 6D and Gram-Schmidted back to SO(3), because quaternions double-cover and Euler wraps.

Time synchronisation becomes a first-class subsystem rather than a detail. Camera, joint bus and policy timer are three free-running clocks; a constant 50 ms camera lag teaches the policy to act early, which is a domain shift in the time axis that looks exactly like 'needs more data'. UMI measures four separate latencies with four different methods and schedules each action to an absolute wall-clock time minus that actuator's latency.

The dataset replaces the specification. There is no correctness proof and no unit test — the only spec is a success rate over N trials with a fixed reset protocol. A 50% policy produces a clean run of three successes about one time in eight, so anecdote is worthless and an evaluation harness is infrastructure, not polish.

The gripper stops being a separate device. The AI config folds gripper_joint_1 into arm_controller's joint list while the standard config gives it its own GripperActionController — because a policy emits one 6-vector per timestep and splitting it would force you to resynchronise two independently-timed command streams.

Configuration lives in metadata, not in flags. fps, normalization statistics and the feature schema must travel with the checkpoint (meta/info.json, meta/stats.json); if train and deploy normalize differently the policy outputs garbage and nothing in the stack will tell you.

Much of this community drops ROS entirely. UMI, Diffusion Policy and core LeRobot use Python multiprocessing with hand-written lock-free shared-memory ring buffers, precisely to own every timestamp with no serialization hop. What they give up — TF, RViz, rosbag, MoveIt, ros2_control's limit enforcement and controller lifecycle — is reimplemented badly or not at all.
beginnerTraps: Skipping mock hardware and going URDF straight to metal. You then debug controller activation, joint-name mismatches, remaps, QoS, TF and your own logic simultaneously with servo limits, bus timing and gravity. Habit: `use_mock_hardware:=true` is the second thing you run, and metal waits until the full graph is green against it.

Believing the URDF about limits. Six identical `lower=-2pi upper=2pi velocity=4.8 effort=1000` entries is the signature of a placeholder nobody filled in; the servo's Min/Max Position Limit registers are the only ones that physically stop the arm. Habit: read the register, then make the URDF agree with it, and generate the other sources from that one table.

Reading a register without checking the mode that gives it meaning. Drive Mode 4 (verified on all six servos) sets bit 2 = TIME-based profile, so Profile Velocity 50 means 50 MILLISECONDS of total duration, not 50 rpm. Habit: dump Operating Mode and Drive Mode first — the units of everything else depend on them.

Enabling torque before reading positions. The arm snaps from wherever gravity left it to whatever stale Goal Position is in RAM. Habit: configure it rather than remember it — disable_torque_at_init: true, read, verify, then activate. And never torque-cycle an extended arm; there are no brakes.

Letting a second process open /dev/ttyACM0 'just to check something'. Half-duplex means two writers do not interleave cleanly, they corrupt each other's status packets, and the symptom is intermittence that correlates with nothing in your code and changes when you add a print. Habit: `sudo fuser -v /dev/ttyACM0` and `docker ps` are the FIRST two commands, before you read any of your own code — and remember s6 may have already started bringup inside the container.

Fixing a reset servo register with a standalone SDK script. That script is the second owner of the bus. Habit: put the value in the <gpio> block so the plugin re-pushes it at every on_activate, and get diagnostics through the plugin's get_dxl_data service. RAM registers reset by design; only EEPROM persists.

Treating an empty `ros2 node list` as a code bug. It means DISCOVERY is broken, which is a much shorter debugging path. Habit: check the middleware before the application — is rmw_zenohd up (ss -ltnp | grep 7447), is RMW_IMPLEMENTATION the same in both shells, is ROS_DOMAIN_ID the same.

Concluding a subscriber should work because `ros2 topic echo` shows data. The CLI subscribes permissively; your node may not, and QoS incompatibility is SILENT by design. The rule is that the offer must dominate: BEST_EFFORT publisher + RELIABLE subscriber never connect, VOLATILE publisher + TRANSIENT_LOCAL subscriber never connect. Habit: `ros2 topic info <topic> --verbose` is the first hypothesis, not the last.

Treating 'no transform from link0 to end_effector_link' as a TF bug. It almost never is. Habit: check in order — is /joint_states publishing, does it contain EVERY joint in the chain, is there a frame_prefix you forgot, did your subscriber join after /tf_static was published with VOLATILE durability, is your lookup timestamp inside the 10 s buffer. `ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames` settles it in seconds.

Calling a service synchronously from inside a callback on the default single-threaded executor. The response can never be processed because the only thread is blocked waiting for it, and it hangs forever with no error. Same family: doing 40 ms of image preprocessing on the same executor as a 100 Hz timer, which silently runs at whatever rate is left over. Habit: measure your loop's actual period rather than trusting the rate you asked for.

Raising the control rate to fix jerkiness. On this arm 100 Hz commands already pass through a ~50 ms servo profile, so you are oversampling a filter. Habit: work out which layer is the bandwidth limit before changing a rate — here it is the servo's profile generator, and the knob is Profile Velocity.

Sending positions with no velocities and blaming the hardware. JTC silently drops to linear interpolation, putting a velocity discontinuity at every waypoint that the position PID turns into a torque step — it looks exactly like mechanical slop. Habit: always populate velocities (central differences), and remember the final point must be zero.

Publishing single-point trajectories every 10 ms to 'match' the 100 Hz loop. You are fighting the interpolator and producing the jerk you were trying to avoid. Habit: send segments with real durations in time_from_start and let JTC do its job.

Gating a policy on per-step ANGLE instead of velocity. The same 6 degrees is gentle at time_scale 8 and violent at 0.5, because the step's duration is DT x time_scale. Habit: gate on |dq|/dt against a real rad/s number — a generous 180 deg/s still catches IK branch flips, which jump far further than any legitimate motion.

Clamping an unsafe action instead of rejecting it. A clamped action is a different action the policy never chose, executed in a state it has never seen — the definition of distribution shift. Habit: reject the whole segment, hold position, and log which step and which number failed.

Assuming the state you read is current. With is_async="true" the /joint_states you receive is at least one 10 ms cycle old plus transport plus the USB round trip that produced it — realistically 15-30 ms. At 1 rad/s that is already 1.1 degrees of anchor error before the network has done anything. Habit: account for observation age in any feedback computation, and stop publishing if the last JointState is older than ~100 ms.

Believing the launch log, or the spawner's exit code. The spawner exits on failure too, so OnProcessExit fires either way and RViz will start happily over a dead arm. Habit: `ros2 control list_controllers` (expect active), `ros2 control list_hardware_interfaces` (see the claims), then the JTC log — three commands that discriminate 'torque off', 'unclaimed' and 'trajectory rejected' in fifteen seconds.

Debugging by reading code and reasoning about what the graph should be doing. Habit: rqt_graph, ros2 topic hz, ros2 control list_controllers, tf2_echo, then PlotJuggler for commanded-vs-measured overlays — cheapest first, and stop guessing the moment a reading surprises you. Most multi-day sessions are a team arguing while a five-second rqt_graph would have shown an unconnected edge.

Changing two things at once, and believing the first successful run. Habit: one variable per run, written down, with the bag filename beside it; and no claim about a policy without at least 20 trials against a fixed reset protocol.
honestNotes: The researchers disagree on where hardware enters the sequence. One argues for a vendor-bringup smoke test as step 3 — get ONE container talking to the arm before you write anything, so it becomes the bisection point for everything after. The others put full description validation, kinematics tests and mock hardware first. Both are defensible; the synthesis above splits the difference by making the early hardware contact read-only (stage 4) and deferring motion until after mock.

Whether ros2_control is the right substrate at all is genuinely contested, and one researcher is blunt about it: the honest reason to keep it on this arm is MoveIt, RViz and the vendor's teleop rig for data collection — NOT determinism. A Python loop calling GroupSyncRead/GroupSyncWrite has comparable worst-case jitter to an async ros2_control USB component, and most imitation-learning codebases (LeRobot, UMI, ALOHA derivatives) do exactly that. What you actually give up, in order of pain: MoveIt, the topic-based observation path (RViz and rosbag go dark), JTC's spline, the register-push-at-init, and the port-exclusivity mechanism.

One researcher recommends absolute joint positions as the action representation for a capstone, 'unless the whole point of the project is UMI-style cross-embodiment' — which would make the team's hand-written analytic 5-DOF kinematics educational but optional. Another treats the Cartesian/relative representation as the defining feature of UMI. This is a real fork and it is the most expensive decision to reverse, because it invalidates the dataset.

Chunk execution has two competing answers to the same jerk-at-chunk-boundary problem, and the choice is coupled to model size. Receding horizon (UMI, Diffusion Policy; Ta=8 found optimal) replans every E<H steps. ACT's temporal ensembling instead queries at EVERY control step and exponentially averages overlapping predictions — which only works because ACT is 52M parameters and ~5 ms per call. LeRobot enforces the coupling by raising NotImplementedError if you set temporal_ensemble_coeff with n_action_steps > 1.

The container is provisioned for real-time and does not claim it: docker-compose.yml grants cap_add SYS_NICE, rtprio 99, rttime -1 and ~8 GB memlock, then docker/s6-services/common/ros2_service_run.sh simply execs `bash -i -c "ros2 launch ..."` with no chrt and no mlockall. One researcher calls this defensible at 100 Hz over async USB (there is no point pinning a thread whose latency is dominated by USB frame scheduling); the point of disagreement is whether to say so out loud rather than assume the ulimits are a guarantee.

The bus arithmetic (1.78 ms/cycle, 562 Hz ceiling, 17.8% utilisation at 100 Hz) is one researcher's calculation from the Protocol 2.0 packet format and is explicitly flagged as unverified. So is the ~1 kHz servo firmware rate, which ROBOTIS does not publish. Treat both as working assumptions, and note the practical ceiling is USB anyway (2-4 ms round trips, 200-300 Hz), not the wire.

Whether to build a real collision layer is a live cost/architecture trade. Adopting MoveIt's PlanningScene with the table modelled is roughly a week and changes your architecture — MoveIt plans, it does not stream. Extending the existing FCL capsule node with a table half-space and re-pointing it at /joint_states is roughly a day and keeps the streaming design. A third researcher argues a z-floor check in the application gate buys most of the practical benefit for a tabletop pick.

Time synchronisation is where the ROBOTIS hybrid visibly pays its price. physical_ai_server's Communicator does NOT use message_filters.ApproximateTimeSynchronizer — each topic callback overwrites a dict entry and get_latest_data returns whatever is newest. One researcher calls this 'a pragmatic choice, not a correct one' and names it the first thing to instrument if a trained policy underperforms its own teleop. UMI treats alignment as the core of the system. Nobody claims the vendor is wrong, only that the gap is real and undocumented.

Devcontainer adoption is genuinely split and nobody should pretend otherwise: heavy in university labs and VS Code monocultures, largely absent in mixed-editor teams and on headless SSH-only robots. The pragmatic middle — a .devcontainer pointing at the EXISTING docker-compose.yml via dockerComposeFile and service — is a recommendation, not a standard. Same for Docker vs Podman vs Apptainer: Podman's rootless userns solves the root-owned-files problem for free, but the compose semantics differ enough that you pick one and do not mix.

Whether to bake the colcon build into the image is a real split. Baking it means the robot boots ready (correct for deployment); mounting src/ and building on first run means the image does not need rebuilding per source change (correct for development). Mature teams do both with two Dockerfile targets. This repo only bakes, which makes iteration miserable if you do not know about the bind mount shadowing the baked clone.

The e-stop recommendation carries an acknowledged cost that nobody resolves: cutting DC power to a brakeless 560 g arm means it falls, and 335 g of it is above joint2. All the researchers still say install it, and pair it with a rule that the arm is never extended over anything you care about. The same asymmetry applies to the servo's own overload/overheat shutdown — it protects the motor, and from the arm's point of view it is an uncommanded torque-off under load at the worst possible moment.

Evidence was thin on two points. First, exact latency figures for this specific Jetson Orin + OpenRB-150 + rmw_zenoh combination: the 15-25 ms to first motion and 65-80 ms to settle are budgeted from component figures, not measured on this rig, and the researchers agree you must measure rather than estimate. Second, the mapping of DXL IDs 11-16 to joint1..joint5+gripper is inferred purely from the positional order of <gpio> blocks in the xacro and is stated nowhere in prose — verify it by backdriving with torque off before trusting it.

components.name: Pinned ROS base image (FROM ros:jazzy-ros-base)
components.role: The bottom of the stack. One line fixes Ubuntu 24.04 Noble, Python 3.12, the ROS 2 Jazzy apt archive, and the ABI that every ros-jazzy-* .deb was compiled against. Everything above it inherits that contract.
components.whyItExists: A ROS distro is not a library, it is a distribution: Jazzy exists only for Noble, Humble only for Jammy, Kilted/Rolling only for Noble/Questing. There is no supported way to run Jazzy on Jammy or Humble on Noble, because every ros-<distro>-* package is built against that release's libstdc++, Python, Boost, and OpenCV. The moment one person on the team has Ubuntu 22.04 on their laptop, they cannot apt-install a single package your robot uses. Docker is near-universal in ROS specifically because it turns 'which Ubuntu do you have' from a team negotiation into a one-line build argument.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/docker/Dockerfile line 4: `FROM ros:jazzy-ros-base AS open-manipulator`. Verified in repo. The ros: images are the OSRF/Docker-Official ones; osrf/ros:jazzy-desktop adds RViz/rqt and is the usual dev-laptop choice.
components.interface: Provides /opt/ros/jazzy (the UNDERLAY), $ROS_DISTRO, and the apt source deb http://packages.ros.org/ros2/ubuntu noble main.
components.rate: Rebuilt when you bump the distro or a security patch lands. Realistically: once per project, then once a year.

components.name: Multi-stage vendor layer (COPY --from=librealsense)
components.role: A second FROM pulls a prebuilt librealsense image and copies only the compiled artifacts (/opt/librealsense, pyrealsense2 dist-packages, two udev .rules files) into the final image. The build toolchain used to produce librealsense never enters the shipped image.
components.whyItExists: Camera SDKs (librealsense, Orbbec, ZED) take 20-40 minutes to compile and drag in a hundred -dev packages. Multi-stage builds exist so the shipped image contains the .so files but not gcc, cmake, and the kernel headers. It also decouples the cadence: RealSense firmware/SDK moves on its own schedule and you re-pin one FROM line instead of re-solving your whole dependency graph.
components.evidence: Dockerfile lines 1 and 33-37: `FROM robotis/ros:jazzy-ros-base-librealsense AS librealsense`, then `COPY --from=librealsense /opt/librealsense /usr/local/` and `COPY --from=librealsense /usr/src/librealsense/config/99-realsense-libusb.rules /etc/udev/rules.d/`. Verified.
components.interface: Filesystem only: shared objects under /usr/local, a Python module on PYTHONPATH, udev rules that are inert inside the container (see the udev component).

components.name: Jetson base image and the NVIDIA container runtime
components.role: On a Jetson Orin you do NOT use ros:jazzy-ros-base. You use an L4T-derived base (nvidia/cuda:*-l4t, dustynv/ros:humble-desktop-l4t-r36.4.0, or a jetson-containers build) and run with runtime: nvidia, so the container borrows CUDA/cuDNN/TensorRT/libnvbuf from the host via the NVIDIA Container Runtime's mount injection.
components.whyItExists: JetPack version-locks the kernel, the display driver, CUDA, cuDNN, TensorRT and the multimedia stack together as one ABI contract established at flash time. A container built against CUDA 12.6 will not run on an r35 host. This is the single most common reason a Jetson robotics team's 'it works on the laptop' image dies on the robot: the Ubuntu release matches, the aarch64 arch matches, and the CUDA userspace still does not. You must know your L4T revision (`cat /etc/nv_tegra_release`, or `dpkg -l nvidia-l4t-core`) before you choose a base image.
components.evidence: General knowledge plus dusty-nv/jetson-containers, which uses --runtime nvidia by default and ships an `autotag` helper precisely because picking the L4T-matching tag by hand is error-prone. NOT verified against this repo: the ROBOTIS Dockerfile targets generic amd64/arm64 via TARGETARCH (lines 6, 18-31) and does not use the NVIDIA runtime, so if your teammate is running this image on the Orin, you have CPU-only ROS in that container and any CUDA work must live in a separate, differently-based image.
components.rate: Re-pinned whenever anyone reflashes the Jetson. Record the JetPack version in the repo README the day you flash it.

components.name: apt layer with cache cleanup
components.role: Installs system dependencies and deletes the apt index in the same RUN so the index never becomes a layer.
components.whyItExists: Two mechanisms. (1) `rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` in a SEPARATE RUN does nothing for image size, because the previous layer already committed the 40MB index; it must be the same RUN. (2) Each RUN is cached on its command string, not on the state of the world, so an apt layer built in March still installs March's package versions until something above it changes. That is why 'rebuild the image' sometimes fixes nothing and sometimes silently changes 60 packages -- you need `docker build --no-cache` or a pinned digest to control which.
components.evidence: Dockerfile lines 12-15 and 40-51: `apt-get update && apt-get install -y ... && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`, installing libusb-1.0-0-dev, ros-${ROS_DISTRO}-rmw-zenoh-cpp, ros-${ROS_DISTRO}-usb-cam, python3-pip. Verified.

components.name: Source-cloning layer with pinned refs
components.role: Clones the five ROBOTIS repos plus realsense-ros into ${COLCON_WS}/src at image build time. Most are pinned to a branch; realsense-ros is pinned to an exact commit.
components.whyItExists: A branch name is not a version. `-b jazzy` means 'whatever jazzy pointed at the day this layer was built', so two teammates who built the image a week apart have different source trees with identical Dockerfiles. The realsense line shows the correct discipline: `git checkout cbd8b8487d4c0126bb590822db9469414496e62a` makes that one dependency byte-identical forever. The reason this matters is the six-months-later bug: you want to reproduce a failure from March, and you cannot, because `git clone -b jazzy` now gives you September's code. In serious teams every external source is pinned to a SHA, in a .repos file, in git.
components.evidence: Dockerfile lines 56-65. Five `git clone -b jazzy` (dynamixel_hardware_interface, dynamixel_interfaces, DynamixelSDK, open_manipulator, robotis_interfaces), one `git clone -b r/4.56.4` + explicit checkout for realsense-ros. Verified. Note the asymmetry is real and is a latent reproducibility hole in this image.
components.rate: Only on image rebuild. Which is exactly the problem: the ref resolves at build time, invisibly.

components.name: rosdep install layer
components.role: Reads every package.xml under src/, maps the abstract dependency keys to Ubuntu package names for this distro, and apt-installs them. `--skip-keys` excludes keys that resolve to nothing because they are being built from source in the same workspace.
components.whyItExists: package.xml declares dependencies in a platform-neutral vocabulary (`<depend>rclpy</depend>`, `<exec_depend>rviz2</exec_depend>`). rosdep's database maps those keys to ros-jazzy-rclpy on Noble, a different name on Fedora, a brew formula on macOS. This is the mechanism that lets one manifest serve every platform, and it is why you NEVER hand-write apt-get install lines for ROS packages: you add a <depend> tag and rosdep derives the apt line. When a new teammate cannot build, the first command is always `rosdep install --from-paths src --ignore-src -r -y`, not 'what did you apt install'.
components.evidence: Dockerfile lines 67-71: `rosdep install -i --from-path src --rosdistro $ROS_DISTRO --skip-keys="librealsense2 robotis_interfaces" -y`. Also enforced in CI: .github/workflows/ros-ci.yml runs `rosdep check` after install and exits 1 if any key is unresolvable. Verified. That rosdep-check-as-a-gate is the good habit to copy.
components.interface: Input: all package.xml files in the tree. Output: apt packages installed into the image.

components.name: colcon build layer (--symlink-install, Release)
components.role: Builds the whole workspace once at image build time, producing build/, install/, log/ inside the image so `docker compose up` starts a working robot with no compile step.
components.whyItExists: Baking the build means the robot boots ready. `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` is not cosmetic on a control loop: colcon's default for CMake packages is an empty build type, i.e. no -O2, and unoptimized ros2_control/KDL/Eigen code will miss deadlines on a Jetson. `--symlink-install` makes install/ point back at src/ for files that can be symlinked, so editing a Python node or a launch file on the host takes effect without rebuilding -- that is the fast edit loop.
components.evidence: Dockerfile lines 73-75. Verified. Note the interaction with the bind mount below.
components.rate: Image build: once. Inside the container during development: every time you touch C++ (seconds to minutes), never for symlinked Python.

components.name: The --symlink-install trap
components.role: symlink-install symlinks what it can, but setup.py data_files are resolved by `glob()` at build time and (for directories not adjacent to setup.py) are copied rather than symlinked in several colcon versions. So editing an existing launch file may take effect live while ADDING a new launch file or config does nothing until you rebuild.
components.whyItExists: This exists because Python packaging has no concept of an editable data file. The failure mode is maximally confusing: your edit works, your colleague's new file does not, same flag, same workspace. The rule that falls out is: after adding ANY file (new node, new launch, new yaml), run `colcon build --packages-select <pkg>` before you believe anything. And there is a worse variant where a data file in the source dir becomes a symlink to itself, corrupting your source tree -- colcon-core issues #300 and #407.
components.evidence: open_manipulator_bringup/setup.py uses `glob('launch/*.py')` and 14 separate `glob('config/<robot>/*')` entries, all under os.path.join('share', package_name, ...) -- exactly the pattern the colcon issues describe. Repo structure verified; the copy-vs-symlink behavior is from the colcon issue tracker, not something I executed here.

components.name: Underlay / overlay sourcing in ~/.bashrc
components.role: Two `source` lines stacked in order: /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash (underlay, the distro) then /root/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash (overlay, your workspace). Plus ROS_DOMAIN_ID=30 and RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp.
components.whyItExists: Sourcing prepends to AMENT_PREFIX_PATH, so the LAST sourced wins. That is the entire mechanism of the overlay: build your own fork of ros2_controllers in your workspace, source it after the distro, and your version shadows the installed one with no uninstall step. The failure this prevents is the one where you patch a vendor package by editing files under /opt/ros -- which works until the next apt upgrade silently reverts it and nobody can reproduce your fix. Corollary: sourcing in the wrong order, or sourcing an overlay built against a different underlay, produces ABI crashes that look like memory corruption. Never source install/setup.bash before the distro.
components.evidence: Dockerfile lines 77-85. Verified. Also re-done at runtime by the s6 service scripts (docker/s6-services/common/ros2_service_run.sh: `source /opt/ros/${ROS_DISTRO}/setup.bash` then `source ${COLCON_WS}/install/setup.bash`), because a supervised process gets no login shell.
components.interface: Environment variables: AMENT_PREFIX_PATH, CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, PYTHONPATH, ROS_DISTRO.

components.name: pip inside the ROS image (break-system-packages)
components.role: The Dockerfile globally disables PEP 668 protection (`pip config set global.break-system-packages true`) and then pip-installs cyclo_manager's requirements with --ignore-installed straight into the system interpreter.
components.whyItExists: Ubuntu 24.04 ships /usr/lib/python3.12/EXTERNALLY-MANAGED, which makes pip refuse system-wide installs, because apt and pip both manage /usr/lib/python3/dist-packages and neither knows about the other. ROS is the worst case for this: ros-jazzy-* debs install Python modules there, so a pip install of numpy or PyYAML can silently replace the version rclpy was built against and every node starts failing with an import or ABI error that no one can attribute. --ignore-installed makes it worse by suppressing the conflict warning. This is why the standing advice in ROS teams is: system Python deps come from rosdep, and anything pip-only either goes in a virtualenv with --system-site-packages, or gets a rosdep key, or lives in a SEPARATE container that talks over a topic. The imitation-learning stack (torch, lerobot, diffusers, transformers) is exactly the case where 'separate container' wins.
components.evidence: Dockerfile lines 94-95. Verified. The PEP 668 mechanism and rosdep's own documented workaround (PIP_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES) are from rosdep's docs, not from this repo.

components.name: s6-overlay as PID 1 and service supervisor
components.role: Replaces the container's entrypoint with /init, which runs an s6-rc supervision tree. Each ROS launch is an s6 'longrun' service with its own run/finish scripts, a logging companion service, and a down-signal.
components.whyItExists: A container's PID 1 does not reap zombies and does not forward signals to a process group. A bare `CMD ros2 launch ...` means docker stop sends SIGTERM to the launch wrapper, the wrapper dies, and the ros2_control node keeps the serial port open as an orphan -- your port is now held by a process with no parent. s6 fixes this: `down-signal: SIGINT` gives ros2 launch the signal it actually handles for clean shutdown, the run script records its PGID to /run/<service>.pgid so the finish script can kill the whole group, and services restart under supervision instead of taking the container down. This is the difference between a demo container and one that survives a power cycle on a robot.
components.evidence: Dockerfile lines 8-31 (s6 install, arch-switched on TARGETARCH), 98-118 (service install), 128 (`ENTRYPOINT ["/init"]`). docker/s6-services/open_manipulator_bringup/{type=longrun, down-signal=SIGINT, producer-for=open_manipulator_bringup-log}. docker/s6-services/common/ros2_service_run.sh writes PGID to /run/${SERVICE_NAME}.pgid. Verified.
components.rate: Supervision is continuous; services restart on exit.

components.name: network_mode: host and ipc: host
components.role: The container shares the host's network namespace and SysV/POSIX IPC namespace. No NAT, no bridge, no port publishing -- the container's sockets ARE the host's sockets.
components.whyItExists: Classic DDS discovery (Fast DDS, Cyclone) announces participants over UDP multicast on 239.255.0.1. Docker's default bridge does not forward multicast, so on a bridge two containers on the SAME HOST cannot see each other's nodes and `ros2 topic list` comes back empty with no error. `network_mode: host` is the blunt fix. `ipc: host` plus the /dev/shm mount is the OTHER half: DDS uses shared memory for same-host large messages (camera frames), and without a shared IPC namespace it silently falls back to loopback UDP, which for a 1280x720 RGB stream at 30 Hz is a measurable CPU and latency cost. The cost of host networking is real: ROS_DOMAIN_ID becomes a machine-wide global (this image hardcodes 30), so two teammates on the same LAN with the same domain ID see each other's nodes and can command each other's robot.
components.evidence: docker-compose.yml: `network_mode: host`, `ipc: host`, volumes include `/dev/shm:/dev/shm` (redundant given ipc: host but harmless). Dockerfile sets `export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=30`. Verified. Multicast/bridge behavior is general knowledge.
components.interface: All DDS/zenoh traffic, and the zenoh router's TCP port 7447.

components.name: rmw_zenoh and the router that must exist first
components.role: This image sets RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp and aliases `zenohd` to `ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd`. Unlike DDS, nodes here do not find each other by multicast; they connect to a router process which gossips peer information.
components.whyItExists: rmw_zenoh deliberately disables UDP multicast scouting by default, precisely because misconfigured networks, OSes and CONTAINERS break multicast discovery. So the ROBOTIS stack traded 'discovery mysteriously fails inside Docker' for 'discovery fails deterministically until you start one named process'. That is a better trade -- a hard, nameable prerequisite beats an intermittent one -- but it means the router is now a first-class piece of your bringup: it must start before nodes, exactly once per machine, and it is the thing to check when `ros2 node list` is empty. That is the thing nobody warned you about, and the reason is that it is a design decision inherited from the middleware, not from ROS.
components.evidence: Dockerfile lines 81, 84-85 (`alias zenohd=...`, `export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp`), apt installs ros-${ROS_DISTRO}-rmw-zenoh-cpp (line 47). container.sh prints a banner saying rmw_zenoh_cpp has been the default since v5.0.0. Verified in repo; the multicast-disabled-by-default rationale is from the ros2/rmw_zenoh design docs.

components.name: /dev:/dev plus privileged: true
components.role: Mounts the host's entire device tree into the container and disables the device cgroup, seccomp and AppArmor confinement. Every serial port, camera, GPU node and block device on the Jetson is visible and writable from inside.
components.whyItExists: It exists because it always works and nobody has to think. The principled alternative is `devices: [/dev/ttyACM0:/dev/ttyACM0]` plus `device_cgroup_rules: ['c 166:* rmw']` (166 is the cdc_acm major; 188 is usb-serial/FTDI), which grants exactly the class of device you need and, unlike a `devices:` entry, survives the device being unplugged and replugged while the container runs. The cost of privileged is not only security: it hides the fact that you have a hardware dependency at all, so nothing fails loudly when the arm is not plugged in, and it means a bug in your node can write to /dev/sda.
components.evidence: docker-compose.yml: `volumes: - /dev:/dev` and `privileged: true`. Verified. The device_cgroup_rules alternative is general Docker knowledge.

components.name: THE CONTAINER BOUNDARY DOES NOT COVER THE SERIAL BUS
components.role: This is the crucial limit. A container isolates the PID, mount, network (not here -- host), user and UTS namespaces. It does NOT isolate devices. /dev/ttyACM0 inside the container and /dev/ttyACM0 on the host are the same character device, the same kernel driver instance, the same single half-duplex RS-485 bus with six DYNAMIXELs on it.
components.whyItExists: Because there is no 'serial namespace' in Linux. And worse: opening a tty twice is NOT an error. DynamixelSDK's PortHandlerLinux opens with `open(port_name_, O_RDWR|O_NOCTTY|O_NONBLOCK)` and does not set TIOCEXCL, so two processes -- yours in the container, your teammate's on the host, or two containers, or an s6-supervised bringup you forgot was running -- both succeed, both write instruction packets, and the bytes interleave on the wire. The symptom is not 'port busy'. The symptom is intermittent CRC errors, phantom timeouts, a servo that responds to a status read with another servo's answer, and a bug that vanishes when you add a print statement. Exactly what bit this team. The fixes are all coordination, not code: (1) exactly ONE process owns the bus, always, and it is the ros2_control hardware interface -- everything else talks to it over topics/services; (2) `sudo fuser -v /dev/ttyACM0` or `lsof /dev/ttyACM0` before you start anything; (3) if you must, wrap with `flock /dev/ttyACM0 -c '...'` so the second opener at least fails loudly.
components.evidence: omx_f.ros2_control.xacro declares the DynamixelHardware plugin with `<param name="port_name">` and `baud_rate 1000000`, i.e. one hardware component owns the port. docker/workspace/dummy_exec/omx_probe.py opens /dev/ttyACM0 directly at 1000000 baud -- that script and a running bringup are mutually exclusive and nothing enforces it. Verified in repo. The absence of TIOCEXCL in DynamixelSDK's port_handler_linux setupPort is from the upstream source, not executed here.
components.rate: The DYNAMIXEL read/write cycle runs at the controller_manager update_rate, typically 100-500 Hz. Every one of those cycles is a chance to collide.

components.name: udev rules and stable device names
components.role: Rules in /etc/udev/rules.d on the HOST set permissions and (should) create stable symlinks when a device appears. container.sh writes 99-u2d2.rules and reloads udev before starting the container.
components.whyItExists: ttyACM0 / ttyUSB0 are assigned in enumeration order. Plug the camera in before the arm and your arm is ttyACM1; reboot with the leader arm attached and everything shifts. Any launch default that names a raw ttyACM number is a time bomb. The robust form is a SYMLINK rule keyed on the device's serial number, giving you /dev/omx_follower, which you then pass as port_name. Also: udev runs on the HOST, in the host's namespace -- the .rules files COPYed into this image at /etc/udev/rules.d are inert, because there is no udevd in the container. That is a genuinely confusing boundary: the file is in the image, and it does nothing.
components.evidence: Two real problems verified in this repo. (1) open_manipulator_bringup/open-manipulator-cdc.rules contains `KERNEL=="ttyACM*", DRIVERS=="ftdi_sio"` -- but a ttyACM device is driven by cdc_acm, never ftdi_sio, so that line can never match. The ttyUSB line is fine. (2) Three sources disagree on the port: open_manipulator_bringup/launch/omx_f.launch.py:61 defaults to /dev/ttyACM0, omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py:71 to /dev/ttyACM0, omx_l_leader_ai.launch.py:60 to /dev/ttyACM2, and open_manipulator_description/ros2_control/omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:3 defaults to /dev/ttyACM1. Neither rule creates a SYMLINK. That is your 'three sources disagreed' experience, reproduced on disk.
components.interface: Creates /dev/<name>, sets MODE/GROUP, sets ATTR{device/latency_timer}.

components.name: X11 / Wayland forwarding for RViz
components.role: DISPLAY passthrough, the X socket bind-mounted, an Xauthority file, QT_X11_NO_MITSHM=1, and `xhost +local:docker` on the host before launch.
components.whyItExists: GUI tools run in the container but must draw on the host's display server. Three distinct things must line up: the SOCKET (/tmp/.X11-unix), the AUTHORIZATION (xhost or a copied .Xauthority cookie), and the GL PATH. QT_X11_NO_MITSHM=1 disables the MIT-SHM X extension because Qt's shared-memory path assumes client and server share a /tmp and an IPC namespace. The GL path is the one that produces the exact failure this team hit: a window that exists in the taskbar and never paints. That is the signature of Mesa selecting a hardware driver it cannot fully load -- it finds the device node and fails on the vendor .so -- and it fails silently because GLX errors go to a stream nobody reads. `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1` forces llvmpipe and sidesteps the whole question; for a 5-DOF arm the scene is trivial and software rendering costs nothing. On Wayland the modern equivalent is passing $WAYLAND_DISPLAY and mounting $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, or just running RViz under XWayland.
components.evidence: docker-compose.yml: `DISPLAY=${DISPLAY}`, `QT_X11_NO_MITSHM=1`, mounts /tmp/.X11-unix and /tmp/.docker.xauth. container.sh runs `xhost +local:docker` in both start and enter. And the team's OWN docker-compose.override.yml (dated later than the vendor files, commented in English, not part of the ROBOTIS repo) sets LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 and explains the /dev/dxg-without-/usr/lib/wsl diagnosis exactly. Verified -- this file is the single best piece of engineering documentation in the repo.

components.name: docker-compose.override.yml as the deviation mechanism
components.role: Compose automatically merges docker-compose.override.yml on top of docker-compose.yml when you run `docker compose up` with no -f flag. It is the sanctioned place for local, per-machine, per-developer deviations from the vendor configuration.
components.whyItExists: The alternative is editing the vendor's docker-compose.yml, which means your working tree is permanently dirty, `git pull` conflicts every release, and the reason for your change lives only in your head. An override file is additive, greppable, and can carry a comment explaining WHY. Note the trap the team already half-hit: container.sh calls `docker compose -f "${SCRIPT_DIR}/docker-compose.yml" up -d` with an explicit -f, and an explicit -f SUPPRESSES automatic override merging. So `./container.sh start` does NOT apply the override; only a bare `docker compose up -d` run from docker/ does. That is worth knowing before debugging why LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE 'did not take'.
components.evidence: docker/docker-compose.override.yml exists and is gitignore-adjacent (docker/.gitignore only ignores workspace/, so the override IS tracked). container.sh start_container() and stop_container() both pass -f explicitly. Verified by reading both files.

components.name: Volume mounts: the bind mount that shadows the baked clone
components.role: `../:/root/ros2_ws/src/open_manipulator/` mounts the host checkout over the copy the Dockerfile cloned from GitHub. `./workspace:/workspace` is a scratch area for code that is not a ROS package.
components.whyItExists: This is the mechanism that makes the container a development environment rather than a shipping unit: you edit on the host with your real editor, and the container sees it instantly. But understand what it does to the prebuilt install/. The image's install/ was built from the BAKED clone; at runtime that path is the bind mount, so --symlink-install's symlinks now resolve to YOUR files -- which is why editing an existing launch file works live. Adding a new file does not, because the data_files globs were evaluated at build time. And any C++ change needs `cb` (the aliased colcon build). The second lesson is the docker/workspace/dummy_exec directory: the team's own nodes live there as loose .py files, outside any ROS package, run by path. That works for a spike and stops working the moment you want ros2 launch, parameters, or a colleague to run it. The graduation step is a real ament_python package under src/.
