components.evidence: docker-compose.yml volumes list. docker/.gitignore contains exactly `workspace/`, so the team's dummy_exec code is NOT under version control from this repo's perspective -- and __pycache__/*.cpython-311.pyc files are sitting in it. Verified.

components.name: Realtime knobs: cap_add SYS_NICE, ulimits rtprio/rttime/memlock
components.role: Grants the container permission to raise thread priority into the SCHED_FIFO range, run RT threads without being killed by the RT throttler, and lock ~8GB of memory.
components.whyItExists: A control loop that is preempted by a Chrome tab produces jitter that looks like a mechanical problem. ros2_control's controller_manager can put its update thread on SCHED_FIFO, but only if the process has CAP_SYS_NICE and an rtprio ulimit above 0 -- inside a default container both are absent and the priority request fails silently, so you get a 'realtime' controller running at normal priority and never know. memlock matters because a page fault in the control thread is an unbounded latency spike. These three lines are the difference between a control loop with a 200 microsecond jitter and one with a 20 millisecond tail.
components.evidence: docker-compose.yml: `cap_add: [SYS_NICE]`, `ulimits: {rtprio: 99, rttime: -1, memlock: 8428281856}`. Verified. 8428281856 bytes is 7.85 GiB, sized for an 8GB Jetson.

components.name: User ID mapping (conspicuously absent here)
components.role: The convention is to create a container user whose UID/GID match the host user (ARG USER_UID=1000, useradd -u ${USER_UID}, USER ros), so files the container writes are owned by you on the host.
components.whyItExists: This image runs everything as root: COLCON_WS=/root/ros2_ws, ~/.bashrc is root's. With `../:/root/ros2_ws/src/open_manipulator/` bind-mounted, every build artifact, every log, every file a node writes into the source tree lands root-owned on the host. Then your host-side editor cannot save, `git clean` fails, and someone reaches for sudo, which is how a repo ends up with a mix of root-owned and user-owned files that nobody can untangle. On Linux hosts this is the single most common daily annoyance of containerized ROS. (On WSL2 and Docker Desktop the ownership semantics differ and it often does not bite, which is why the vendor may not have noticed.) The fix is either UID-matched user in the Dockerfile, `user: "${UID}:${GID}"` in compose, or Podman's rootless userns mapping.
components.evidence: Dockerfile writes to ~/.bashrc and sets COLCON_WS=/root/ros2_ws; no useradd, no USER directive. docker-compose.yml has no `user:` key. Verified by absence.

components.name: colcon workspace layout: src/ build/ install/ log/
components.role: src/ is the ONLY directory you edit or commit. build/ holds per-package intermediate objects and CMake caches. install/ holds the resulting FHS-like tree (lib/, share/, include/) plus setup.bash. log/ holds per-invocation build logs.
components.whyItExists: The separation exists so that 'my build is broken' has a one-command answer: `rm -rf build install log && colcon build`. You never edit install/ because it is generated, and with --symlink-install half of it is symlinks INTO src/, so editing 'install/share/pkg/launch/foo.launch.py' may be editing your source file through a symlink and may be editing a throwaway copy -- you cannot tell by looking. Three .gitignore lines (build/, install/, log/) are non-negotiable. COLCON_IGNORE is the escape hatch for directories that contain package.xml-like content but must not be built.
components.evidence: docker/COLCON_IGNORE and docker/AMENT_IGNORE both exist as empty marker files in this repo -- verified -- so that the docker/ directory (which sits inside the repo that gets mounted into src/) is not scanned as a ROS package. That is exactly the pattern to copy when you park a dataset, a notebook directory, or a vendored third-party tree inside src/.
components.interface: install/setup.bash is the only thing the rest of the system consumes.

components.name: vcstool and the .repos file
components.role: A YAML manifest listing every external repository and the exact ref to check out. `vcs import src < robot.repos` reproduces the whole source tree; `vcs export src > robot.repos` snapshots what you currently have, SHAs and all.
components.whyItExists: This is the answer to 'pin your dependencies' for source-built ROS workspaces, and it is the thing that makes the six-months-later reproduction possible. The discipline is: one .repos file per deployment target, checked into git, with `version:` set to a SHA (not a branch) for anything you depend on being stable. Then `vcs export --exact src > frozen.repos` before a demo or a data collection run, and commit that file. If you do one thing from this whole answer, do this one -- it costs ten minutes and it is the difference between 'we can rebuild the robot we had on demo day' and 'we cannot'.
components.evidence: open_manipulator_ci.repos exists but is minimal (2 repos, both `version: main` -- a branch, not a SHA) and is used only by CI, not by the Dockerfile, which re-clones by hand. Verified. So the repo demonstrates the tool without demonstrating the discipline; your team should do better than the vendor here.

components.name: CI as the reproducibility check
components.role: GitHub Actions builds the workspace from scratch on a clean ubuntu:noble container on every push and PR, using ros-tooling/setup-ros and action-ros-ci, and runs eight ament linters in parallel.
components.whyItExists: CI is not about catching logic bugs in robotics -- there is no robot in CI. It is about catching environment drift: the missing <depend> tag, the header that only compiles because it happens to be installed on your laptop, the package that builds only in the order you happen to build it. Any dependency you forgot to declare fails here and nowhere else. The `rosdep check ... || exit 1` step is the specific gate that enforces 'package.xml is complete'.
components.evidence: .github/workflows/ros-ci.yml (matrix over ros_distribution, currently just jazzy on ubuntu:noble; humble and rolling commented out) and ros-lint.yml (cppcheck, cpplint, uncrustify, flake8, pep257, lint_cmake, xmllint, copyright). Verified.
components.rate: Every push to jazzy/main and every PR.

components.name: Devcontainers: what they are and who actually uses them
components.role: .devcontainer/devcontainer.json describes a container that VS Code (or the devcontainer CLI, or now several other editors) builds and attaches to, with the extension set, mounts, runArgs and post-create commands declared alongside.
components.whyItExists: It solves the last mile that compose does not: the EDITOR lives inside the container too, so clangd finds /opt/ros/jazzy/include, Python intellisense finds rclpy, and the debugger can attach. Without it you get red squiggles on every ROS include and a team that turns off the linter. Usage is genuinely split: university labs and mid-size robotics companies with VS Code monocultures use them heavily; teams with mixed editors, or whose robots are headless Jetsons reached over SSH, tend to stay on plain compose plus `docker exec -it`. A common compromise is `"dockerComposeFile": "../docker/docker-compose.yml"` with `"service": "open_manipulator"`, so the devcontainer is a thin editor attachment to the SAME container definition the robot runs -- one source of truth, two front doors. That is what I would recommend here.
components.evidence: This repo has NO .devcontainer (verified by find). The vendor ships container.sh instead -- a hand-rolled start/enter/stop wrapper that also does the xhost and udev setup a devcontainer would put in initializeCommand.

components.name: Image tagging and the registry
components.role: `image: robotis/open-manipulator:5.1.1` plus `docker compose pull` in container.sh: the normal path is to DOWNLOAD the vendor's built image, not build it. `build:` is there as a fallback.
components.whyItExists: Building this image takes 30+ minutes and requires network access to six git remotes. Pulling a tagged image takes two minutes and every team member gets bit-identical bytes. The version in the tag is kept in sync with open_manipulator/package.xml, and container.sh compares it against the GitHub releases API to nag you about updates. The convention to copy: tag images with the git SHA or a semver that maps to a git tag, push to a registry (ghcr.io is free for your team), and make 'what image is the robot running' a question with a one-word answer. `docker inspect --format '{{.Config.Image}}' open_manipulator` should tell you, and it should match a tag in git.
components.evidence: docker-compose.yml `image: robotis/open-manipulator:5.1.1`; container.sh get_current_version() parses <version> out of open_manipulator/package.xml and get_latest_version() hits the GitHub releases API. Verified. Important consequence: because both `image:` and `build:` are present, `docker compose up` uses the LOCAL image if one exists with that tag and only builds if none does -- so a stale local 5.1.1 will be used forever without warning.

components.name: Team coordination over the one physical robot
components.role: Not software. A convention, written down: who owns the arm right now, who may power-cycle it, which branch is on it, and a no-surprises rule about the serial port.
components.whyItExists: Two processes on one serial bus is a scheduling problem wearing a software costume. No amount of Docker fixes it, because Docker does not isolate /dev. What actually works, in order of how much teams underestimate it: (1) A physical or Slack-channel BOOKING for the arm -- one person at a time, with a stated end time. (2) One machine is the robot machine; nobody else's laptop ever opens the port, they read topics over the network. (3) `ros2 launch` bringup is started ONCE and left running; everyone else's code is a node that connects to it. If your workflow requires restarting bringup to test your change, your change is in the wrong process. (4) A pre-flight command everyone runs: `docker ps`, `sudo fuser -v /dev/ttyACM0`, `ros2 node list`. (5) Distinct ROS_DOMAIN_ID per developer when simulating, and a single agreed one for the real robot -- with host networking, the domain ID is the ONLY thing keeping your sim nodes out of the robot's graph. (6) Branch discipline: the robot runs a named branch (here, jazzy / main); feature work happens on branches and reaches the arm only via that branch, so 'what is on the robot' is always answerable from git. (7) The servo RAM-register problem is the same category: RAM registers reset on power cycle by design, EEPROM ones persist, so 'who set the PID gains and did they survive the reboot' must be a startup step in a launch file or a config yaml, never a thing someone typed once.
components.evidence: Repo evidence for the branch convention: git branches are named feature-omx, feature-collision-rev5, feature-moveit-srdf etc., all merged into main via PRs (git log shows 'Merge pull request #378 from ROBOTIS-GIT/feature-fix-dockerfile'). CONTRIBUTING.md requires DCO sign-off on every commit. The booking/ownership conventions are general practice, not verifiable here.

orderOfOperations: 1. Fix the substrate FIRST, before any code: which Ubuntu, which ROS distro, which JetPack/L4T on the Jetson. Write the three answers in the repo README on day one. `lsb_release -a`, `echo $ROS_DISTRO`, `cat /etc/nv_tegra_release`. Everything downstream inherits these and none of them can be changed later without a rebuild of everything.

2. Choose the base image from those answers, not from a tutorial. Generic amd64/arm64 dev box: ros:jazzy-ros-base (headless) or osrf/ros:jazzy-desktop (RViz included). Jetson with GPU work: an L4T base matching your flashed revision, run with the NVIDIA container runtime. Verify with one command before writing a Dockerfile: `docker run --rm ros:jazzy-ros-base ros2 --help`.

3. Get ONE container to talk to the hardware before you write a single node. Start the vendor container, `ros2 launch <bringup>`, watch /joint_states tick. This is the bisection point for everything afterwards: if the arm moves under vendor bringup, every later failure is yours; if it does not, stop and fix the environment. Teams that skip this spend weeks unable to tell an IK bug from a udev bug.

4. Pin the sources. Convert the ad-hoc `git clone -b jazzy` lines into a .repos file with SHAs, commit it, and make the Dockerfile do `vcs import src < robot.repos`. Do this BEFORE the workspace grows, because retro-pinning requires knowing what you had, and by then you will not.

5. Declare dependencies in package.xml and prove it with rosdep, not by apt-installing until it builds. The test is: `rm -rf build install log && rosdep install --from-paths src --ignore-src -r -y && colcon build`. If that passes on a fresh container, your environment is reproducible. If you cannot run it because it takes 40 minutes, that is a signal to split the workspace, not a reason to skip the check.

6. Only now write the compose file, adding capabilities one at a time and testing after each. Start minimal; add network_mode: host when discovery fails; add the device when the port is missing; add cap_add/ulimits when the controller complains about priority. Adding everything at once (which is what `privileged: true` is) means you never learn which line does what, and you cannot tighten it later.

7. Make the device name stable before you make anything else work. Write a udev SYMLINK rule keyed on the USB serial number, reload, unplug, replug, confirm /dev/omx_follower exists, and then make EVERY config point at that name -- launch default, xacro default, your scripts. Right now three files in this repo disagree (ttyACM0, ttyACM1, ttyACM2) and that is a bug waiting for a reboot.

8. Establish the single-owner rule for the bus, in writing, before two people ever run code simultaneously. One process owns /dev/<port>; everything else is a ROS node. Add `sudo fuser -v /dev/ttyACM0` to the team's pre-flight checklist. This is step 8 and not step 20 because the debugging cost of violating it is enormous and the symptoms do not point at the cause.

9. Bring up the display path and confirm RViz RENDERS, not merely opens. A window in the taskbar that never paints is the failure mode; `glxinfo | grep renderer` inside the container tells you which driver Mesa picked, and LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 is the fast answer when the hardware path is broken.

10. Put your own code in a real ROS package under src/, with package.xml, setup.py and a launch file, the moment it stops being a one-off script. The forcing function is: can a teammate run it with `ros2 launch`? Loose .py files run by path (docker/workspace/dummy_exec/) cannot take parameters, cannot be composed, cannot be launched with the rest of the system, and are invisible to rosdep and CI.

11. Wire up CI that builds from scratch on every push. Not to test behavior -- to catch the undeclared dependency the day it appears rather than the day a new teammate clones the repo. rosdep check as a hard gate, ament linters as advisory at first.

12. Tag and push an image at every milestone, and record image tag + git SHA + .repos snapshot together. `vcs export --exact src > frozen-$(date +%F).repos` before every data-collection session or demo. Six months later this file is the only thing that lets you reproduce a bug.

13. Only after all of the above: add the ML container. The torch/lerobot/diffusers stack does not belong in the ROS image -- different Python version pressure, different CUDA pressure, different update cadence. Run it as a second container on the same host (ipc: host, network_mode: host so DDS/zenoh still works) and let it talk to the robot over topics. This keeps a `pip install -U torch` from breaking your robot's ability to move.
keyFacts: ROS distro to Ubuntu is a hard 1:1 binding: Jazzy = Ubuntu 24.04 Noble + Python 3.12; Humble = 22.04 Jammy + Python 3.10; Kilted/Rolling = 24.04/newer. There is no supported cross-combination. This single fact is why Docker is not optional in ROS -- it is the only practical way for a team on mixed machines to share one ABI.

VERIFIED in this repo: the launch files and the xacro disagree on the serial port. open_manipulator_bringup/launch/omx_f.launch.py:61 and omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py:71 default to /dev/ttyACM0, omx_l_leader_ai.launch.py:60 to /dev/ttyACM2, and open_manipulator_description/ros2_control/omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:3 to /dev/ttyACM1. The launch argument normally wins (it is passed as `port_name:=` into xacro), but any path that instantiates the macro without the argument silently gets ttyACM1.

VERIFIED in this repo: open_manipulator_bringup/open-manipulator-cdc.rules line 1 is `KERNEL=="ttyACM*", DRIVERS=="ftdi_sio"` -- a contradiction. ttyACM devices are driven by cdc_acm; ftdi_sio produces ttyUSB. That rule can never match, so your /dev/ttyACM0 gets no MODE=0666 from it. If the port works without sudo, it is because privileged + /dev:/dev bypassed the permission entirely, not because the rule worked.

Opening a Linux tty twice succeeds. DynamixelSDK's PortHandlerLinux::setupPort calls open() with O_RDWR|O_NOCTTY|O_NONBLOCK and does not set TIOCEXCL, so two processes both get a valid fd on /dev/ttyACM0 and their writes interleave on the half-duplex bus. You will never see 'device busy'; you will see CRC failures and phantom timeouts.

rmw_zenoh disables UDP multicast scouting BY DEFAULT, explicitly to avoid broken discovery in misconfigured networks and containers. That is why `ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd` must exist before nodes can see each other -- it is a deliberate design trade, not a bug.

Docker's default bridge network does not forward UDP multicast, which is how classic DDS discovery works. That is the whole reason `network_mode: host` appears in essentially every robotics compose file. The cost is that ROS_DOMAIN_ID becomes machine-wide and LAN-visible; this image hardcodes 30 (Dockerfile line 84).

`ipc: host` is a separate and equally important line: DDS uses POSIX shared memory for same-host transport of large messages. Without a shared IPC namespace it falls back to loopback UDP, which for camera streams is a real CPU and latency cost and produces no error message.

VERIFIED: this Dockerfile pins exactly one dependency properly. realsense-ros gets `git checkout cbd8b8487d4c0126bb590822db9469414496e62a` (line 64). The other five repos use `-b jazzy`, a moving branch, so two people building the same Dockerfile a week apart get different source.

colcon's default CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE is empty -- no optimization. `--cmake-args -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` is what makes the control path fast enough on a Jetson. This repo does it (Dockerfile line 75) and aliases it as `cb`.

VERIFIED: docker/docker-compose.override.yml exists and Compose merges it automatically -- but ONLY when you run `docker compose up` with no -f flag. container.sh passes `-f docker-compose.yml` explicitly, which suppresses the merge. So `./container.sh start` does not apply your LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE fix; a bare `docker compose up -d` from the docker/ directory does.

VERIFIED: docker-compose.yml declares both `image: robotis/open-manipulator:5.1.1` and `build:`. Compose uses an existing local image with that tag and only builds when none exists -- so a stale local 5.1.1 is reused indefinitely, silently, even after you change the Dockerfile. Force with `docker compose build --no-cache` or `docker compose up --build`.

VERIFIED: this image runs everything as root (COLCON_WS=/root/ros2_ws, no useradd, no USER, no `user:` in compose) while bind-mounting your host checkout at /root/ros2_ws/src/open_manipulator/. On a Linux host, every file the container writes into the source tree becomes root-owned on the host.

`ulimits: {rtprio: 99, memlock: 8428281856}` with `cap_add: [SYS_NICE]` is what allows ros2_control to put its update thread on SCHED_FIFO. Without these the priority request fails SILENTLY and you get a 'realtime' loop running at normal priority. 8428281856 bytes = 7.85 GiB, sized for an 8GB Jetson.

VERIFIED: docker/COLCON_IGNORE and docker/AMENT_IGNORE are empty marker files that stop colcon from scanning the docker/ directory when the whole repo is mounted into src/. This is the standard way to park non-package directories (datasets, notebooks, vendored trees) inside a workspace.

PEP 668 puts /usr/lib/python3.12/EXTERNALLY-MANAGED on Noble, which makes pip refuse system-wide installs. This image disables that globally (`pip config set global.break-system-packages true`, Dockerfile line 94) and then installs with --ignore-installed, which also suppresses the conflict warning. Anything you pip-install after that can silently replace a module that ros-jazzy-* debs own.

JetPack version-locks kernel, driver, CUDA, cuDNN, TensorRT and multimedia together at flash time. A container built against a different L4T revision will fail on the Orin even though the Ubuntu release and CPU architecture match. Record the JetPack version the day you flash.

s6-overlay exists in this image because container PID 1 does not reap children or forward signals to process groups. `down-signal: SIGINT` (verified in docker/s6-services/open_manipulator_bringup/) is what gives ros2 launch the signal it actually handles, and the run script records its PGID to /run/<service>.pgid so the finish script can kill the whole tree. Without this, `docker stop` leaves an orphan holding your serial port.

CI in this repo (.github/workflows/ros-ci.yml) runs `rosdep check --from-paths ros_ws/src --ignore-src` as a hard gate that exits 1 on any unresolvable key. That one step is what keeps package.xml honest; copy it.
beginnerMistakes: Editing files under install/ because that is where the error message pointed. install/ is generated. With --symlink-install some of it is symlinks into src/ and some is copies, and you cannot tell which by looking -- so half your edits take effect and half vanish on rebuild. Correct habit: only ever edit src/, and treat `rm -rf build install log` as a free, always-safe action.

Assuming --symlink-install means 'no rebuild ever'. It symlinks what it can; setup.py data_files globs are evaluated at build time, so a NEW launch file or config yaml does not appear until you rebuild. Correct habit: after ADDING any file, run `colcon build --packages-select <pkg>` before you believe a negative result.

Apt-installing packages until the build succeeds, and never adding the <depend> tag. It works on your machine forever and fails on the next clone. Correct habit: add the tag, then prove it with `rm -rf build install log && rosdep install --from-paths src --ignore-src -r -y && colcon build` in a fresh container.

pip installing into the ROS environment -- especially numpy, PyYAML, setuptools, or anything torch drags in. It can replace a module that rclpy was built against, and the resulting ImportError or segfault points nowhere near the cause. Correct habit: system deps via rosdep; ML deps in a separate container, or a venv created with --system-site-packages that you activate only for training, never for a ROS node.

Reaching for `privileged: true` and `/dev:/dev` at the first permission error. It always works, which is exactly the problem -- you never learn what you actually needed, and your compose file no longer documents your hardware dependency. Correct habit: add the narrowest thing that fixes it (`devices:` plus `device_cgroup_rules:`), one line at a time, testing after each.

Believing the container isolates the robot. It does not. Devices are shared, the network here is host, and the serial port is exclusive across the whole machine regardless of how many container boundaries sit between the two openers. Correct habit: treat /dev/ttyACM0 as a machine-global mutex with no enforcement, and coordinate it socially.

Debugging a flaky arm as a mechanical or kinematics problem when it is a second process on the bus. The signature is intermittence that correlates with nothing in your code and changes when you add prints. Correct habit: `sudo fuser -v /dev/ttyACM0` and `docker ps` are the FIRST two commands, before you read any of your own code.

Hardcoding /dev/ttyACM0 in a script. Enumeration order is not stable across reboots, replugs, or plugging the camera in first. Correct habit: a udev SYMLINK rule keyed on the device serial, then use /dev/omx_follower everywhere -- launch defaults, xacro defaults, scripts.

Running your own code as loose .py files next to the workspace instead of as a package. It is fine for the first spike and becomes a wall the moment you want parameters, launch integration, or a teammate to run it. Correct habit: promote to an ament_python package under src/ as soon as a second person or a second file is involved. The forcing question is 'can a teammate run this with ros2 launch?'

Rebuilding the Docker image expecting fresh packages. Layer caching keys on the command string, so `apt-get install` returns March's versions until something above it invalidates. Correct habit: know that `docker compose up --build` may be a no-op, and use `docker compose build --no-cache` when you actually mean it.

Thinking git branch = version. `git clone -b jazzy` today and `-b jazzy` in six months give different code with an identical Dockerfile, which is exactly why the bug you saw in March cannot be reproduced in September. Correct habit: SHAs in a .repos file, committed, plus `vcs export --exact` before every demo or data-collection run.

Sourcing install/setup.bash without sourcing the distro first, or sourcing an overlay built against a different underlay. The result is ABI crashes that look like memory corruption. Correct habit: underlay then overlay, always, and when in doubt open a fresh shell rather than un-sourcing anything -- there is no un-source.

Treating an empty `ros2 topic list` as a code bug. With rmw_zenoh it almost always means the router is not running; with DDS in a bridge network it means multicast is not forwarded. Correct habit: check the middleware layer before the application layer -- is zenohd up, is RMW_IMPLEMENTATION the same in both shells, is ROS_DOMAIN_ID the same.

Configuring a servo by typing into a tool once. RAM registers reset on power cycle by design; only EEPROM persists. Correct habit: every register you depend on is set from a config yaml at bringup, or it does not exist. If a setting only survives because nobody unplugged the arm, it is not a setting, it is a coincidence.
communityDifferences: Research labs: one workspace, one branch, `colcon build` on a laptop, often no container at all until a second person joins and nothing builds. When they do containerize, it is one big privileged image with everything in it, built by whoever set it up, and nobody else can rebuild it. Pinning is rare, CI is rare, and the .repos file (if any) points at branches. This is the repo you are looking at, culturally -- the ROBOTIS Dockerfile pins one dependency out of six.

Industrial / product robotics: images are built in CI and pulled by digest, never built on the robot. Two compose files -- a dev one with RViz and GUI passthrough, a slim runtime one with no X11, no build tools, narrow `devices:` entries and no privileged flag. Non-root user, read-only root filesystem where possible, a health-check on the bringup service, and an OTA story (balena, Mender, or a plain systemd unit that pulls a tag). The serial port question is settled in hardware: a fixed USB topology, a udev rule with SYMLINK, and a wiring diagram.

The imitation-learning / LeRobot / UMI crowd: almost always TWO environments, not one. A conda or uv environment for the policy stack (torch, diffusers, transformers, wandb) and a separate ROS container for the robot, communicating over topics, a websocket, or a shared-memory ring. The reason is a genuine conflict: LeRobot and friends move fast, want recent Python and recent torch, and reinstall constantly; ROS wants a frozen system interpreter. Trying to make one image satisfy both is the single most common way this community breaks a working robot. Notably, much of this community does NOT use ros2_control or MoveIt at all -- they drive the arm from a Python SDK at 10-30 Hz and treat ROS as optional glue. Whether that is a shortcut or a legitimate architecture is genuinely contested; it works for tabletop manipulation and does not scale to anything with safety requirements.

Devcontainers specifically: heavily used in university labs and mid-size companies with a VS Code monoculture, largely absent in teams with mixed editors or headless SSH-only robots. The pragmatic middle -- and what I would recommend for a capstone team -- is a .devcontainer that references the EXISTING docker-compose.yml via `dockerComposeFile` and `service`, so the editor attaches to exactly the container the robot runs. One definition, two front doors.

Docker vs Podman vs Apptainer: Docker dominates, but Podman is gaining in labs that care about rootless containers (its user-namespace mapping makes the root-owned-files problem disappear without a UID-matching dance), and Apptainer/Singularity is standard in HPC-adjacent research where you cannot have a daemon. The compose semantics differ enough that you should pick one and not mix.

Whether to bake the build into the image at all. One camp bakes it (this repo does) so the robot boots ready -- correct for deployment. The other mounts src/ and builds on first run -- correct for development, because the image does not need rebuilding for every source change. Mature teams do both, with two Dockerfile targets or two compose services sharing a base stage. Doing only the first makes iteration miserable; doing only the second means the robot cannot boot unattended.

components.name: Stage 0 — Workspace skeleton and container image (before a single line of robot code)
components.role: Create the colcon workspace layout (src/ with one package per concern: _description, _bringup, _moveit_config, _teleop, plus a .repos file), and the Dockerfile that pins the ROS distro and builds the dependency tree. Nothing robot-specific is written yet; you are fixing the substrate everything else will be diffed against.
components.whyItExists: Robotics dependencies are not pip-shaped: a hardware plugin is a compiled pluginlib .so discovered at runtime through an XML manifest and the AMENT_PREFIX_PATH, so 'it works on my machine' is usually an environment-variable difference, not a code difference. The container exists so that a teammate's apt state cannot change your controller's behaviour. The .repos file exists so that 'which commit of dynamixel_hardware_interface' is a tracked fact rather than whatever was on main the day someone cloned.
components.interface: Out: a built install/ tree and a setup.bash that sets AMENT_PREFIX_PATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, PYTHONPATH. In: src/*/package.xml dependency keys resolved by rosdep against the distro's index.
components.rate: Rebuilt on dependency change; `colcon build --symlink-install` per edit for Python/config, full rebuild for C++.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/docker/Dockerfile (FROM ros:jazzy-ros-base, ENV COLCON_WS=/root/ros2_ws, `rosdep install -i --from-path src --rosdistro $ROS_DISTRO --skip-keys=...`, then `colcon build --symlink-install --cmake-args -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`); open_manipulator/open_manipulator_ci.repos pins dynamixel_hardware_interface and robotis_interfaces by URL+branch; docker-compose.yml bind-mounts `../:/root/ros2_ws/src/open_manipulator/` so the host checkout is the overlay source.

components.name: Stage 0b — Host-side device and privilege plumbing (udev, serial latency, RT scheduling, RMW)
components.role: Install udev rules so the arm appears at a stable path with sane driver settings, grant the container the capabilities a control loop needs, and fix the RMW and domain so nodes can actually discover each other.
components.whyItExists: Three separate real failures, each of which looks like a code bug: (1) the FTDI/CDC default latency_timer is 16 ms, which caps a serial round trip at ~60 Hz and silently destroys a 100 Hz loop — the rule sets it to 1 ms; (2) without SYS_NICE and an rtprio ulimit the controller_manager thread cannot get real-time priority and you get jitter that looks like mechanical slop; (3) rmw_zenoh_cpp requires a router process to exist before any node can see any other node — which is exactly the 'zenoh router had to exist first' surprise. ROS_DOMAIN_ID isolates your graph from a teammate's on the same LAN.
components.interface: Out: /dev/ttyACM0 with mode 0666 and latency_timer=1; a running `rmw_zenohd`; ROS_DOMAIN_ID and RMW_IMPLEMENTATION exported identically in every shell and every container.
components.rate: Once per machine (udev); once per boot (zenoh router, supervised).
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_bringup/open-manipulator-cdc.rules: `KERNEL=="ttyACM*", DRIVERS=="ftdi_sio", MODE="0666", ATTR{device/latency_timer}="1"`; installer at open_manipulator_bringup/open_manipulator_bringup/om_create_udev_rules.py; docker-compose.yml: `cap_add: [SYS_NICE]`, `ulimits: {rtprio: 99, rttime: -1, memlock: 8428281856}`, `network_mode: host`, `ipc: host`, `/dev:/dev`; Dockerfile writes `export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=30`, `export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp` and `alias zenohd='ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd'` into ~/.bashrc.

components.name: Stage 1 — Robot description (URDF via xacro): the single source of geometric truth
components.role: Write the kinematic tree as xacro macros: links with visual/collision/inertial, joints with parent, child, origin, axis, and limits. Parameterise everything that differs between deployments (prefix, port, sim-vs-mock-vs-real) as xacro args so ONE description serves all three backends.
components.whyItExists: Every downstream consumer — robot_state_publisher for TF, MoveIt for planning, the collision checker, ros2_control for the joint/interface list, Gazebo for physics — reads the SAME URDF. If they each had their own copy of the geometry you get the classic failure where RViz shows the arm in one place and the planner thinks it is somewhere else. Xacro exists because raw URDF has no variables, so a 6-joint arm becomes 400 lines of copy-paste in which one wrong origin is invisible.
components.interface: Out: a single expanded XML string published as the `robot_description` parameter (ROS 2 Jazzy: a parameter on robot_state_publisher and on ros2_control_node, not a global). In: nothing — this is the root.
components.rate: Expanded once at launch time via a `Command([FindExecutable('xacro'), ...])` substitution; never re-read at runtime.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_description/urdf/omx_f/omx_f.urdf.xacro (declares args prefix, use_sim, use_mock_hardware, port_name, ros2_control_type; includes the arm macro, the gazebo macro, and the selected ros2_control macro); open_manipulator_description/urdf/omx_f/omx_f_arm.urdf.xacro holds the actual links/joints — e.g. joint3 `<origin xyz="0.0415 0 0.11315"/> <axis xyz="0 1 0"/> <limit velocity="4.8" effort="1000" lower="${-pi*2.0}" upper="${pi*2.0}"/>`, and link0 carries a real measured `<inertial>` (mass 0.2238905 kg, full 6-term inertia tensor).

components.name: Stage 1b — Description validation harness (prove the URDF before anything stands on it)
components.role: Run the description through four independent checks in ascending cost: `xacro file.urdf.xacro > /tmp/r.urdf` (does it even expand), `check_urdf /tmp/r.urdf` (is the tree well-formed, one root, no cycles), `urdf_to_graphiz /tmp/r.urdf` (does the parent/child chain match the physical arm), and a description-only launch with robot_state_publisher + joint_state_publisher_gui + RViz (do the axes point where you think, do the limits feel right when you drag the sliders).
components.whyItExists: A wrong `<axis>` sign or a 5 mm error in an `<origin>` produces FK that is subtly wrong everywhere, and you will discover it as 'the IK never converges' or 'the arm misses the object by a centimetre' three weeks later. The slider GUI catches sign errors in seconds because a joint visibly rotates the wrong way. Note the ORDER within the stage: check_urdf proves syntax, graphiz proves topology, RViz+sliders proves geometry and sign. Each one is a strictly weaker claim than the next, and each is cheaper.
components.interface: Out: /joint_states (sensor_msgs/JointState) from the GUI at ~10 Hz, /tf and /tf_static from robot_state_publisher, the `robot_description` parameter. NOTHING touches hardware.
components.rate: joint_state_publisher_gui publishes at its `rate` param (default 10 Hz); robot_state_publisher recomputes TF on every JointState.
components.evidence: The vendor ships this harness as a separate launch file precisely for this purpose: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_description/launch/omx_f.launch.py spawns only robot_state_publisher, rviz2 (-d open_manipulator_description/rviz/open_manipulator.rviz) and joint_state_publisher_gui — no controller_manager, no hardware. Run it as `ros2 launch open_manipulator_description omx_f.launch.py`.

components.name: Stage 1c — Collision geometry and the SRDF allowed-collision matrix
components.role: Give each link a SIMPLIFIED collision shape (box/cylinder/sphere/capsule, or a convex hull of the visual mesh), separate from the pretty visual mesh. Then write the SRDF: planning groups, named poses, the end-effector, and the disable_collisions list.
components.whyItExists: Collision checking runs inside the planner's inner loop — MoveIt's OMPL planners evaluate tens of thousands of states per plan, and FCL mesh-vs-mesh on a 20k-triangle STL is orders of magnitude slower than sphere-vs-capsule. The ACM exists because adjacent links ALWAYS touch at their joint, so without disabling those pairs every configuration reports a collision and the planner returns 'start state in collision' forever. This repo is a live example of the tradeoff: the URDF uses the SAME high-poly STL for `<visual>` and `<collision>` on every link, and the vendor then wrote a SEPARATE C++ node that re-approximates the links as FCL capsules to get a fast runtime self-collision check. That second node is the cost of not simplifying the first time.
components.interface: Out: SRDF consumed by MoveIt (planning groups, ACM); /collision_flag (std_msgs/Bool) and /…/MarkerArray from the capsule checker. In: /joint_states.
components.rate: Self-collision node recomputes per incoming JointState (so ~100 Hz when joint_state_broadcaster is up).
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_description/urdf/omx_f/omx_f_arm.urdf.xacro — `<collision>` re-uses `follower_01_base.stl` etc. verbatim; open_manipulator/open_manipulator_collision/src/self_collision_node.cpp + include/.../self_collision_node.hpp uses `fcl::Capsuled`, subscribes /joint_states, publishes /collision_flag; open_manipulator/open_manipulator_moveit_config/config/omx_f/omx_f.srdf has group 'arm' (joint1..joint5 + end_effector_joint), group_state 'home' = [0, -1.57, 1.57, 1.57, 0], `<passive_joint name="gripper_joint_2"/>`, and 9 disable_collisions entries tagged Adjacent/Never/Always.

components.name: Stage 2 — Kinematics: choose a solver and prove it numerically, off-robot
components.role: Decide between an analytic closed-form IK you derive yourself and a numerical plugin (KDL, TRAC-IK, bio_ik, pick_ik). Analytic is worth it when the arm has a decomposable structure (spherical wrist, or in your case a planar 3R sub-chain with a yaw base), when you need determinism and sub-millisecond latency, and when you need to CHOOSE the branch (elbow-up vs elbow-down) rather than get whatever the optimiser landed on. Numerical is worth it the moment the geometry stops being nice, or when you need arbitrary cost terms.
components.whyItExists: An imitation-learning executor calls IK at the chunk rate — for H=16 steps replanned every few steps, that is hundreds of IK calls per second, inside a node that must also hold a real-time publishing deadline. KDL's default timeout here is 5 ms; sixteen of those is 80 ms of worst-case latency in a 40 ms control step. Analytic IK is microseconds and never fails nondeterministically. The other half of the reason is branch stability: a numerical solver seeded from the current state will usually stay on one branch, but 'usually' means that once per hundred chunks the arm flips its elbow through the table. Analytic lets you pick the branch explicitly and reject the other.
components.interface: In: a 4x4 target pose (or position-only). Out: a joint vector, plus an explicit failure reason. For MoveIt the boundary is the `kinematics_solver` pluginlib class in kinematics.yaml.
components.rate: Called at whatever rate the layer above plans; for a UMI-style chunk decoder, H calls per replan.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_moveit_config/config/omx_f/kinematics.yaml: `kinematics_solver: kdl_kinematics_plugin/KDLKinematicsPlugin`, `kinematics_solver_timeout: 0.005`, `kinematics_solver_search_resolution: 0.005`, and crucially `position_only_ik: True`. Alternatives: TRAC-IK (dual-threaded Newton + SQP, better at joint limits than KDL), bio_ik and pick_ik (PickNik's reimplementation of bio_ik, supports arbitrary goal cost functions). https://moveit.picknik.ai/main/doc/how_to_guides/pick_ik/pick_ik_tutorial.html ; https://github.com/PickNikRobotics/ik_benchmarking

components.name: Stage 2b — position_only_ik and what underactuation actually costs you
components.role: On a 5-DOF arm, accept that the reachable set is a 5-manifold in a 6-dimensional SE(3) and decide explicitly how to project a 6-DOF target onto it. The usual choice for a yaw-base + planar-elbow + roll-wrist arm: honour x, y, z and the approach pitch, drop the free yaw-about-approach (or vice versa), and make the projection an explicit, testable function.
components.whyItExists: Ask a 5-DOF arm for a full 6-DOF pose and a numerical solver will fail, or worse, converge to something 15 degrees off with no error. `position_only_ik: True` is MoveIt's blunt version of this: it tells KDL to zero the orientation rows of the Jacobian, so the solver only chases position. That is honest but throws away orientation entirely, which is wrong for a pick where approach angle matters. The competent version is your own projection with a documented policy, because then 'the policy asked for an unreachable orientation' becomes a logged rejection instead of a silent 15-degree error.
components.interface: In: desired SE(3). Out: achievable SE(3) + a residual you can threshold and log.
components.rate: Same as IK.
components.evidence: kinematics.yaml sets position_only_ik: True for the omx_f 'arm' group. The team's own code already does the explicit version: open_manipulator/docker/workspace/dummy_exec/action_format.py documents `R = Rz(yaw) @ Ry(pitch) @ Rx(roll)` as the OMX composition order with 'joint1 supplies yaw, joints 2/3/4 sum to pitch, joint5 is roll' — that sentence IS the projection policy, written down.

components.name: Stage 2c — Kinematics test harness (the first thing in the repo with real unit tests)
components.role: Three tests, no robot required. (1) Round trip: sample q uniformly inside limits, FK to T, IK back to q', FK again to T', assert ||T - T'|| < tol — compare POSES not joint vectors, because multiple q map to the same T. (2) Workspace sampling: grid the reachable volume, record IK success rate and solve time per cell, and plot it — this is how you learn your arm's actual reachable set rather than the one in your head. (3) Branch continuity: walk a dense Cartesian path and assert no joint jumps more than a threshold between consecutive solutions.
components.whyItExists: FK is easy to get right and easy to get subtly wrong; IK is the reverse. Without the round trip you find the sign error on hardware. Without workspace sampling you write a demo script whose waypoints happen to sit in a low-manipulability region and then blame the controller when the arm shudders. Without the continuity test you ship an executor that occasionally flips branches at 180 deg/s.
components.interface: Pure functions in, numbers out. Runs in CI on a laptop in seconds.
components.rate: Every commit.
components.evidence: The team already built the scaffolding for this: open_manipulator/docker/workspace/dummy_exec/omx_kinematics.py plus a `--dry-run` path in chunk_executor_node.py ('Run without ROS to check the maths: python chunk_executor_node.py --dry-run'). That dry-run flag is the right instinct; it should become a pytest under a `test/` directory so CI runs it.

components.name: Stage 3 — mock_components/GenericSystem: the whole node graph, zero hardware
components.role: Flip one xacro arg and the ros2_control hardware plugin becomes `mock_components/GenericSystem`, which mirrors every command interface straight back to the corresponding state interface. Everything above it — controller_manager, JointTrajectoryController, joint_state_broadcaster, robot_state_publisher, MoveIt, your executor node, RViz — runs completely unchanged.
components.whyItExists: This is the single highest-leverage step in the whole arc and the one beginners skip. It proves: the controller spawns and activates; the joint names in your YAML match the joint names in your URDF (a mismatch here is the #1 'controller failed to activate' cause); the JointTrajectory you publish is accepted and not rejected for a velocity/timestamp violation; the TF tree is complete; your topic remappings are right; MoveIt's controller manager can talk to your action server. None of that needs physics, let alone metal. It costs nothing to run and it catches perhaps 70% of integration bugs. ros2_control's own documentation states the recommendation flatly: develop with mock hardware first, then simulation, then real hardware.
components.interface: Identical to real hardware: command interfaces in, state interfaces out, /joint_states at the controller_manager update_rate, /arm_controller/follow_joint_trajectory action server.
components.rate: controller_manager `update_rate: 100` Hz — the mock loop runs at the real loop's rate, so timing-shaped bugs still show up.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_description/ros2_control/omx_f.ros2_control.xacro: `<xacro:if value="${use_mock_hardware}"><plugin>mock_components/GenericSystem</plugin><param name="mock_sensor_commands">…</param><param name="state_following_offset">0.0</param></xacro:if>`. Launch it with `ros2 launch open_manipulator_bringup omx_f.launch.py use_mock_hardware:=true start_rviz:=true`. https://control.ros.org/jazzy/doc/ros2_control/hardware_interface/doc/mock_components_userdoc.html

components.name: Stage 3b — Physics simulation (Gazebo Harmonic / MuJoCo / Isaac), and its honest limits
components.role: Add contact, gravity, inertia and a camera. Gazebo Harmonic is the ROS 2 Jazzy pairing and integrates through gz_ros2_control, so again the SAME controller stack runs on top. MuJoCo is the imitation-learning community's default (fast, good contact, ROBOTIS ships MuJoCo models in robotis_mujoco_menagerie). Isaac Sim/Lab is where you go for photorealistic rendering and massively parallel RL rollouts.
components.whyItExists: Mock hardware cannot tell you whether the gripper will actually hold the object, whether the arm droops under its own weight, or whether the planned path sweeps through the table. Sim answers those cheaply. But be explicit about what sim does NOT catch, because this is where teams lose months: it will not reproduce your serial bus's timing, your servo's PID response, stiction at low velocity, backlash, thermal torque derating, camera exposure and rolling shutter, or gravity droop of a specific gearbox. Your arm's URDF rates every joint `effort="1000"` — a thousand newton-metres, versus roughly 1.5 Nm stall on an XL430 — so any Gazebo run using those numbers is simulating a robot that does not exist.
components.interface: gz_ros2_control's `gz_ros2_control/GazeboSimSystem` presents the identical hardware_interface API; the plugin block is parameterised by the same controller YAML.
components.rate: Sim steps at its own dt; ros2_control still runs at 100 Hz against it; `use_sim_time: true` must be set on every node or TF timestamps diverge.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_description/urdf/omx_f/omx_f.urdf.xacro embeds `<plugin filename="gz_ros2_control-system" name="gz_ros2_control::GazeboSimROS2ControlPlugin">` pointing at the same hardware_controller_manager.yaml; ready-made launch at open_manipulator_bringup/launch/omx_f_gazebo.launch.py and world at open_manipulator_bringup/worlds/empty_world.sdf. https://control.ros.org/jazzy/doc/simulators/simulators.html

components.name: Stage 4 — First hardware session: read-only before write, harmless write before motion
components.role: A strict ladder, each rung proving one thing. (a) Power the arm, confirm the bus enumerates: `ls -l /dev/ttyACM*`, `dmesg | tail`. (b) With the ROS stack STOPPED, run a read-only scan: ping every ID, dump the control table, read Present Position. (c) Torque OFF, backdrive the arm by hand, watch the positions change — this proves your tick-to-radian conversion and your ID-to-joint mapping simultaneously, and costs nothing. (d) Write something harmless: an LED, or Return Delay Time. (e) Torque ON one joint, command +2 degrees, with a finger on the power switch. (f) All joints, small amplitude. (g) Only then hand the bus to ros2_control.
components.whyItExists: Three specific failures. The port is exclusive: two processes on /dev/ttyACM0 produce checksum errors that look like a hardware fault but are a teammate's node — so the discipline is 'one owner of the bus, and you know who it is before you start'. The ID-to-joint mapping is nowhere in the vendor description as a statement; it is POSITIONAL, inferred from the order of gpio blocks, so guessing wrong means joint3's command goes to joint4's servo. And torque-on-first is how people bend links: the arm snaps from wherever gravity left it to whatever Goal Position was stale in RAM.
components.interface: Raw DYNAMIXEL Protocol 2.0 over half-duplex serial. Addresses that matter: Torque Enable 64 (1 byte), Present Position 132 (4), Goal Position 116 (4), Min/Max Position Limit 52/48 (4), Operating Mode 11 (1), Position P/I/D Gain 84/82/80 (2).
components.rate: Human-paced. Deliberately.
components.evidence: The team already wrote exactly this tool: open_manipulator/docker/workspace/dummy_exec/omx_probe.py — 'Writes nothing, moves nothing… Run with the ros2_control stack STOPPED -- only one process may hold the port.' It resolves the three things its own docstring names: which joint is which DXL id, what the real limits are, and whether ticks convert correctly (CENTER=2048, TICKS_PER_TURN=4096, `(ticks-2048)/4096*2π`). IDs 11..16 map to joint1..joint5 + gripper.

components.name: Stage 4b — Handing the bus to ros2_control, and the register-push that fixes 'RAM resets on power cycle'
components.role: Swap the mock plugin for the real one and let the hardware interface own the port. The right hardware plugin does not just read and write positions — it PUSHES the full per-servo configuration (operating mode, gains, profile velocity/acceleration, current limits, position limits) into each servo at activation, every time.
components.whyItExists: DYNAMIXEL RAM registers (Position P/I/D Gain, Profile Velocity/Acceleration, Goal Current, Torque Enable) revert to their EEPROM defaults on every power cycle. If your code assumes the gains you set last Tuesday are still there, the arm behaves differently after someone unplugs it, and you spend a day debugging a 'flaky' controller. The cure is not to remember to re-set them; it is to make activation idempotent — declare the desired register state in config and push it every time. That is precisely what the `<gpio>` blocks are. The second thing this plugin gets right is `disable_torque_at_init: true`: the stack comes up torque-off, reads the true positions, and only then enables — which is Stage 4's discipline encoded in software. Third, `is_async="true"` decouples the serial read/write thread from the 100 Hz control loop, because a sync-read plus sync-write of 6 servos on a half-duplex 1 Mbps bus does not reliably fit inside 10 ms.
components.interface: In: `robot_description` (which carries the ros2_control block) + hardware_controller_manager.yaml. Out: /joint_states at 100 Hz via joint_state_broadcaster; services dynamixel_hardware_interface/{set_dxl_torque, reboot_dxl, get_dxl_data, set_dxl_data}; /dynamixel_hardware_interface/dxl_state.
components.rate: 100 Hz control loop; serial I/O asynchronous to it.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_description/ros2_control/omx_f.ros2_control.xacro: `<ros2_control name="${name}" type="system" is_async="true">`, plugin `dynamixel_hardware_interface/DynamixelHardware`, params port_name, `baud_rate=1000000`, `error_timeout_ms=500`, `disable_torque_at_init=true`, `number_of_joints=6`; then one `<gpio name="dxl11">`…`<gpio name="dxl16">` block per servo carrying ID, Operating Mode, Return Delay Time 0, Position P/I/D Gain 1000/0/1000, Profile Velocity 50, Profile Acceleration 25, and for dxl16 `Current Limit 600`, `Goal Current 600`, `Shutdown 21`.

components.name: Stage 5 — Calibration part 1: joint zero / homing offsets
components.role: Establish the mapping from raw encoder ticks to the URDF's joint angle convention. Physically place the arm in a known pose (a machined jig, a straightedge, or the mechanical hard stops), read the ticks, and store the offset. Verify by commanding the URDF's named 'home' pose and measuring the real arm against the RViz render.
components.whyItExists: Everything downstream is a rigid-body chain, so a constant offset on joint2 translates into a position error at the tip that grows with reach and rotates with configuration — it will never look like a constant offset, it will look like 'IK is inaccurate'. Doing this AFTER the URDF is validated and BEFORE any data collection is mandatory, because a demonstration dataset recorded against a wrong zero is unusable: the policy learns the offset as part of the task.
components.interface: Out: a per-joint offset (ticks or radians) stored in config, applied in exactly one place.
components.rate: Once per mechanical rebuild, and re-verified after any servo swap or horn re-seat.
components.evidence: The mechanism exists in the vendor stack as `offsets` on the broadcaster: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_l_leader_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml → joint_trajectory_command_broadcaster has `offsets: [0.0 x6]` and `reverse_joints: [gripper_joint_1]`. Named poses to check against are in open_manipulator_moveit_config/config/omx_f/omx_f.srdf ('init' all-zeros, 'home' [0,-1.57,1.57,1.57,0]) and open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_f/initial_positions.yaml (step1/step2 with duration 5.0, epsilon 0.15).

components.name: Stage 5b — Calibration part 2: gravity and friction identification
components.role: Identify the per-joint torque needed to hold the arm against gravity and the Coulomb/viscous friction that has to be overcome before a joint moves at all. Practically: sweep each joint slowly in both directions, record commanded current versus velocity, and fit. The result is a set of scalars in the controller config.
components.whyItExists: Two consumers. First, a leader arm in a teleoperation rig must feel weightless in the operator's hand, which means a controller cancelling gravity and stiction in real time — without it the operator fights the arm and the demonstrations are jerky, which the policy then imitates. Second, gravity droop is a real position error on the follower: this team already hit it, where the arm settled ~6.5 mm short of a waypoint whose tolerance was 4 mm and the script deadlocked. That is a calibration problem masquerading as a control problem.
components.interface: Out: per-joint scalars consumed by an effort-mode controller; in: position and velocity state interfaces.
components.rate: Controller runs at the 100 Hz loop rate; identification itself is an offline fit.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_l_leader_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml → gravity_compensation_controller with `command_interfaces: [effort]`, `torque_scaling_factors: [200.0, 350.0, 300.0, 300.0, 300.0]`, `kinetic_friction_scalars: [0.0005, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15]`, `friction_compensation_velocity_thresholds: [100.0, 3.5, 3.5, 3.5, 3.5, 3.5]`. Note joint1's friction scalar is 300x smaller than the rest — joint1 rotates about the vertical axis and carries no gravity load, which is the physics showing up in the config. Implementation: open_manipulator/ros2_controller/om_gravity_compensation_controller/src/gravity_compensation_controller.cpp

components.name: Stage 5c — Calibration part 3: camera intrinsics, then hand-eye extrinsics (strictly in that order)
components.role: First solve the camera alone: checkerboard or ChArUco, `ros2 run camera_calibration cameracalibrator`, producing fx, fy, cx, cy and distortion coefficients published on camera_info. Only then solve where the camera sits relative to the robot: eye-in-hand (camera bolted to the wrist — solve T_flange_camera) or eye-to-base / eye-to-hand (camera on a tripod — solve T_base_camera). Collect 15+ well-spread poses, check that the estimate has converged, and publish the result as a static_transform_publisher in your launch.
components.whyItExists: The order is forced by the mathematics: hand-eye solves AX = XB where the B terms come from the camera's estimate of the target pose, and that estimate is computed using the intrinsics. Bad intrinsics silently poison the extrinsics and you get an answer that converges confidently to the wrong transform. Eye-in-hand versus eye-to-base is not a preference — it changes which TF edge you are solving for and which link the result attaches to, and getting it backwards produces a transform that is self-consistent and useless. Expect roughly 1-3 mm and under a degree with a good rig and a rigid mount; a 3D-printed bracket that flexes puts a hard floor under your accuracy that no amount of sampling removes.
components.interface: Out: sensor_msgs/CameraInfo (intrinsics) and one /tf_static edge (extrinsics). In: image stream + a known-geometry target.
components.rate: Once per optics or mount change. Re-verify after anything is unbolted.
components.evidence: Camera launch files already present: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_bringup/launch/camera_realsense.launch.py and camera_usb_cam.launch.py; the Dockerfile installs librealsense, realsense-ros pinned to r/4.56.4 at commit cbd8b8487d, `ros-jazzy-usb-cam` and `ros-jazzy-image-transport-plugins`. Tools: ROS 2 `camera_calibration`; https://github.com/marcoesposito1988/easy_handeye2 (ROS 2 port, supports eye-in-hand and eye-on-base, can auto-move the robot via MoveIt to sample); moveit_calibration provides an RViz plugin for the same job.

components.name: Stage 6 — Teleoperation before autonomy: leader-follower and why it comes first
components.role: Stand up a human-in-the-loop path: a leader arm (gravity-compensated, backdrivable, torque-off-ish) whose joint states are broadcast as a command stream, and a follower running a JointTrajectoryController that tracks it. Get a human doing the task through the robot, reliably, dozens of times.
components.whyItExists: Four reasons, in order of importance. (1) It proves the task is physically possible with this gripper and this workspace — if a skilled human cannot do it through the arm, no policy will. (2) It is your data source; imitation learning has no substitute for demonstrations. (3) It exercises the entire real-time path at task speed with a human safety monitor holding the leader, so failures are recoverable. (4) It defines the action space: whatever the leader publishes IS what the policy will be trained to emit, so the representation choice gets made here, empirically, rather than being invented later at training time. Notice the follower_ai config folds the gripper into the SAME JointTrajectoryController as the arm, unlike the standalone config which gives the gripper its own GripperActionController — because for imitation you need the gripper commanded at the same timestamps as the arm, not through a separate asynchronous action server.
components.interface: Leader publishes joint_trajectory_command_broadcaster output; follower's arm_controller consumes trajectory_msgs/JointTrajectory. Both sides run their own controller_manager at 100 Hz, in separate processes, on separate serial ports.
components.rate: 100 Hz command stream; recording typically downsampled to 25-30 Hz to match the camera.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_bringup/launch/omx_ai.launch.py orchestrates the three-step sequence (follower up → joint_trajectory_executor drives it to the init pose → leader up) using RegisterEventHandler/OnProcessStart/OnProcessExit; leader at open_manipulator_bringup/launch/omx_l_leader_ai.launch.py defaults `port_name:=/dev/ttyACM2` while the follower defaults /dev/ttyACM0 — two arms, two ports, one bus each. Follower config open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml lists `joints: [joint1..joint5, gripper_joint_1]` all under arm_controller.

components.name: Stage 6b — Time synchronisation and dataset format
components.role: Decide the canonical clock and stamp everything against it. Cameras and joint streams arrive on different threads with different latencies; you must either hardware-trigger, or use message_filters ApproximateTimeSynchronizer with an explicit slop, or record raw with honest header stamps and align offline. Then write to a format the training code reads natively.
components.whyItExists: A 50 ms constant offset between image and action teaches the policy to act 50 ms early, which on a 40 ms control step is more than one action step of pure, systematic, unrecoverable error — and it looks exactly like 'the policy is a bit imprecise'. This is the single most common silent killer in imitation-learning datasets. Format choice matters less than consistency, but it matters: ALOHA-lineage code uses per-episode HDF5; the Hugging Face ecosystem uses LeRobotDataset, whose v3.0 revision moved from one parquet file per episode to chunked parquet with many episodes per file, MP4 video shards per camera, and unified parquet metadata — and requires an explicit `dataset.finalize()` or the parquet writers never close and the dataset silently will not load. rosbag2 is the ROS-native capture and remains the right thing to record alongside, because it captures the FULL graph including the topics you did not know you would need.
components.interface: In: /joint_states, /…/joint_trajectory, /camera/color/image_raw, /camera/color/camera_info, /tf. Out: an MCAP/sqlite3 bag and/or a LeRobotDataset on disk.
components.rate: Cameras 30 Hz, joints 100 Hz, recorded episodes typically resampled to a single 25-30 Hz timeline.
components.evidence: `ros2 bag record -a -o pick_001` (default storage MCAP in Jazzy), `ros2 bag info`, `ros2 bag play --clock`. ROBOTIS's own data-collection layer is https://github.com/ROBOTIS-GIT/physical_ai_tools, referenced from open_manipulator/README.md. LeRobotDataset v3.0 spec: https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/en/lerobot-dataset-v3 and https://huggingface.co/blog/lerobot-datasets-v3 ; ROS 2 bridges: https://github.com/ycheng517/lerobot-ros and https://github.com/sacovo/lerobot_ros

components.name: Stage 7 — Policy inference node, latency budget, and the safety wrapper
components.role: Wrap the trained model in a ROS 2 node that: reads observations, runs inference, decodes an action chunk, executes the first k steps of it, then replans (receding horizon). Around that, put a wrapper that validates every number before it reaches the controller.
components.whyItExists: Three distinct pressures. Latency: a chunk of H steps at DT seconds gives you H*DT of lookahead; inference must finish well inside k*DT or the arm runs off the end of the chunk and stutters. Chunking exists precisely so inference latency and control rate are decoupled — you buy H*DT of slack with one forward pass. Receding horizon (execute k < H, then replan) exists because executing the whole chunk makes the robot open-loop for H*DT and it cannot react; replanning every step makes the commanded trajectory jitter as successive chunks disagree. The safety wrapper exists because a neural network's output is an arbitrary float vector: it must be checked against joint limits, per-step velocity, workspace bounds, and IK feasibility, and rejected with a LOGGED REASON, before it becomes a JointTrajectory. Where inference runs is a real architectural choice — on the Jetson beside the controller (lowest latency, hardest deployment) or on a workstation over the network (easier iteration, adds a variable network delay into the loop that you must measure, not assume).
components.interface: In: /joint_states + camera topics. Out: trajectory_msgs/JointTrajectory to the follower's arm_controller (or a remapped topic). Internal boundary: `chunk = policy(observation)` returning [H, action_dim].
components.rate: H=16, DT=0.04 s → 0.64 s of lookahead; replan every 3 steps → 8.3 Hz inference, 120 ms budget per forward pass.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/docker/workspace/dummy_exec/chunk_executor_node.py — `H = 16`, `DT = 0.04`, `EXECUTE_STEPS = 3`, `PUBLISH_STEPS = 8`, `MAX_JOINT_VEL = radians(180.0)`, `TIME_SCALE = 2.0`. Its comments record two hard-won mechanisms worth generalising: JointTrajectoryController falls back to LINEAR interpolation when a point has no velocity (so supply velocities to get the cubic spline back), and the FINAL point must have zero velocity or JTC rejects the entire message (`allow_nonzero_velocity_at_trajectory_end` defaults false) — hence publishing 8 steps but executing 3, keeping the zero-velocity tail beyond the replan point. dummy_policy.py is the stand-in with the same signature, which is the right way to build this: the executor is fully debugged before the model exists.

components.name: Stage 8 — The observability toolbox, and when you reach for each
components.role: A small set of tools, each answering a different question. `ros2 node list` / `ros2 topic list`: does the thing exist. `rqt_graph`: who is connected to whom (the fastest way to spot a missing remap or a QoS mismatch showing as an absent edge). `ros2 topic hz` and `ros2 topic info -v`: is it publishing at the rate you think, with the QoS you think — QoS incompatibility is silent by design, so hz returning nothing on a topic that exists is the classic symptom. `ros2 topic echo --once`: what is the actual payload. `ros2 control list_hardware_interfaces` / `list_controllers`: which interfaces are claimed and which controller is active (this is where 'the controller spawned but nothing moves' resolves). `ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames` and `ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo a b`: is the TF tree connected and is the transform what you expect. PlotJuggler: overlay commanded versus measured joint positions on one time axis — this is how tracking error, latency and oscillation become visible rather than felt. `ros2 bag record` then replay into PlotJuggler: the only way to debug an intermittent failure you cannot reproduce on demand. `ros2 doctor --report`: environment sanity (RMW, domain id, network).
components.whyItExists: Every one of these replaces a guess with a measurement. The discipline is to reach for them in order of cheapness and to STOP GUESSING after the first surprising reading. Most multi-day robotics debugging sessions are a team reasoning about what the graph should be doing while a 5-second rqt_graph would have shown them an unconnected edge.
components.interface: All read-only observers on the same DDS/zenoh graph.
components.rate: Interactive.
components.evidence: `ros2 control list_controllers` against the controller_manager configured in open_manipulator/open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_f/hardware_controller_manager.yaml should show joint_state_broadcaster, arm_controller and gripper_controller all `active`. `ros2 topic hz /joint_states` should read ~100 Hz, matching `update_rate: 100`. Note the RViz caveat this team already documented in docker/docker-compose.override.yml: a window that exists but paints nothing is a GL driver problem (LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 forces llvmpipe), not a ROS problem — which is itself a lesson in isolating the layer before debugging it.

components.name: Stage 9 — Testing and CI: the three tiers, and the one that can only be tested on metal
components.role: Tier 1, pure unit tests with no ROS: kinematics round-trips, action decoding, the safety wrapper's reject logic. Fast, run on every commit, no hardware, no network. Tier 2, launch_testing: bring up the real launch file against mock_components, wait for controllers to reach 'active', publish a trajectory, assert /joint_states converges. This tests the WIRING — joint names, remaps, parameter files, spawn ordering — which is where most integration bugs live. Tier 3, on-metal: current draw, thermal derating, bus timing under load, contact forces, gravity droop, repeatability over hundreds of cycles.
components.whyItExists: The split is defined by what each tier can possibly observe. A unit test can prove your IK is correct but can never prove your YAML joint names match your URDF. launch_testing can prove that, but can never prove the servo will hold 200 g at full extension without overheating. Trying to test tier-3 things in tier 1 produces elaborate mocks that pass while the robot fails; trying to test tier-1 things on hardware wastes the scarcest resource you have. The vendor repo is an honest illustration of the gap: its CI runs `rosdep check` as a hard gate and eight ament linters as a matrix, and builds every package — but ships no launch_testing and essentially no unit tests, which is typical of vendor stacks and is exactly the gap a capstone team should fill for their own code.
components.interface: In: source tree. Out: pass/fail per package, per linter, per test.
components.rate: Every push and pull request.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/.github/workflows/ros-ci.yml — ros-tooling/setup-ros@v0.7 + ros-tooling/action-ros-ci@v0.3, target jazzy on ubuntu:noble, `vcs-repo-file-url` pointing at open_manipulator_ci.repos, and an explicit `rosdep check --from-paths ros_ws/src --ignore-src` that exits 1 on failure. open_manipulator/.github/workflows/ros-lint.yml — a matrix of cppcheck, cpplint, uncrustify, flake8, pep257, lint_cmake, xmllint, copyright. Local equivalents: `colcon test --packages-select <pkg>` then `colcon test-result --verbose`.

orderOfOperations: 1. Pin the environment before writing robot code. Create the colcon workspace, the Dockerfile with the ROS distro pinned, and the .repos file with dependency commits pinned. PROVES: every subsequent failure is a change you made, not a change apt made. If you skip this, every later bisect is contaminated — you cannot tell a regression in your code from a silent upgrade of ros2_controllers.

2. Fix the host plumbing next: udev rules for the serial device (including latency_timer=1), container privileges for real-time scheduling, and the RMW/domain settings identical everywhere. PROVES: the transport and the device path are constants. This must precede any node work because a discovery failure and a logic failure look identical from inside a node, and you will burn days attributing one to the other. This is the layer where the 'zenoh router must exist first' and 'teammate's process owns the port' surprises live — they are environment facts, so pin them as environment facts.

3. Write the URDF/xacro. PROVES: the geometry is stated once, in a form every consumer reads. It goes before kinematics because your FK is a claim ABOUT this description, and before simulation because sim loads it, and before hardware because the ros2_control joint list is embedded in it. There is no version of this order where description is not first — it is the root of the dependency graph, literally and figuratively.

4. Validate the URDF in four ascending steps before trusting anything on it: xacro expands → check_urdf passes → urdf_to_graphiz matches the physical chain → joint_state_publisher_gui + RViz shows correct axes, senses and limits. PROVES, in order: syntax, topology, geometry, sign. Each check is cheaper than the next and each failure it catches would otherwise surface as a subtle numerical error three stages later. Run `ros2 launch open_manipulator_description omx_f.launch.py` — no controllers, no hardware. The reason for this order is that a sign error found by dragging a slider costs ten seconds; the same error found as 'IK does not converge on the real arm' costs a week.

5. Simplify collision geometry and write the SRDF (groups, named poses, allowed-collision matrix). PROVES: the planner can evaluate a state in microseconds rather than milliseconds, and that adjacent links touching does not read as a collision. Do this immediately after the URDF and before any planning, because 'start state in collision' with a missing ACM is an unfalsifiable-looking error that stops everything.

6. Build and TEST kinematics off-robot. Round-trip FK→IK→FK on poses (not joint vectors), sample the workspace for success rate and solve time, and check branch continuity along dense paths. PROVES: your maths is right, independently of ROS, hardware, timing and transport. This precedes bringup because kinematics failures and hardware failures produce the same symptom — the arm goes to the wrong place — and you want exactly one candidate explanation at a time. For an underactuated arm, also decide and write down the 6-DOF→5-DOF projection here, so an unreachable orientation becomes a logged rejection instead of a silent error.

7. Bring up the ENTIRE node graph on mock_components/GenericSystem before any physics and before any metal. One xacro arg: `use_mock_hardware:=true`. PROVES: controllers spawn and activate, joint names in YAML match joint names in URDF, your JointTrajectory messages are accepted, remaps are correct, the TF tree is complete, MoveIt can reach your action server. This is the highest-value step in the arc and the most commonly skipped one. It goes before simulation because it is faster to start, has no physics to misconfigure, and isolates a strictly smaller set of causes — if something breaks here it is wiring, full stop.

8. Then physics simulation (Gazebo Harmonic via gz_ros2_control, or MuJoCo). PROVES: contact, gravity and reachability against a table; your planned paths do not sweep through the world. It comes after mock because sim adds an entire new failure surface (world SDF, physics parameters, use_sim_time on every node) and you do not want to debug that surface simultaneously with your controller config. Be explicit about the ceiling: sim will not reproduce serial bus timing, servo PID response, stiction, backlash, thermal derating, or camera exposure — and in this repo it cannot even reproduce torque limits, because the URDF rates every joint at effort=1000 Nm against roughly 1.5 Nm of real stall torque.

9. First hardware session, as a strict ladder with the ROS stack STOPPED: enumerate the device → read-only scan of every servo ID and control table → torque OFF and backdrive by hand, watching positions change → write something harmless → torque ON one joint, +2 degrees → all joints, small amplitude. PROVES, rung by rung: the bus works; the ID-to-joint mapping (which the vendor xacro never states — it is positional); the tick-to-radian conversion AND the mapping simultaneously and for free; write path works; one closed loop works; all six coexist on one half-duplex bus. The ordering principle here is the whole discipline in one line: read before write, harmless write before motion, one joint before six, small before large.

10. Hand the bus to ros2_control with a hardware plugin that pushes full register configuration at every activation and starts with torque disabled. PROVES: the stack owns the port exclusively, and the servo configuration is idempotent rather than remembered. This directly closes the 'RAM registers silently reset on power cycle' failure — not by remembering to re-set gains, but by declaring the desired register state in the ros2_control <gpio> blocks so activation re-establishes it every single time.

11. Calibrate, and calibrate in this internal order: joint zeros first, then gravity/friction, then camera intrinsics, then hand-eye extrinsics. Joint zeros first because every later measurement is expressed in joint space and a constant offset propagates into everything as a configuration-dependent tip error. Gravity/friction next because it is what makes a leader arm backdrivable and what explains follower droop (this team already lost time to ~6.5 mm of droop against a 4 mm tolerance). Intrinsics strictly before extrinsics, because hand-eye solves AX=XB where the B terms are computed FROM the intrinsics — bad intrinsics produce a confidently converged and completely wrong extrinsic.

12. Teleoperate before you automate. Stand up leader-follower, gravity-compensate the leader, and have a human do the task through the robot dozens of times. PROVES: the task is physically achievable with this gripper and this workspace; the real-time path holds at task speed with a human able to stop it; and — critically — it DEFINES the action space, because whatever the leader publishes is what the policy will be trained to emit. Attempting autonomy before this means you are simultaneously validating the task, the pipeline and the model, and cannot attribute a failure to any of them.

13. Nail time synchronisation BEFORE recording a single episode you intend to train on. Decide the canonical clock, stamp honestly, and measure the camera-to-joint offset rather than assuming it is zero. PROVES: the dataset does not contain a systematic lie. A 50 ms constant offset on a 40 ms control step is more than one full action step of unrecoverable error baked into every episode, and it is invisible in the data — you will only see it as a policy that is mysteriously 'imprecise'. Re-recording a dataset is expensive; discovering the offset afterwards means every episode is worthless.

14. Record, then train, then deploy inference behind a safety wrapper. Build the executor against a DUMMY policy with the real signature first, so the receding-horizon path (anchor → compose → project → IK → publish → replan) is fully debugged before a model exists. PROVES: the deployment path is correct independently of model quality, so when the real policy underperforms you know it is the policy. The wrapper validates every number — joint limits, per-step velocity, workspace bounds, IK feasibility — and rejects with a logged reason, because a network's output is an arbitrary float vector and must be treated as untrusted input to the control layer.

15. Instrument continuously, not at the end. Reach for tools cheapest-first — `ros2 node list`, `rqt_graph`, `ros2 topic hz`, `ros2 topic info -v`, `ros2 control list_controllers`, `tf2_echo`, then PlotJuggler for commanded-vs-measured overlays, then rosbag2 record/replay for anything intermittent. The rule is: stop guessing after the first surprising reading. Most multi-day robotics debugging is a team reasoning about what the graph should be doing while a five-second rqt_graph would have shown an unconnected edge.

16.
