Keep three tiers of tests running the whole way, added as each layer is built rather than retrofitted: pure unit tests for kinematics and decoding (every commit, seconds), launch_testing against mock hardware for wiring (every PR, minutes), and a documented on-metal checklist for what only hardware can answer — current draw, thermal derating, bus timing under load, contact forces, repeatability over hundreds of cycles. The tiers are defined by what each can possibly observe, so a test placed in the wrong tier either passes while the robot fails or wastes your scarcest resource.
keyFacts: The controller loop for this arm is 100 Hz (`update_rate: 100` in open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_f/hardware_controller_manager.yaml), i.e. a 10 ms budget per cycle, on a half-duplex DYNAMIXEL bus at 1,000,000 baud with six servos. That is why the ros2_control block is declared `is_async="true"` — serial I/O runs on its own thread so a slow bus transaction cannot overrun the control cycle.

The default FTDI/USB-serial latency_timer is 16 ms, which alone caps your round-trip rate at about 60 Hz. The vendor udev rule sets it to 1: `ATTR{device/latency_timer}="1"` in open_manipulator_bringup/open-manipulator-cdc.rules. This single byte is the difference between a 100 Hz loop and mystery jitter.

Joint limits genuinely live in THREE places in this repo and they disagree. (a) URDF: `lower="${-pi*2.0}" upper="${pi*2.0}"` on every joint — effectively unlimited. (b) DYNAMIXEL registers in the ros2_control xacro: dxl12/joint2 `Min Position Limit 830`, `Max Position Limit 3129`, which at 4096 ticks per revolution centred on 2048 is -1.868 rad (-107.1 deg) to +1.658 rad (+95.0 deg); dxl13/joint3 is 1024..3140 = -1.571 rad (-90.0 deg) to +1.675 rad (+96.0 deg). (c) MoveIt joint_limits.yaml sets no position limits at all, and sets `max_velocity: 5.0` which is HIGHER than the URDF's `velocity="4.8"`. The servo registers are the only ones the hardware actually enforces.

Servo-to-joint mapping is positional and stated nowhere in prose: DXL IDs 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 map to joint1..joint5 plus the gripper, inferred purely from the order of `<gpio>` blocks in open_manipulator_description/ros2_control/omx_f.ros2_control.xacro.

Operating modes differ per joint and matter: dxl11 (joint1) runs Operating Mode 4 = extended position (multi-turn, no limits); dxl12-15 run mode 3 = position; dxl16 (gripper) runs mode 5 = current-based position with `Current Limit 600` and `Goal Current 600`, which is how the gripper grasps compliantly instead of crushing or stalling.

`disable_torque_at_init: true` in the hardware plugin config means the stack comes up torque-off, reads true positions, then enables. This is the 'torque off first, read before write' discipline encoded in configuration rather than in a human's memory.

DYNAMIXEL RAM registers (Position P/I/D Gain, Profile Velocity/Acceleration, Goal Current, Torque Enable) revert to EEPROM defaults on every power cycle. The fix is not to remember — it is the `<gpio>` blocks, which the hardware interface pushes at every activation, making bringup idempotent.

`position_only_ik: True` in open_manipulator_moveit_config/config/omx_f/kinematics.yaml is MoveIt's answer to 5 DOF: it zeroes the orientation rows of the Jacobian so KDL only chases position. KDL's timeout there is 5 ms per call, which for an H=16 action chunk is up to 80 ms of worst-case latency inside a 40 ms control step — the arithmetic argument for analytic IK in an imitation-learning executor.

This repo's collision geometry is NOT simplified — `<visual>` and `<collision>` reference the identical high-poly STL for every link. The consequence is visible in the repo: a separate C++ node (open_manipulator_collision) re-approximates the arm as FCL capsules to get a runtime self-collision check that is fast enough to run per JointState.

The URDF rates every joint `effort="1000"` (1000 Nm) against roughly 1.5 Nm of real stall torque on an XL430. Any Gazebo run or gravity-compensation calculation that trusts that number is simulating a robot that does not exist.

Gravity compensation is calibrated per joint and the numbers show the physics: `kinetic_friction_scalars: [0.0005, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15]` — joint1's is 300x smaller than the rest because joint1 rotates about the vertical axis and carries no gravity load. `torque_scaling_factors: [200.0, 350.0, 300.0, 300.0, 300.0]`.

The imitation-learning follower config puts the gripper in the SAME JointTrajectoryController as the arm (`joints: [joint1..joint5, gripper_joint_1]` in config/omx_f_follower_ai/), whereas the standalone config gives it a separate `position_controllers/GripperActionController`. The reason is timestamp alignment: a policy emits arm and gripper at the same instants, so they must be commanded through one message.

JointTrajectoryController falls back to LINEAR interpolation when a trajectory point carries no velocity, putting a velocity discontinuity at every waypoint; and it REJECTS the entire message if the final point has nonzero velocity (`allow_nonzero_velocity_at_trajectory_end` defaults to false). The standard workaround is to publish further ahead than you execute, so the zero-velocity tail always sits beyond the replan point.

Receding horizon arithmetic for this team's executor: H=16 steps, DT=0.04 s → 0.64 s of lookahead per chunk; executing 3 steps before replanning → 8.3 Hz inference, a 120 ms budget per forward pass. Chunking exists specifically to decouple inference latency from control rate.

LeRobotDataset v3.0 changed the on-disk layout: chunked parquet with MANY episodes per file (data/chunk-000/file-000.parquet) instead of one file per episode, MP4 video shards per camera, unified parquet metadata instead of scattered JSON — and it requires an explicit `dataset.finalize()` or the parquet writers never close and the dataset silently fails to load. https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/en/lerobot-dataset-v3

The vendor's CI (.github/workflows/) gates on `rosdep check` exiting nonzero and runs eight ament linters as a matrix (cppcheck, cpplint, uncrustify, flake8, pep257, lint_cmake, xmllint, copyright), but ships no launch_testing and essentially no unit tests. That is typical of vendor stacks and is exactly the gap a team should fill for its own code.

ros2_control's own documentation states the development order explicitly: start with mock hardware, then move to simulation, then to real hardware. https://control.ros.org/jazzy/doc/ros2_control/hardware_interface/doc/mock_components_userdoc.html

Gazebo Harmonic is the version paired with ROS 2 Jazzy, integrated through gz_ros2_control, which presents the identical hardware_interface API — so the same controllers and the same YAML run against mock, sim and metal. https://control.ros.org/jazzy/doc/simulators/simulators.html
beginnerMistakes: Skipping mock hardware entirely and going URDF → real arm. This is the single most expensive mistake available. You then debug controller activation, joint-name mismatches, remaps, QoS, TF and your own logic simultaneously with servo limits, bus timing and gravity. Correct habit: `use_mock_hardware:=true` is the second thing you run after the description-only launch, and you do not touch the arm until the full graph is green against it.

Trusting the URDF without validating it, because it came from the vendor. Vendor descriptions ship with real defects — in this one, collision meshes are unsimplified and effort limits are off by roughly three orders of magnitude. Correct habit: run check_urdf, urdf_to_graphiz and the slider GUI on any description you did not derive yourself, and read the numbers, not just the picture.

Reading joint limits from the datasheet or the URDF and believing them. Correct habit: read them off the servo, from the machine, with a read-only probe, and treat the servo registers as authoritative because they are the only ones that physically stop the arm. Write down which source wins and put it in a comment.

Enabling torque before reading positions. The arm snaps from wherever gravity left it to whatever stale Goal Position is in RAM. Correct habit: torque off → read → verify → torque on one joint → small move. Configure it rather than remember it (`disable_torque_at_init: true`).

Letting two processes open /dev/ttyACM0. The symptom is checksum and timeout errors that look exactly like a loose cable or a dying servo. Correct habit: exactly one owner of the bus at a time, and make 'is the stack running?' the first question of every hardware debugging session — as this team's own omx_probe.py docstring already says.

Treating IK as solved because it returned a number. Correct habit: round-trip in POSE space (FK→IK→FK, compare transforms, not joint vectors, because multiple joint vectors map to one pose), and sample the workspace so you know where IK is reliable before you write waypoints into a demo script.

Asking a 5-DOF arm for a 6-DOF pose and not noticing. Correct habit: write the projection from SE(3) to the reachable 5-manifold as an explicit named function with a residual you threshold and log, so an unreachable request is a logged rejection rather than a silent 15-degree error.

Assuming camera and joint streams are synchronised because they arrive close together. Correct habit: measure the offset before recording anything you plan to train on, and treat a constant offset as a dataset-destroying bug, not a rounding error. On a 40 ms control step, 50 ms of skew is more than one full action step of systematic error baked into every episode.

Calibrating hand-eye extrinsics before camera intrinsics have converged. The optimiser will happily converge to a confident, wrong transform. Correct habit: intrinsics first, verify reprojection error, then 15+ well-spread poses for extrinsics, then check convergence of the estimate rather than accepting the first answer.

Debugging by reading code and reasoning about what the graph should be doing. Correct habit: rqt_graph, `ros2 topic hz`, `ros2 control list_controllers`, `tf2_echo` — cheapest first — and stop guessing the moment a reading surprises you. A missing edge in rqt_graph resolves in five seconds what code-reading resolves in two days.

Fixing an environment problem inside the application. This team's RViz-window-that-never-renders was a GL driver issue under WSLg (solved with LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 in a compose override), not a ROS problem — attacking it in RViz config would have been endless. Correct habit: isolate which LAYER is failing (kernel/device, container, transport, ROS graph, node logic) before choosing a tool.

Hand-tuning servo registers over the serial console and then wondering why behaviour changes after a power cycle. Correct habit: every register you care about goes in the ros2_control <gpio> block and gets re-pushed at activation. Configuration you typed once is configuration you will lose.

Building the policy before building the executor. Correct habit: write a dummy policy with the real signature and the real output shape first, and debug the entire receding-horizon path against it. This team did exactly that (dummy_policy.py alongside chunk_executor_node.py) and it is the right instinct — when the trained model later underperforms, you know it is the model.

Treating a model's output as trusted input to the controller. Correct habit: a safety wrapper that checks joint limits, per-step velocity (this team caps at 180 deg/s specifically to catch IK branch flips, which jump far more), workspace bounds and IK feasibility, and rejects with a reason you can read in the log.

Writing zero tests because 'robotics can't be tested without hardware'. Correct habit: three tiers. Kinematics and decoding are pure functions and belong in pytest. Wiring belongs in launch_testing against mock hardware. Only current draw, thermal behaviour, contact forces and repeatability genuinely need metal — and those belong in a written checklist, not in someone's head.
communityDifferences: Where the description lives. Industrial teams treat the URDF as a controlled document derived from CAD with measured inertials, versioned against the mechanical drawing, and changed through review — because a geometry error propagates into safety-rated workspace limits. Research labs treat it as editable scratch and frequently carry local uncommitted tweaks. The imitation-learning crowd increasingly does not have a URDF at all: if the policy maps pixels to joint deltas and the only IK is the leader arm's own kinematics, nothing in the pipeline reads a URDF. That is a real and defensible position, but it costs you RViz, MoveIt, collision checking and any pose-space debugging — and it is why UMI-style work that DOES use Cartesian actions (as this team's does) has to reintroduce a description it could otherwise skip.

Planning versus policy. Industrial and classical-research stacks put MoveIt in the loop: plan a collision-free trajectory, time-parameterise it, execute through FollowJointTrajectory, and treat the planner as the arbiter of safety. The imitation-learning crowd generally bypasses MoveIt entirely — the policy emits a stream of end-effector deltas or joint targets at 10-30 Hz and goes straight to a trajectory controller or even a raw position interface, because a planner's replanning latency (tens to hundreds of ms) does not fit inside a reactive visuomotor loop. Both work; the tradeoff is that you give up guaranteed collision avoidance and inherit the obligation to build your own safety wrapper.

Simulation. Industrial teams are the most sim-skeptical of the three: cell layouts are fixed, cycle times are validated on the real line, and sim is used for reach studies and offline programming rather than for closing the loop. Classical robotics research standardised on Gazebo because of its ROS integration and model ecosystem. The learning community runs MuJoCo (fast, differentiable-adjacent, excellent contact) and Isaac Sim/Lab (photorealistic rendering, thousands of parallel environments on one GPU) and largely ignores Gazebo — and ROBOTIS follows that split, shipping both gz_ros2_control launch files and a separate robotis_mujoco_menagerie of MuJoCo models. If you are doing imitation from real demonstrations, note that you may need sim far less than an RL team would: your data comes from the physical arm, so sim's role shrinks to collision sanity-checking and offline pipeline testing, and mock hardware covers most of what you actually need.

Determinism and real-time. Industrial deployments care intensely about a bounded, jitter-free control cycle: PREEMPT_RT kernels, isolated CPU cores, locked memory, no dynamic allocation in the control loop, and ros2_control with an RT-safe RMW configuration. Research labs run stock Ubuntu and accept jitter. The IL community is closer to the research end and often runs inference in Python on a shared machine, accepting tens of milliseconds of variance because action chunking absorbs it — which is itself an argument for chunking. Note that this repo's compose file (SYS_NICE, rtprio 99, memlock) is reaching toward the industrial end while the Python executor on top is firmly at the research end; that combination is fine, but be conscious that your real jitter is set by the Python side.

Data and reproducibility. Industrial practice records everything for traceability and audit and keeps it in vendor-specific logs. Classical robotics research records rosbags and mostly does not publish them. The imitation-learning community has converged hard on shareable, standardised datasets — LeRobotDataset on Hugging Face, ALOHA-lineage HDF5 — because the dataset IS the contribution. For a capstone, record BOTH: rosbag2 for debugging the graph (it captures topics you did not know you would need) and a LeRobotDataset export for training. They answer different questions and the conversion is one-directional.

Testing culture. Industrial robotics has formal verification, safety standards (ISO 10218 / TS 15066 for collaborative arms), and hardware-in-the-loop rigs. ROS-community packages lean on linters, build-success CI and launch_testing — visible in this repo, whose CI runs eight ament linters and a full build but zero functional tests. The IL community's 'test' is largely the evaluation protocol: N rollouts, success rate, which is a statistical claim about a policy and says nothing about whether your launch file spawns the right controllers. These are complementary, not substitutes, and the IL crowd's habit of measuring only end-to-end success rate is why integration bugs there often go undiagnosed for weeks — the number goes down and nobody can say which layer moved.

IK solver choice. Industrial vendors ship analytic IK for their own arms because it is deterministic, fast, and lets them enumerate and select solution branches — properties a certification argument needs. The ROS research default is KDL (fast, Newton-based, poor around joint limits), with TRAC-IK the usual upgrade (dual-threaded Newton + SQP, markedly better with joint limits) and bio_ik/pick_ik the choice when you need arbitrary cost terms such as 'stay near this posture' or 'keep the camera pointed there'. For a 5-DOF arm inside a chunk executor, deriving your own analytic solution — as this team did — is the industrially-shaped choice and is the right one, for determinism and branch control as much as for speed.

components.name: L0 — Commutation / PWM stage (inside each DYNAMIXEL)
components.role: The bottom of the stack. An ARM Cortex-M MCU inside the servo case drives an H-bridge inverter with a PWM duty cycle, turning a signed duty number into average voltage across the motor windings. Everything above it exists only to choose that one number.
components.whyItExists: Because a DC motor has no notion of 'position'. The only physical actuator input is voltage-over-time. Every layer above is a scheme for computing a duty cycle 1000 times a second without a human in the loop. Once you see that the entire stack — OMPL, TOTG, JTC, ros2_control, the serial bus — collapses into one saturating integer per motor per millisecond, the rest of the architecture stops being mysterious.
components.interface: IN: signed PWM duty, integer, clamped by PWM Limit (addr 36, range 0..885, 885 = 100% duty on X-series). OUT: winding voltage, motor torque.
components.rate: PWM carrier tens of kHz; the duty value is refreshed at the firmware main-loop rate (see L1).
components.evidence: PWM Limit at addr 36 is read by the team's own probe: open_manipulator/docker/workspace/dummy_exec/omx_probe.py:31. ROBOTIS block diagram: 'The final PWM value is applied to the motor through an Inverter, and the horn of DYNAMIXEL is driven.' (emanual.robotis.com/docs/en/dxl/x/xm430-w350/)

components.name: L1 — Current / velocity / position PID (inside each DYNAMIXEL, ~1 kHz)
components.role: The cascaded feedback loops. On X-series the Position PID and the velocity PI both terminate in a PWM value; there is no separately tunable current loop on XL430/XL330 (current is capped, not servoed, except in Operating Mode 0/5). Position error in *pulses* goes in, PWM goes out. Feedforward 1st gain (addr 90) multiplies the profile's desired velocity; Feedforward 2nd (addr 88) multiplies desired acceleration.
components.whyItExists: Servoing must be closer to the motor than any network can be. A 1 kHz loop across a 1 Mbps serial link shared by six devices is arithmetically impossible (see the bus math below), so the tight loop is pushed inside the actuator and the host only gets to move the setpoint. This is the single most important structural fact about smart-servo robots and the reason they feel different from EtherCAT industrial arms, where the current loop is in the drive but the position loop can legitimately live on the host at 1–4 kHz.
components.interface: IN: Goal Position (addr 116, 4 bytes, unit 1 pulse = 0.088°, 4096 pulses/rev). OUT: PWM duty. Gains are raw integers with fixed denominators: KPP = PosP/128, KPI = PosI/65536, KPD = PosD/16.
components.rate: ~1 kHz. ROBOTIS does not publish the exact figure; treat 1 kHz as the working assumption, not a datasheet number.
components.evidence: Configured in open_manipulator/open_manipulator_description/ros2_control/omx_f.ros2_control.xacro — every joint gets Position P Gain 1000, Position I Gain 0, Position D Gain 1000. Arithmetic: KPP = 1000/128 = 7.8125 PWM-units per pulse; PWM saturates at 885, so 885/7.8125 = 113.3 pulses = 113.3 x 0.088° = 9.97°. **Roughly 10 degrees of tracking error commands 100% motor power from the P term alone.** KPD = 1000/16 = 62.5. KPI = 0, so there is deliberately no integral action: steady-state droop under gravity is a design choice, not a fault. Gain denominators from emanual XM430-W350 control table.

components.name: L2 — The servo's own trajectory profile generator (Drive Mode bit 2)
components.role: Between the Goal Position register and the position PID sits a profile generator that will not let the setpoint step. It builds a trapezoidal or triangular velocity profile from present position to goal. Drive Mode (addr 10) bit 2 selects how it is parameterised: clear = velocity-based (Profile Velocity is a speed cap in 0.229 rpm units, Profile Acceleration in 214.577 rev/min² units); set = time-based (Profile Velocity is the TOTAL DURATION in ms, Profile Acceleration is the ACCELERATION TIME in ms).
components.whyItExists: So that a host which crashes, stalls, or sends a wild setpoint cannot produce an instantaneous commanded jump. It is the last line of mechanical defence and it is inside the actuator where nothing you write can disable it by accident. It is also why sparse commanding works at all on hobby-grade buses.
components.interface: IN: Goal Position (pulses) + Drive Mode / Profile Velocity / Profile Acceleration (RAM registers). OUT: an interpolated position setpoint stream feeding L1, plus the desired velocity/acceleration that the feedforward gains consume.
components.rate: Regenerated on every Goal Position write; internally evaluated at the ~1 kHz firmware rate.
components.evidence: omx_f.ros2_control.xacro sets `Drive Mode 4` (bit 2 set = **time-based**), `Profile Velocity 50`, `Profile Acceleration 25` on all six servos. Time-based units are milliseconds, and the firmware constraint is 'Profile Acceleration will not exceed 50% of Profile Velocity' — 25 is exactly 50 x 0.5, so the constraint is saturated: **25 ms accelerating, 25 ms decelerating, 50 ms total, zero cruise phase — a pure triangular velocity profile.** Now compose that with a 100 Hz controller: a new Goal Position arrives every 10 ms but each one starts a 50 ms profile, so every profile is superseded after 20% of its life. The servo is acting as a ~50 ms smoothing filter on the command stream. That is a hard floor on this arm's command-to-motion bandwidth, roughly 10 Hz of meaningful content; a policy chunk finer than that is filtered away before it reaches the motor.

components.name: L3 — Half-duplex TTL bus + Protocol 2.0 (the fieldbus)
components.role: One 3-wire daisy chain carries all six servos. Every exchange is master-initiated and strictly turn-taking: the host transmits, releases the line, each addressed servo answers in ID order. Sync Read (0x82) and Sync Write (0x83) exist so that six devices cost one packet instead of six round trips.
components.whyItExists: Half duplex means a collision is not a retry, it is corrupted torque commands to a live arm. Protocol 2.0's CRC-16 and the strict master-slave discipline are what make a shared line safe. This is also the mechanism behind the failure the team already hit: **exactly one process may hold the port.** There is no arbitration, no lock, no error — two writers simply interleave bytes and both see CRC failures. It is not a ROS problem or a Docker problem; it is a property of the physical layer.
components.interface: IN (Sync Write): start address + length + [ID, 4-byte Goal Position] x 6. OUT (Sync Read status): per device, 11 bytes of framing + N data bytes. Units are raw control-table integers throughout — pulses, 0.229 rpm, 2.69 mA.
components.rate: Configured 1,000,000 bps, 8N1.
components.evidence: `<param name="baud_rate">1000000</param>` in omx_f.ros2_control.xacro. **Bus arithmetic, 6 servos, 8N1 so 10 bit-times per byte at 1 µs/bit:** Sync Read of 8 contiguous bytes (Present Velocity @128 + Present Position @132): instruction packet = 3 header + 1 reserved + 1 ID(0xFE) + 2 length + 1 instr + 2 addr + 2 len + 6 IDs + 2 CRC = 20 bytes; each status packet = 3+1+1+2+1+1+8+2 = 19 bytes, x6 = 114; total 134 bytes = 1340 µs. Sync Write of 4-byte Goal Position to 6: 3+1+1+2+1+2+2+(6x5)+2 = 44 bytes = 440 µs, no status returned. **Cycle total 1.78 ms → hard ceiling 562 Hz; at the configured 100 Hz that is 17.8% bus utilisation.** A 1 kHz host loop is not slow, it is *impossible* here: 1.78 ms > 1 ms. The OMY arms run the identical traffic at 6.25 Mbps (omy_f3m_smooth.ros2_control.xacro:20) = 285 µs, which is why that platform can go faster.

components.name: L4 — USB transport (OpenRB-150 / U2D2), the layer that actually limits you
components.role: The TTL bus does not reach the Jetson directly. An OpenRB-150 running the usb_to_dynamixel passthrough sketch enumerates as /dev/ttyACM0 (USB CDC-ACM) and store-and-forwards bytes between USB and the half-duplex line. On U2D2-based setups it is an FTDI chip at /dev/ttyUSB0 instead.
components.whyItExists: Nobody's SBC has a TTL half-duplex transceiver. But the bridge is where the latency budget is quietly spent, and it is invisible in every architecture diagram. USB Full-Speed schedules transfers on 1 ms frames: your OUT lands in one frame, the bridge forwards it, six servos answer, and the IN transfer lands on a later frame. Realistic round trip is 2–4 ms regardless of baud rate. The 562 Hz bus ceiling is therefore fantasy — **200–300 Hz is the honest practical ceiling and 100 Hz is where the vendor sensibly landed.**
components.interface: Opaque byte stream both ways. Nothing semantic crosses here, which is exactly why it gets forgotten.
components.rate: 1 ms USB frame granularity; 2–4 ms observed round trip.
components.evidence: port_name default `/dev/ttyACM0` in omx_l.ros2_control.xacro and omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py; OpenRB-150 supports up to 1 Mbps with the usb_to_dynamixel sketch, matching the configured baud. The FTDI variant has a documented trap: **default latency_timer is 16 ms**, which caps you near 60 Hz no matter the baud. The vendor writes a udev rule for exactly this — `docker/container.sh` installs `KERNEL=="ttyUSB*", DRIVERS=="ftdi_sio", MODE="0666", ATTR{device/latency_timer}="1"`. CDC-ACM has no such knob; you are at the mercy of USB scheduling.

components.name: L5 — Hardware component: dynamixel_hardware_interface/DynamixelHardware
components.role: The ros2_control plugin that owns the port. It implements on_init (parse the gpio blocks, push Drive Mode / Operating Mode / gains / Profile registers into servo RAM), on_activate (torque on), read() (one Sync Read → fill state interfaces in SI units), write() (one Sync Write from command interfaces). It converts pulses↔radians and 0.229 rpm↔rad/s.
components.whyItExists: It is the single point where raw registers become SI units and where *exactly one* owner of the serial port is established. The 'teammate's process fighting mine over /dev/ttyACM0' failure is structurally prevented by making the hardware component the sole holder — and structurally guaranteed to recur the moment anyone runs a Python SDK script alongside it. The team's own probe script already documents the rule: 'Run with the ros2_control stack STOPPED -- only one process may hold the port.'
components.interface: DOWN: Protocol 2.0 packets. UP: state interfaces `<joint>/position` (rad), `<joint>/velocity` (rad/s); command interfaces `<joint>/position` (rad). Plus a `dxl_state` topic and get/set/reboot/torque services for out-of-band register access.
components.rate: Once per controller_manager cycle — but see is_async below.
components.evidence: omx_f.ros2_control.xacro declares the plugin, `error_timeout_ms 500`, `disable_torque_at_init true`, `dynamixel_model_folder /param/dxl_model`, and one `<gpio>` block per servo carrying the register writes. **The registers listed there are RAM, not EEPROM — this is precisely why servo settings 'silently reset on power cycle': they are re-pushed at every on_init and only at on_init.** Joint→ID mapping is positional and undocumented, which is why omx_probe.py exists.

components.name: L5a — is_async="true": the detail that makes 100 Hz work
components.role: With `is_async="true"`, read() and write() run on a dedicated thread instead of inline in the controller_manager update loop. controller_manager triggers them and moves on; it does not block on the 2–4 ms USB round trip.
components.whyItExists: Without it, a 10 ms control period containing a 4 ms blocking USB transaction burns 40% of the budget and any USB hiccup directly overruns the cycle. With it, the control loop keeps its period and the comms jitter is absorbed by the async thread. **The price is honesty about staleness: controllers now read state that is at least one cycle old, and commands land whenever the thread gets to them.** You trade determinism for non-blocking, which is the right trade on a USB-serial arm and the wrong trade on EtherCAT.
components.interface: Same interfaces; only the scheduling changes. Defaults: thread_priority 50, scheduling_policy 'synchronized', affinity any core.
components.rate: Triggered at the controller_manager rate, executed asynchronously.
components.evidence: `<ros2_control name="${name}" type="system" is_async="true">` — omx_f.ros2_control.xacro line 4. Note the leader arm (omx_l.ros2_control.xacro line 4) is **not** async, because it only reads.

components.name: L6 — Resource Manager and the interface claim mechanism
components.role: Holds every state and command interface as a named double, and enforces that at most one controller may claim a given command interface at a time. Claiming happens at controller activation.
components.whyItExists: This is the software analogue of the serial-port exclusivity problem, one level up. Two controllers writing joint1/position would be as bad as two processes writing the bus. The claim mechanism turns a race into a startup error message. It is also what makes controller *chaining* expressible: a chained controller exports its own command interfaces that another controller claims, so a cascade is built from the same primitive.
components.interface: Named strings: `joint1/position` (command), `joint1/velocity` (state). The interface name *is* the contract; there is no type system beyond double.
components.rate: N/A — claims are made at activation, not per cycle.
components.evidence: The `<command_interface>` / `<state_interface>` tags in omx_f.ros2_control.xacro are exactly these declarations. Note the omx_f follower declares only `position` as a command interface — no velocity, no effort — which forecloses the entire class of impedance/torque control on this arm without a config change.

components.name: L7 — controller_manager update cycle (100 Hz)
components.role: The heartbeat. Each tick: read() all hardware → update() all active controllers in claim order → write() all hardware. Runs in ros2_control_node, one process.
components.whyItExists: A single ordered loop gives you a well-defined data-flow: every controller in a cycle sees state from the same read(). Without it you get controllers sampling different instants and fighting each other. The rate is chosen as the slowest thing that still discretises your motion acceptably — not the fastest you can manage.
components.interface: Nothing crosses; it orchestrates. Configured by one number.
components.rate: `update_rate: 100  # Hz` → 10 ms period.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml line 4. Identical in omx_f/, omx_l_leader_ai/, and every other variant in that directory — 100 Hz is this vendor's platform-wide answer.

components.name: L8 — JointTrajectoryController: what it actually computes
components.role: Takes a sparse trajectory_msgs/JointTrajectory (waypoints with time_from_start), fits splines between consecutive points, and at every 10 ms tick samples that spline at 'now minus trajectory start' to produce one position per joint. That is the whole job: **sparse waypoints in, dense setpoints out.**
components.whyItExists: It is the impedance-matcher between a planner that thinks in seconds and a bus that must be fed every 10 ms. The spline order is chosen by what you supply, and this is the rule that bites everyone: **positions only → LINEAR interpolation, which puts a velocity discontinuity at every waypoint; positions + velocities → CUBIC, velocity-continuous; + accelerations → QUINTIC.** A policy that publishes positions only gets a visibly jerky arm and blames the servo.
components.interface: IN: trajectory_msgs/JointTrajectory on `~/joint_trajectory`, or control_msgs/FollowJointTrajectory action on `~/follow_joint_trajectory`. Positions in rad, velocities rad/s, time_from_start as builtin_interfaces/Duration. OUT: one double per joint into the claimed command interface, in rad.
components.rate: Sampled at the controller_manager rate, 100 Hz here.
components.evidence: hardware_controller_manager.yaml declares `type: joint_trajectory_controller/JointTrajectoryController`, `command_interfaces: [position]`, `state_interfaces: [position, velocity]`, `allow_partial_joints_goal: true`. Two defaults worth memorising: **`allow_nonzero_velocity_at_trajectory_end` defaults to false — the last point's velocity must be zero or the whole message is rejected**, and `interpolation_method` defaults to 'splines'. The team's chunk_executor_node.py already encodes both rules in its PUBLISH_STEPS=8 / EXECUTE_STEPS=3 design: publish further ahead than you execute so the mandatory zero-velocity tail always sits beyond the replan point and the arm never actually decelerates into it. That is the correct trick. Also note `gains.*` PID parameters are inert when the command interface is position — JTC only closes its own loop for velocity/effort command interfaces.

components.name: L9 — joint_state_broadcaster
components.role: Not a controller in the control sense. It claims state interfaces only and republishes them as sensor_msgs/JointState on /joint_states. Everything else in ROS — RViz, robot_state_publisher, MoveIt, the team's policy — feeds off this one topic.
components.whyItExists: Separating 'publish the truth' from 'command the robot' means the observation path survives a controller crash, and means you can run zero controllers and still see the arm. It is also the reason /joint_states appears at exactly the controller_manager rate and not faster: it is sampled in the same 100 Hz loop.
components.interface: OUT: sensor_msgs/JointState {name[], position[] rad, velocity[] rad/s, effort[] N·m}, at 100 Hz.
components.rate: 100 Hz (inherits update_rate).
components.evidence: Spawned alongside arm_controller in open_manipulator_bringup/launch/omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py. The team's chunk_executor_node.py subscribes to `/joint_states` and does FK on it to get its anchor pose.

components.name: L10 — robot_state_publisher
components.role: Subscribes /joint_states, walks the URDF kinematic tree, publishes /tf. Pure kinematics, no control.
components.whyItExists: So that exactly one component owns the URDF→TF mapping and everything else can ask TF instead of reimplementing FK. Worth stating plainly to this team: you wrote your own analytic FK/IK, which is correct and fast for a 5-DOF arm, but it means your FK and RViz's FK are two independent implementations that can silently disagree. Compare them once, deliberately.
components.interface: IN: /joint_states. OUT: /tf (geometry_msgs/TransformStamped, metres + quaternions), /robot_description (latched std_msgs/String).
components.rate: Republishes on every /joint_states message → 100 Hz.
components.evidence: open_manipulator_bringup/launch/omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py instantiates it with the xacro-expanded URDF.

components.name: L11 — MoveIt move_group: planning scene, OMPL, TOTG
components.role: The deliberative layer, and a *separate process*. Maintains the planning scene (robot model + octomap + attached objects), runs a sampling-based planner (OMPL: RRTConnect and friends) to find a collision-free path in joint space, then runs the response adapter chain that time-parameterises it. Sends the result to JTC over the FollowJointTrajectory action.
components.whyItExists: Planning is a *search*, and search has unbounded worst-case time. You cannot put unbounded worst-case time in a loop that must finish in 10 ms, so it gets its own process and its own timescale. The separation is not stylistic, it is the only way to have both guarantees. OMPL is also probabilistically complete but not deterministic: the same goal can produce different paths and different durations on consecutive calls, which is why you never plan inside a feedback loop.
components.interface: IN: moveit_msgs/MotionPlanRequest (goal pose or joint state, m and rad), /planning_scene, /joint_states, /tf. OUT: control_msgs/FollowJointTrajectory goal — a trajectory_msgs/JointTrajectory whose waypoints are **spaced 0.1 s apart** by TOTG's default resample_dt, i.e. 10 Hz waypoints that JTC then interpolates up to 100 Hz.
components.rate: Plan calls take roughly 0.05–2 s for a 5-DOF arm. Call it 1 Hz-ish as an order of magnitude, with a long tail.
components.evidence: open_manipulator_moveit_config/config/ompl_planning.yaml lists `default_planning_response_adapters/AddTimeOptimalParameterization` — that is TOTG, whose constructor default resample_dt is 0.1 s. config/omx_f/moveit_controllers.yaml wires `arm_controller` with `type: FollowJointTrajectory, action_ns: follow_joint_trajectory`. config/omx_f/kinematics.yaml uses KDL with **`position_only_ik: True`** — the standard and necessary concession for a 5-DOF arm, which cannot reach arbitrary 6-DOF poses. That is the same geometric fact your analytic IK handles by projecting the commanded pose onto the reachable 5-DOF subspace.

components.name: L12 — MoveIt Servo: the middle ground
components.role: Reactive Cartesian jogging. Takes a twist or joint-velocity command, does damped-least-squares inverse kinematics on the *current* state, checks singularities and collisions, and emits a short JointTrajectory every cycle. No search, no planning scene rebuild, bounded time.
components.whyItExists: Because there is a real gap between 'plan a whole motion in 1 second' and 'servo at 100 Hz', and visual servoing, teleop and reactive policies live in it. Servo fills it by giving up global optimality and obstacle avoidance-by-planning in exchange for a bounded per-cycle cost. **For an imitation-learning team this is the closest existing component to what your policy does**, and reading its source is the fastest way to see how a 100 Hz reactive layer is built correctly.
components.interface: IN: geometry_msgs/TwistStamped on ~/delta_twist_cmds (m/s, rad/s) or control_msgs/JointJog on ~/delta_joint_cmds. OUT: trajectory_msgs/JointTrajectory (or Float64MultiArray) to the controller's topic interface.
components.rate: publish_period default 0.01 s = 100 Hz; collision_check_rate 10 Hz; incoming_command_timeout 0.1 s.
components.evidence: MoveIt 2 servo_parameters.yaml defaults: publish_period 0.01, scale.linear 0.4 m/s, scale.rotational 0.8 rad/s, lower_singularity_threshold 17.0, hard_stop_singularity_threshold 30.0, leaving_singularity_threshold_multiplier 2.0, self_collision_proximity_threshold 0.01 m, scene_collision_proximity_threshold 0.02 m, joint_limit_margins [0.1], smoothing via online_signal_smoothing::ButterworthFilterPlugin. Note the collision check runs at 10 Hz while commands go out at 100 Hz — it *scales down velocity* as you approach a collision rather than checking every command.

components.name: L13 — Application / policy layer (your chunk executor)
components.role: Non-realtime, Python, GPU-bound. Reads /joint_states, runs the network, decodes the action chunk, does IK, publishes a JointTrajectory. Hands work down and immediately returns; it never blocks anything below it.
components.whyItExists: Inference latency is unbounded and jittery — CUDA sync, page faults, GC, the occasional 200 ms outlier. The whole point of the layered architecture is that this jitter is absorbed by JTC's spline (which keeps interpolating whatever it last received) and by the servo's 50 ms profile, so a late chunk degrades smoothness rather than causing a discontinuity. **The receding-horizon pattern — publish 8 steps, execute 3, replan — is the correct structural answer and you already found it.**
components.interface: IN: sensor_msgs/JointState (rad). OUT: trajectory_msgs/JointTrajectory with positions (rad), velocities (rad/s), time_from_start. Crosses via DDS/zenoh, not shared memory.
components.rate: Your configured replan period is EXECUTE_STEPS 3 x DT 0.04 x TIME_SCALE 2.0 = 0.24 s → **4.17 Hz**, publishing a 0.64 s horizon each time. At TIME_SCALE 1.0 that becomes 8.3 Hz. UMI-class policies typically target 10–30 Hz inference.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/docker/workspace/dummy_exec/chunk_executor_node.py — DEFAULT_TOPIC '/leader/joint_trajectory', PUBLISH_STEPS 8, EXECUTE_STEPS 3, TIME_SCALE 2.0; DT 0.04 and H 16 in dummy_policy.py. The topic works because omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py remaps `/arm_controller/joint_trajectory` → `/leader/joint_trajectory`: **your policy is literally occupying the leader arm's slot in the vendor's teleop architecture.** That is a clean insertion point, not a hack.

components.name: L14 — The realtime substrate (and what it actually means)
components.role: Not a layer with an interface — a property the lower layers need. 'Realtime' means **bounded worst-case latency, not low average latency or high throughput.** A loop that runs in 0.2 ms 99.9% of the time and 40 ms once a minute is not realtime; a loop that always finishes in 3 ms is. Concretely: a PREEMPT_RT kernel, the control thread on SCHED_FIFO with a priority above every other thread on the box, mlockall(MCL_CURRENT|MCL_FUTURE) so no page fault stalls the loop, and no malloc/free, no logging to disk, no unbounded queue, no lock shared with a non-realtime thread inside the cycle.
components.whyItExists: Because the failure mode of missing a deadline on a robot is not a dropped frame, it is a setpoint discontinuity that the position PID turns into a torque spike. Recall the arithmetic: ~10° of error saturates PWM. A 40 ms stall while the arm is moving at 1 rad/s creates 2.3° of error instantly — survivable. The same stall on a stiff 1 kHz torque-controlled arm is not.
components.interface: N/A.
components.rate: Deadline is the controller_manager period: 10 ms here.
components.evidence: The vendor's container is *provisioned* for this and then does not use it, which is worth seeing plainly. docker/docker-compose.yml grants `cap_add: [SYS_NICE]`, `ulimits: {rtprio: 99, rttime: -1, memlock: 8428281856}` — i.e. permission to run SCHED_FIFO up to priority 99 and lock ~8 GB — plus `ipc: host` and `/dev/shm:/dev/shm` so DDS can use shared-memory transport, and `privileged: true` + `/dev:/dev` for the serial port. But docker/s6-services/common/ros2_service_run.sh just `exec bash -i -c "ros2 launch ..."` with no chrt, no priority. **The capability is granted; nothing claims it.** At 100 Hz over async USB that is a defensible choice — there is no point pinning a thread whose latency is dominated by USB frame scheduling. Say it out loud rather than assuming the container is realtime because it has rtprio in it.

components.name: ALTERNATIVE — the direct-driver loop (Python + DynamixelSDK)
components.role: One process, one while-loop: `groupSyncRead.txRxPacket()` → compute → `groupSyncWrite.txPacket()` → sleep. No ros2_control, no controller_manager, no plugin, no URDF. Your omx_probe.py is already 80% of this.
components.whyItExists: Because for a 6-servo arm driven by a learned policy, most of ros2_control's machinery is solving problems you do not have. You get: total clarity about what byte goes where and when, trivial debugging, no plugin lifecycle, no XML, sub-second iteration. **This is what most imitation-learning codebases actually do** — LeRobot, the original UMI/Diffusion Policy stacks, and essentially every ALOHA derivative talk to DYNAMIXELs directly from Python.
components.interface: Same registers, same units, straight from your process. You write the pulses↔radians conversion yourself (0..4095 spans ±π with 2048 at zero, per the .model files).
components.rate: Realistically 50–100 Hz from CPython. The GIL and USB latency, not the bus, are the limits.
components.evidence: omx_probe.py:20-44 already has the full control table. **What you give up, concretely and in order of how much it will hurt:** (1) MoveIt — no collision checking, no planning, no RViz motion planning panel; (2) the topic-based observation path, so RViz, rosbag and every ROS tool go dark unless you republish /joint_states yourself; (3) JTC's spline — you must generate dense setpoints yourself or accept velocity steps; (4) the register-push-at-init behaviour, so you own the 'RAM resets on power cycle' problem explicitly; (5) the exclusive-port discipline, which becomes a convention instead of a mechanism. **What you should NOT claim you give up:** realtime guarantees. A Python loop and an async ros2_control USB component have comparable worst-case jitter here. The honest reason to stay with ros2_control on this arm is MoveIt, RViz and the vendor's existing leader-follower teleop for data collection — not determinism.

orderOfOperations: **0. Establish exclusive ownership of the bus before anything else.** Write down who owns /dev/ttyACM0 and how you know. On this arm that means: ros2_control_node is running, OR your Python script is running, never both. `fuser -v /dev/ttyACM0` or `lsof /dev/ttyACM0` before every debugging session. This is first because every diagnosis downstream is worthless if two processes are interleaving bytes — you will chase phantom CRC errors, phantom joint limits and phantom jitter for days. Your own omx_probe.py docstring already states the rule; institutionalise it.

**1. Read the servo, do not read the datasheet.** Run a read-only probe against every ID and dump Drive Mode, Operating Mode, Min/Max Position Limit, the PID gains, Profile Velocity/Acceleration and Present Position. The servos' RAM is the only authority on what the robot will actually do. Datasheet, URDF and xacro are three *claims*; the register is the *fact*. Do this before every session on a robot that has been power-cycled, because those are RAM registers and only on_init rewrites them.

**2. Reconcile the limit sources and pick one as canonical, in writing.** On this arm there are at least five and they disagree: (a) omx_f_arm.urdf.xacro lines 37/72/107/142/177 say every joint is ±2π at 4.8 rad/s — obviously a placeholder, all six identical; (b) omx_f.ros2_control.xacro says joint2 is ticks 830..3129 = **-107.1°..+95.0° = [-1.868, +1.658] rad** and joint3 is 1024..3140 = **-90.0°..+96.0° = [-1.571, +1.675] rad**, while joint4/joint5 get 0..4095 which is no limit at all; (c) MoveIt joint_limits.yaml says max_velocity 5.0 and max_acceleration 5.0 but with default_velocity_scaling_factor 0.1, so the effective limit is 0.5 rad/s; (d) the servo's own time-based profile imposes a 50 ms transit; (e) your chunk_executor_node.py MAX_JOINT_VEL is π rad/s. The URDF is the one MoveIt and RViz believe; the registers are the one the hardware enforces. **Make the URDF match the registers, then everything above agrees by construction.** Do this before planning anything, because a planner that believes a ±2π joint will happily plan straight through a hard stop.

**3. Bring up the stack in strict dependency order and verify each layer before adding the next.** The order is forced by what depends on what: discovery middleware (the zenoh router — `ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd`; with rmw_zenoh nodes genuinely cannot see each other without it, and this is a real change from Fast DDS's routerless discovery) → ros2_control_node with the URDF → joint_state_broadcaster (verify: `ros2 topic hz /joint_states` reads ~100) → robot_state_publisher (verify: `ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames`) → arm_controller (verify: `ros2 control list_controllers` shows it active and `ros2 control list_hardware_interfaces` shows the claims) → move_group → RViz → your policy node. Each step has a one-command verification; do not skip them, because a failure three layers up is indistinguishable from a failure one layer up if you never checked layer one.

**4. Prove the full command path with a motion of zero.** Publish exactly the pose the arm is already in and confirm nothing moves. Your `--hold` mode does this and it is the single best-designed thing in your codebase. It exercises joint_states in → FK → IK → JointTrajectory out → controller accepts, with no risk. **If the arm twitches, your joint ordering or your angle convention is wrong, and you have learned it while stationary rather than at 1 rad/s.** Every competent robotics team has some version of this ritual.

**5. Then move one joint, slowly, in open air, with a hand on the power switch.** Not a trajectory — a single JointTrajectory with one point, 5 seconds out, 0.1 rad away. Confirm direction of rotation matches your sign convention. Do this per joint. Sign errors are the most common and most expensive class of bug in a new kinematics implementation and they are free to find this way.

**6. Only now raise speed, and raise it by lowering TIME_SCALE one step at a time.** You already have the right knob. Each halving roughly doubles peak joint velocity and quadruples the tracking error the position PID must absorb. Watch for the specific failure: with Position I Gain 0 there is no integral term, so under load the arm will *settle short of the goal* rather than oscillating. That is droop, it is expected, and it is not fixed by moving faster.

**7. Close the loop on latency before you tune anything.** Measure, do not estimate: timestamp your publish, log /joint_states, and find the actual transport delay. On this arm the budget is roughly — DDS/zenoh hop 0.2–1 ms; JTC sample, up to one 10 ms cycle; async hardware thread pickup, up to another 10 ms; USB round trip 2–4 ms; wire time 1.78 ms; servo profile ~25 ms to peak velocity and 50 ms to complete; servo loop ~1 ms. Call it **15–25 ms to first motion and 65–80 ms to settle.** Until you know your real number you cannot tell a policy problem from a plumbing problem, and you will tune the wrong one.

**8. Record the environment as code the same day you get it working.** Image tag, colcon workspace layout, the exact commit of every cloned repo, ROS_DOMAIN_ID, RMW_IMPLEMENTATION. The vendor's Dockerfile pins six repos by branch and one by SHA (`realsense-ros` at cbd8b848…) — that asymmetry is a lesson: **branches drift, SHAs do not.** A capstone that cannot be rebuilt from scratch in one command is a capstone that will fail in week eleven for reasons nobody can reconstruct.
keyFacts: **The configured stack is 100 Hz, everywhere.** `update_rate: 100  # Hz` in open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml, and identically in omx_f/, omx_l_leader_ai/ and every sibling directory. Not 1 kHz. Anyone who tells you robot control means 1 kHz is describing EtherCAT industrial arms, not smart-servo arms.

**Bus arithmetic, 6 servos at 1 Mbps, 8N1 (10 bit-times/byte):** Sync Read of 8 bytes = 20-byte instruction + 6 x 19-byte status = 134 bytes = 1340 µs. Sync Write of 4-byte Goal Position = 44 bytes = 440 µs, no status returned. **Total 1.78 ms/cycle → 562 Hz hard ceiling → 17.8% utilisation at the configured 100 Hz.** A 1 kHz host loop is arithmetically impossible on this bus, not merely difficult. The OMY platform runs the same traffic at 6.25 Mbps (285 µs), which is the actual reason it can go faster.

**The real ceiling is USB, not the bus.** /dev/ttyACM0 is an OpenRB-150 in USB CDC-ACM passthrough. USB Full-Speed schedules on 1 ms frames and the bridge stores and forwards, so round trips are 2–4 ms regardless of baud. Practical ceiling ~200–300 Hz. On the FTDI/U2D2 variant there is a worse trap: **default latency_timer is 16 ms, capping you near 60 Hz**, which is exactly why docker/container.sh installs `ATTR{device/latency_timer}="1"` in a udev rule.

**Drive Mode 4 means time-based profile, and the units change meaning.** With bit 2 set, Profile Velocity (addr 112) is the total profile DURATION in **milliseconds** and Profile Acceleration (addr 108) is the acceleration TIME in milliseconds — not rpm and not rev/min². The configured 50 and 25 sit exactly at the firmware's 'accel ≤ 50% of span' constraint, giving a **pure triangular velocity profile, 25 ms up + 25 ms down, no cruise.** If you ever read Profile Velocity 50 and think '50 rpm', you have misread the register by a factor of everything.

**The 100 Hz command stream and the 50 ms profile interact.** A new Goal Position lands every 10 ms; each one launches a 50 ms profile that is superseded after 20% of its life. Net effect: the servo is a ~50 ms low-pass filter on your commands, so the arm's usable command bandwidth is around 10 Hz. **A policy chunk finer than ~100 ms of detail is filtered out inside the actuator before it reaches the motor.** This is the number that should govern your DT choice.

**Gain arithmetic, from the configured P=1000, I=0, D=1000:** KPP = 1000/128 = 7.8125 PWM-units per position pulse; KPD = 1000/16 = 62.5; KPI = 0/65536 = 0. PWM Limit maxes at 885, so **885/7.8125 = 113.3 pulses = 113.3 x 0.088°/pulse = 9.97° — roughly ten degrees of tracking error commands full motor power from the P term alone.** And with I = 0 there is deliberately no integral action: the arm will settle short of its goal under gravity. That droop is configured, not broken.

**`is_async="true"` is why 100 Hz works and why your state is stale.** omx_f.ros2_control.xacro line 4. read()/write() run on their own thread (default thread_priority 50, scheduling_policy 'synchronized'), so a 2–4 ms USB transaction does not eat 40% of a 10 ms cycle. The cost is that controllers see state at least one cycle old and commands land asynchronously. The leader arm's component is *not* async, because it only reads.

**JTC's spline order is chosen by what you send.** Positions only → LINEAR, which puts a velocity step at every waypoint. Positions + velocities → CUBIC. + accelerations → QUINTIC. And `allow_nonzero_velocity_at_trajectory_end` **defaults to false** — a final point with nonzero velocity gets the entire message rejected, not clamped. Your PUBLISH_STEPS 8 / EXECUTE_STEPS 3 design is the standard way around this: keep the mandatory zero-velocity tail beyond the replan point so the arm always lives in the smooth middle of the spline.

**MoveIt hands JTC 10 Hz waypoints, not 100 Hz setpoints.** TOTG's default resample_dt is 0.1 s, so a planned trajectory arrives as waypoints 100 ms apart and JTC interpolates the 10x. This is the canonical sparse→dense boundary in the whole stack, and seeing it makes the whole architecture click: planning is 1 Hz-ish, trajectory waypoints are 10 Hz, control setpoints are 100 Hz, servo loops are 1 kHz. **Each layer is roughly 10x the one above it.**

**Your arm is 5 DOF, and both MoveIt and your own code handle that the same way.** open_manipulator_moveit_config/config/omx_f/kinematics.yaml sets `position_only_ik: True` on the KDL solver — the standard concession, because 5 joints cannot realise arbitrary 6-DOF poses. Your analytic IK's projection step is the same fact expressed differently. Any tutorial that assumes a full 6-DOF pose goal will mislead you.

**The registers in the xacro's `<gpio>` blocks are RAM, not EEPROM.** That is the whole mechanism behind 'servo settings silently reset on power cycle'. They are pushed by the hardware component at on_init and at no other time. If you power-cycle the arm without restarting ros2_control_node, the servos are running factory defaults while your config file says otherwise.

**The container is provisioned for realtime but does not claim it.** docker-compose.yml grants SYS_NICE, rtprio 99, rttime -1, memlock ~8 GB, plus ipc: host and /dev/shm for shared-memory DDS. Then docker/s6-services/common/ros2_service_run.sh simply `exec bash -i -c "ros2 launch ..."` — no chrt, no SCHED_FIFO, no mlockall. Defensible at 100 Hz over async USB, but do not mistake the ulimits for a guarantee.

**Your policy occupies the leader arm's slot.** omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py remaps `/arm_controller/joint_trajectory` → `/leader/joint_trajectory`. The vendor's teleop has a leader arm publishing JointTrajectory into the follower's JTC; your chunk executor publishes to the same topic. That is a genuinely clean architectural insertion point — the same seam the data-collection rig uses — and it means the teleop and the policy paths are interchangeable by construction.

**Realtime means bounded worst-case latency, not speed.** Concretely: PREEMPT_RT kernel, control thread on SCHED_FIFO above every other thread, mlockall(MCL_CURRENT|MCL_FUTURE), and no allocation, no disk logging, no unbounded queue and no lock shared with a non-realtime thread inside the cycle. A loop averaging 0.2 ms that stalls 40 ms once a minute is *not* realtime. A loop that always finishes in 3 ms is.
beginnerMistakes: **Believing the URDF about joint limits.** In this repo every joint in omx_f_arm.urdf.xacro carries the identical `lower=-2π upper=+2π velocity=4.8 effort=1000` — six identical values is the signature of a placeholder nobody filled in. The enforcing authority is the servo's Min/Max Position Limit register, and for joint2 that is 830..3129 ticks = [-1.868, +1.658] rad, less than a third of what the URDF claims. **Habit: read the register, then make the URDF agree with it.** Everything above the URDF inherits its lie otherwise.

**Trying to raise the control rate to fix jerkiness.** The instinct is 'more Hz = smoother'. On this arm 100 Hz commands already pass through a 50 ms servo profile, so going to 200 Hz changes nothing you can see — you are oversampling a filter. **Habit: before changing a rate, work out which layer is actually the bandwidth limit.** Here it is L2, the servo's profile generator, and the fix is Profile Velocity, not update_rate.

**Sending positions with no velocities and blaming the hardware for the result.** JTC silently drops to LINEAR interpolation, which means a velocity discontinuity at every single waypoint, which the position PID turns into a torque step. It looks exactly like a mechanical problem. **Habit: always populate `velocities` in JointTrajectoryPoint** (your build_segment's central-difference approach is the right way), and know that the final point's velocity must be zero or the whole message is rejected.

**Assuming 'realtime' means 'fast'.** Beginners chase average latency and tune the mean. **Habit: measure the worst case and the tail, never the mean.** `ros2 topic hz` reporting 100.0 Hz tells you almost nothing; the standard deviation and the max gap are the numbers that matter. A single 40 ms stall matters more than a 2 ms average improvement.

**Running a Python DynamixelSDK script while ros2_control_node holds the port.** There is no lock, no error, no warning — the two writers interleave bytes and both see CRC failures that look like a flaky cable. **Habit: `lsof /dev/ttyACM0` before touching the arm, every time.** This is the exact failure the team already hit; the lesson is that it is a property of half-duplex serial, not of ROS or Docker, and it will recur forever unless it becomes a reflex.

**Tuning the servo's PID gains before checking Operating Mode and Drive Mode.** Doubling Position P Gain on a servo that is in Current-based Position Control (mode 5, which is what dxl16 the gripper uses) with Goal Current 600 does something quite different from the same change on a servo in mode 3. **Habit: dump Operating Mode and Drive Mode first; the gain's meaning depends on them.**

**Putting planning inside a feedback loop.** OMPL is a sampling planner: probabilistically complete, non-deterministic, unbounded worst case. Calling it at 10 Hz produces a robot that occasionally freezes for 2 seconds and takes a different path each time. **Habit: planning is a one-shot request; reactive control is Servo or your own IK loop. Never confuse them.** If you need to react, you need bounded-time IK, not a planner.

**Testing new kinematics by commanding a real motion.** Sign errors, frame errors and joint-ordering errors are the most common bugs in hand-written FK/IK, and the cheapest possible test is to command the pose the arm is already in and confirm stillness. **Habit: the zero-motion test first, then one joint, then trajectories.** Your `--hold` mode is exactly this; use it before every kinematics change, not just the first one.

**Treating `docker run` as reproducibility.** A container that builds from `git clone -b jazzy` pulls a different commit every week. The vendor's own Dockerfile pins realsense-ros to SHA cbd8b848… and leaves the other six on branches — the asymmetry is instructive. **Habit: pin every dependency by SHA, and record the image digest, not the tag.** `robotis/open-manipulator:5.1.1` is a moving target; its sha256 is not.

**Assuming state you read is current.** With `is_async="true"` the /joint_states you receive is at minimum one 10 ms cycle old, plus DDS transport, plus the USB round trip that produced it — realistically 15–30 ms stale by the time your policy sees it. **Habit: in any feedback computation, account for the age of your observation.** For a UMI-style policy that does FK on /joint_states to build an anchor pose, a 20 ms-old anchor while the arm moves at 1 rad/s is already 1.1° of error before the network has done anything.

**Not distinguishing the three kinds of 'it doesn't move'.** Torque disabled (`disable_torque_at_init: true` is set in this repo, so the arm is limp until on_activate), controller not claimed (`ros2 control list_hardware_interfaces` shows unclaimed), or trajectory rejected (JTC logs it, but only at the right log level). **Habit: three commands, always in this order — `ros2 control list_controllers`, `ros2 control list_hardware_interfaces`, then check the JTC log.** They discriminate the three cases in about fifteen seconds.
communityDifferences: **Where the tight loop lives — and this is the real fault line.** Industrial (UR, KUKA, Franka, anything EtherCAT): the drive closes current at 10–20 kHz, the host closes position/torque at 1–4 kHz over a hard-realtime fieldbus with a PREEMPT_RT kernel and SCHED_FIFO threads; ros2_control genuinely runs at 1 kHz and `is_async` would be a bug. Smart-servo (this arm, and most academic manipulators): the entire cascade is inside the actuator, the host moves setpoints at 50–200 Hz over USB-serial, and 'realtime' is aspirational. **Tutorials, textbook figures and conference talks overwhelmingly describe the first world while most people's hardware is in the second.** That mismatch is the single largest source of confusion for teams in your position, and it explains why everything you read said 1 kHz while your config file says 100.

**Whether ros2_control is used at all.** Industrial and most ROS-native research: yes, invariably — the vendor ships a hardware component and MoveIt integration and you would be mad to reimplement it. **Imitation learning: mostly no.** LeRobot, the original UMI and Diffusion Policy stacks, and essentially every ALOHA derivative talk to DYNAMIXELs directly from Python with the SDK, because the policy wants a numpy array of joint angles at 30 Hz and ros2_control's plugin/lifecycle/XML machinery is overhead against that. Neither camp is wrong; they are optimising for different things. **You are in an unusual and actually good position: the vendor gave you a working ros2_control stack, so you get MoveIt and RViz for free, and the `/leader/joint_trajectory` remap gives you a clean seam to inject a policy without touching any of it.**

**Sparse goals versus dense setpoints — the design question you asked.** *Hand sparse goals to the servo's profile generator when:* the motion is point-to-point, you do not care about the path between endpoints, the host link is slow or jittery (USB-serial, WiFi, a Python process), and you want a host stall to be harmless — the servo just finishes its profile and stops. This is the right default for a 6-servo arm on USB. *Send dense interpolated setpoints when:* the path matters (Cartesian straight lines, welding, contact tasks), you need coordinated multi-joint timing so the end effector follows a specific trajectory rather than each joint arriving whenever, you are doing impedance or force control (where the servo's position profile is actively fighting you and must be bypassed via Operating Mode 0), or you are visually servoing and the goal moves faster than a profile completes. **The trade-off in one line: sparse goals buy you robustness to host jitter and cost you path control; dense setpoints buy you path control and make you responsible for every deadline.** On this arm, with a 50 ms triangular profile and 2–4 ms USB, sparse-to-moderately-dense is correct and your 8-waypoint 0.64 s horizon at 4 Hz is a reasonable point on that spectrum. If you later want true Cartesian paths, the move is not 'send faster' — it is to set Profile Velocity/Acceleration to 0 (disabling the internal profile entirely) and take full responsibility for smoothness at 100 Hz. Do that only once you have measured your worst-case loop time.

**How much the policy layer is allowed to know about the robot.** Classical ROS: the policy emits Cartesian goals, MoveIt owns IK and collision checking, and the application never touches joint angles. Imitation learning: the policy emits joint or end-effector deltas directly, IK is a 20-line analytic function in the same file, and MoveIt is not in the loop at all — because the policy was trained on demonstrations in exactly that action space and inserting a planner between policy and robot changes the distribution the policy expects. **Your architecture is the second kind and that is correct for UMI.** The honest cost is that you have no collision checking anywhere in the runtime path; the vendor's SRDF (open_manipulator_moveit_config/config/omx_f/omx_f.srdf) has the self-collision matrix already computed, and if you ever want a safety layer, running a collision check against that model as a veto on your published trajectory is far cheaper than adopting MoveIt wholesale.

**What counts as done.** Research lab: it worked in the demo video, the paper deadline passed, the repo has a README and no pinned dependencies. Industrial: it has run 10^6 cycles, every failure mode has a documented recovery, the software is version-locked and the E-stop is certified. Imitation learning specifically: success rate over N trials on a held-out object set, with the honest admission that nobody can tell you why it failed the other 1-N times. **For a capstone, borrow the industrial habit of pinning and the IL habit of reporting success rate over trials rather than showing one good run** — the second is what makes your result mean anything, and the first is what makes it survive to demo day.

components.name: rmw_zenohd — the router daemon (separate process, must exist FIRST)
components.role: A standalone Zenoh router listening on tcp/[::]:7447. Every ROS 2 node in the container opens a Zenoh client session to it; the router is the only thing that knows who exists. It is NOT a ROS node — it publishes and subscribes nothing, it has no name in `ros2 node list`, and nothing depends on it in the launch graph. Start it with `ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd` (aliased to `zenohd`).
components.whyItExists: Classic DDS (Fast DDS, Cyclone) discovers peers by UDP multicast to 239.255.0.1 on ports derived from ROS_DOMAIN_ID (discovery port = 7400 + 250*domain). That is peer-to-peer: N participants each announce to N-1 others, so discovery traffic is O(N^2), and it breaks silently whenever multicast breaks — Docker bridge networks, Wi-Fi AP client isolation, VPN interfaces, a firewall. rmw_zenoh deletes multicast entirely and replaces it with one brokered rendezvous point. The cost is that the broker is now a hard dependency with no error message: nodes start perfectly, log nothing, and `ros2 node list` returns empty. That is the exact failure this team lost time to. Nothing in the launch files starts it, because launch has no concept of 'the middleware must be up' — it is infrastructure, not a node.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/docker/Dockerfile:47 installs ros-jazzy-rmw-zenoh-cpp; :81 aliases zenohd; :83 sets RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp. container.sh:130-143 prints a banner warning that zenoh became the default in v5.0.0.
components.interface: TCP 7447. Config via ZENOH_ROUTER_CONFIG_URI (router) and ZENOH_SESSION_CONFIG_URI (each node). Diagnose with `ss -ltnp | grep 7447` before you debug anything ROS-level.
components.rate: n/a (daemon)

components.name: ros2_control_node — the ONE real-time process
components.role: The single OS process that owns /dev/ttyACM0. Inside it live: the ControllerManager, the DynamixelHardware plugin instance, and every loaded controller (joint_state_broadcaster, arm_controller, gripper_controller). It runs a dedicated thread at 100 Hz executing read() -> update() -> write(); a separate executor thread spins the node's services and subscriptions so a slow service call cannot stall the control loop. Executable: `ros2 run controller_manager ros2_control_node`.
components.whyItExists: Because a half-duplex serial bus has exactly one owner. Every additional process that opens the port corrupts framing for the other — this is the teammate-fighting-over-ttyACM0 failure, and the architectural cure is not 'coordinate better', it is 'only one process may ever touch the bus, and everything else talks ROS to it.' Diagnostics included: if you want a servo's raw register, you call the plugin's `/dynamixel_hardware_interface/get_dxl_data` service, you do NOT run a second DynamixelSDK script. Putting the controllers inside the same process as the hardware is also what makes the control loop real-time-able: controller update() reads and writes raw `double*` pointers into the hardware's state/command arrays with zero serialization, zero copies, zero middleware.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_bringup/launch/omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py:138-145. docker-compose.yml:10-15 grants SYS_NICE and rtprio 99 so this process can actually get real-time scheduling.
components.interface: Services: /controller_manager/{list_controllers, load_controller, configure_controller, switch_controller, unload_controller, list_hardware_components, list_hardware_interfaces, set_hardware_component_state} (controller_manager_msgs/srv/*). Parameters: robot_description (URDF string), update_rate.
components.rate: 100 Hz — hardware_controller_manager.yaml:4. That is a 10 ms budget for a full read+update+write of six servos.

components.name: dynamixel_hardware_interface/DynamixelHardware — the hardware interface plugin
components.role: A pluginlib class loaded INTO ros2_control_node (not a node, no topics of its own by default). It implements on_init/on_configure/on_activate/read/write. read() sync-reads Present Position and Present Velocity from IDs 11-16 and writes them into the state interface array; write() sync-writes Goal Position. On activation it also pushes the entire <gpio> parameter block — Operating Mode, Drive Mode, PID gains, Position Limits, Current Limit — into each servo's control table.
components.whyItExists: Two reasons, and both answer a bug this team hit. (1) The plugin is where the URDF becomes the single source of truth for servo configuration. DYNAMIXEL RAM-area registers (PID gains, Profile Velocity, Goal Current) genuinely reset to defaults on power cycle — that is servo firmware behavior, not a bug. The convention is: never poke registers by hand, put them in the ros2_control xacro, and every bringup re-writes them. (2) `is_async="true"` on the <ros2_control> tag runs read()/write() in their own thread, so a serial round trip that overruns 10 ms degrades to a stale sample instead of blowing the control period. On a CDC-ACM device the USB poll interval alone can eat 1-2 ms per transaction; Return Delay Time is set to 0 on every servo for the same reason.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_description/ros2_control/omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:4 (is_async), :18-30 (plugin + port_name + baud_rate 1000000 + error_timeout_ms 500), :75-175 (six <gpio> blocks, IDs 11-16).
components.interface: Exports command interface `<joint>/position` and state interfaces `<joint>/position`, `<joint>/velocity` for joint1..joint5 and gripper_joint_1. Publishes dynamixel_hardware_interface/dxl_state; offers services get_dxl_data, set_dxl_data, reboot_dxl, set_dxl_torque (xacro:26-30).
components.rate: Its own async thread; the 100 Hz loop samples whatever it last produced.

components.name: joint_state_broadcaster — a controller that reads and publishes nothing to hardware
components.role: A lifecycle-managed controller loaded into ros2_control_node. It claims ALL state interfaces and no command interfaces, and each update() publishes the current joint positions/velocities.
components.whyItExists: It is the bridge from the zero-copy real-time world (raw double pointers) into the ROS graph. It is a controller rather than a plain node precisely so it reads the same memory the control loop reads, in the same tick, with no serialization and no time skew. If it is not spawned, /joint_states never exists, so robot_state_publisher publishes no /tf, RViz shows a grey robot at the origin, MoveIt refuses to plan ('Failed to fetch current robot state'), and any policy node waiting for /joint_states hangs forever with no error. It is the most common single cause of 'everything launched fine but nothing works.'
components.evidence: Spawned at omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py:151; type declared at open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml:6-7.
components.interface: Publishes /joint_states (sensor_msgs/msg/JointState) and /dynamic_joint_states (control_msgs/msg/DynamicJointState). Both are global, not node-relative, because use_local_topics defaults to false — the same `topic_name_prefix = use_local_topics ? "~/" : ""` idiom you can read verbatim in this repo at ros2_controller/om_joint_trajectory_command_broadcaster/src/joint_trajectory_command_broadcaster.cpp:112.
components.rate: 100 Hz, locked to controller_manager update_rate.

components.name: arm_controller — joint_trajectory_controller/JointTrajectoryController
components.role: The controller that actually moves the arm. Holds an active trajectory, interpolates it against the real clock every tick, and writes position commands. It claims the position command interface for joint1..joint5 and gripper_joint_1 (all six, because this AI config treats the gripper as just another trajectory joint).
components.whyItExists: Time-parameterized motion needs a component that owns the clock. A naive 'publish a setpoint, servo goes there' loop cannot do blending, cannot report 'goal tolerance violated', and cannot be preempted mid-motion. JTC exists to make a trajectory a first-class object with a lifetime. Note that this AI config folds gripper_joint_1 into arm_controller and drops gripper_controller entirely — the non-AI config keeps them separate. That difference is the imitation-learning crowd's fingerprint: a learned policy emits one 6-vector per timestep, so splitting the gripper into a separate GripperCommand action would force you to re-synchronize two independently-timed streams.
components.evidence: config/omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml:9-10 and :13-32 (six joints incl. gripper). Compare config/omx_f/hardware_controller_manager.yaml:12-13 and :36-39, which splits out a gripper_controller.
components.interface: ACTION SERVER /arm_controller/follow_joint_trajectory (control_msgs/action/FollowJointTrajectory). TOPIC SUBSCRIBER /arm_controller/joint_trajectory (trajectory_msgs/msg/JointTrajectory). PUBLISHER /arm_controller/controller_state (control_msgs/msg/JointTrajectoryControllerState — this was named ~/state in Humble). SERVICE /arm_controller/query_state (control_msgs/srv/QueryTrajectoryState).
components.rate: update() at 100 Hz; goal feedback published at the same rate.

components.name: gripper_controller — position_controllers/GripperActionController (non-AI configs only)
components.role: Exposes a single-joint gripper as a force-limited close/open action rather than a position setpoint.
components.whyItExists: A gripper closing on an object never reaches its commanded position — that is the point. A position controller would report failure or integrate windup forever. GripperCommand has max_effort in the goal and stalled/reached_goal in the result, so 'I stopped because I am holding something' is a success. On this hardware the equivalent trick is done in the servo instead: dxl16 runs Operating Mode 5 (current-based position) with Current Limit and Goal Current both 600, so the firmware itself caps grip force.
components.evidence: config/omx_f/hardware_controller_manager.yaml:12-13, :36-39. omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:165 (Operating Mode 5), :172-174 (Current Limit 600, Goal Current 600, Shutdown 21).
components.interface: ACTION SERVER /gripper_controller/gripper_cmd (control_msgs/action/GripperCommand). Used by open_manipulator_teleop/open_manipulator_teleop/omx_f_teleop.py:46-48.
components.rate: event-driven

components.name: spawner — a transient process that exits, and that is the API
components.role: `ros2 run controller_manager spawner arm_controller joint_state_broadcaster`. It waits for /controller_manager services, then calls load_controller, then configure_controller, then ONE switch_controller to activate all named controllers together, then exits with code 0. It is not part of the running system — after bringup it is gone.
components.whyItExists: Controllers are lifecycle objects with a real state machine, and someone has to drive them through it. Making that driver a short-lived process rather than a launch feature is what lets launch sequence on it: `OnProcessExit(spawner)` is the only reliable 'controllers are now active' event the launch system has. That is exactly how this repo delays RViz and the homing node. The sharp edge: the spawner exits on failure too, so an OnProcessExit handler fires whether the controllers came up or not — RViz will start over a dead arm and look fine. Check `ros2 control list_controllers` (expect `active`), do not trust the launch log.
components.evidence: omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py:147-157 (the spawner), :183-194 (two RegisterEventHandler/OnProcessExit blocks keyed on it). Note the argument order here is arm_controller before joint_state_broadcaster, which is harmless only because a single spawner invocation activates them in one switch_controller call.
components.interface: Client of /controller_manager/load_controller, /configure_controller, /switch_controller. Useful flags it accepts: --controller-manager <ns>, --param-file, --inactive (load+configure but do not activate).
components.rate: once, then exits
