components.name: robot_state_publisher (RSP) — own process
components.role: Parses the URDF string in its `robot_description` parameter into a KDL tree, subscribes /joint_states, and for every message publishes the full chain of parent->child transforms for movable joints on /tf. Fixed joints are computed once and published on /tf_static.
components.whyItExists: This is the question every newcomer asks: why do I need this when I already have joint states? Because /joint_states is a flat list of scalars — `joint2 = -1.57` — and it says nothing about geometry. RSP is the one place the URDF's link lengths and joint origins get applied, and it turns six numbers into a pose tree that every other node can query without any of them parsing the URDF. It exists so that the kinematic model has exactly ONE evaluator. Remove it and nothing errors: /joint_states keeps flowing, the arm keeps moving, and RViz, MoveIt and any TF lookup simply report 'no transform from link0 to end_effector_link' — the classic failure, which is almost never a TF bug and almost always (a) a name prefix you forgot, (b) a joint missing from /joint_states so the chain cannot close, (c) a subscriber that joined after /tf_static was published and used VOLATILE durability, or (d) a lookup timestamp outside the 10 s buffer.
components.evidence: omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py:159-164. Leader variant with frame_prefix at omx_l_leader_ai.launch.py:136-143.
components.interface: SUB /joint_states (sensor_msgs/msg/JointState). PUB /tf (tf2_msgs/msg/TFMessage, RELIABLE depth 100), /tf_static (tf2_msgs/msg/TFMessage, RELIABLE TRANSIENT_LOCAL), /robot_description (std_msgs/msg/String, RELIABLE TRANSIENT_LOCAL depth 1). Params: robot_description, frame_prefix, use_sim_time.
components.rate: /tf at 100 Hz (one per joint_states message); /tf_static exactly once, latched

components.name: joint_state_publisher_gui — development only, and mutually exclusive with real hardware
components.role: A Qt slider panel that FAKES /joint_states so you can inspect a URDF in RViz with no robot present.
components.whyItExists: Because URDF debugging and hardware debugging must never happen at the same time. The failure mode if you leave it running against a live arm is instructive: two publishers on /joint_states, RSP consumes them interleaved, and the TF tree jitters between the real pose and the slider pose. Two publishers on /joint_states is always a bug — the only sanctioned exception is joint_state_publisher itself acting as a designated merger of several partial sources.
components.evidence: open_manipulator_description/launch/omx_f.launch.py:81-85, guarded by IfCondition(use_gui); note :47-49 of the same file force use_mock_hardware:=True so this path can never touch the serial port.
components.interface: PUB /joint_states (sensor_msgs/msg/JointState)
components.rate: ~10 Hz

components.name: move_group — the MoveIt process (ABSENT from the AI pipeline, and that is the point)
components.role: Collision-aware motion planning. Maintains the planning scene, runs OMPL/Pilz/CHOMP, and hands the resulting trajectory to a controller. It is an action CLIENT of /arm_controller/follow_joint_trajectory — MoveIt does not talk to hardware, it talks to ros2_control exactly the way your own code would.
components.whyItExists: To answer 'get from A to B without hitting anything', which is a search problem, not a control problem, and therefore belongs in a different process at a different rate. The load-bearing observation for this team: omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py contains NO move_group. The imitation-learning path deliberately skips planning — the policy emits joint targets directly and JTC executes them. MoveIt lives in a separate launch file you run only when you want planned motion, and it needs robot_description_semantic (SRDF: which links may legitimately touch, named poses, the planning group) which the URDF alone cannot express.
components.evidence: open_manipulator_moveit_config/launch/omx_f_moveit.launch.py:80-92. The controller binding is open_manipulator_moveit_config/config/omx_f/moveit_controllers.yaml:10-18 — type FollowJointTrajectory, action_ns follow_joint_trajectory.
components.interface: ACTIONS served: /move_action (moveit_msgs/action/MoveGroup), /execute_trajectory (moveit_msgs/action/ExecuteTrajectory). SERVICES: /compute_ik, /compute_fk, /plan_kinematic_path (moveit_msgs/srv/GetMotionPlan), /get_planning_scene, /apply_planning_scene. SUB: /joint_states, /tf, /tf_static, /collision_object, /attached_collision_object. PUB: /planning_scene, /monitored_planning_scene, /display_planned_path (moveit_msgs/msg/DisplayTrajectory), /robot_description_semantic (TRANSIENT_LOCAL). CLIENT of /arm_controller/follow_joint_trajectory.
components.rate: event-driven; planning takes 0.1-5 s

components.name: rviz2 — a pure consumer, and a liar about failure
components.role: 3D visualization. Subscribes everything, commands nothing (except the MoveIt MotionPlanning panel, which is an action client of /move_action, and interactive markers).
components.whyItExists: It is the only tool that shows you the TF tree and the robot model in the same frame, which is how you catch a wrong joint sign or a bad link origin in five seconds instead of five hours. Two things newcomers must internalize. First, RViz subscribes to /robot_description with TRANSIENT_LOCAL durability — if RSP is not running when RViz starts, RobotModel stays empty and the error is a small red text in a panel nobody reads. Second, RViz displays let you choose QoS per display, and the default for image displays does not always match what the camera driver offers; `ros2 topic echo` showing data while RViz shows nothing is a QoS mismatch, not a RViz bug. In this container there is a third trap: a window that appears in the taskbar but never paints, because the GPU path is broken.

components.name: joint_trajectory_executor — a transient application node (the 'go home' node)

It also exits when done, which lets launch sequence the next stage on OnProcessExit. components.name: chunk_executor — the policy node (this team's own, and the real subject)
components.role: Subscribes /joint_states, runs the learned policy on the current end-effector pose, decodes the action chunk into joint targets, and publishes a JointTrajectory. Re-plans on a timer at 1/(EXECUTE_STEPS * DT * time_scale) Hz, consuming only the first EXECUTE_STEPS of each chunk before replanning.
components.whyItExists: This is the impedance-matching layer between two worlds that run at incompatible rates, and it is where essentially every imitation-learning bug lives. The policy infers at 5-15 Hz; ros2_control runs at 100 Hz. The chunk executor's job is to keep a valid trajectory in JTC's queue at all times so the arm never stalls waiting for inference, while discarding the tail of each chunk that the next inference will supersede. Two design rules fall out. First, use the TOPIC interface, not the action: each new JointTrajectory should replace the active one with no handshake, and you have no use for a result callback you will cancel 200 ms later. Second, the segment duration is a hard deadline — if inference does not finish inside EXECUTE_STEPS * DT, the arm runs off the end of its trajectory and holds, which looks like stuttering. The --hold mode in this file is the right first-contact test: command exactly the current pose and confirm nothing twitches, which proves frame and joint ORDERING before anything swings.

components.name: MECHANISM — topics vs services vs actions
components.role: Topics: anonymous many-to-many streams, fire-and-forget, no reply. Services: blocking request/response, one server, meant to return in milliseconds. Actions: a goal that takes time — implemented as five underlying topics/services (send_goal, cancel_goal, get_result services; feedback and status topics) presented as one API.
components.whyItExists: The rule is about TIME and OWNERSHIP, not about data. Use a topic when the newest value fully replaces the old one and nobody needs to know it arrived: joint states, images, streaming setpoints. Use a service when you need an answer and it is cheap: 'load this controller', 'give me this servo's register'. Use an action when the operation has duration, because duration forces three things a topic cannot express — FEEDBACK (how far along), RESULT (did it succeed, and why not), and PREEMPTION (a new goal must cancel the old one, and the server must acknowledge the cancel). A trajectory has all three, so FollowJointTrajectory is an action. The deliberate exception is the reason for JTC's topic interface: in a streaming teleop or policy loop you emit a new full trajectory every 20-200 ms, each one superseding the last, and you never wait for a result. Running that through the action protocol would mean a goal handshake and a cancel per tick — pure overhead with no benefit. So ros2_control offers both and lets the caller pick by usage pattern. This repo uses both, in the right places: the action for homing, the topic for teleop and for the policy.

components.name: MECHANISM — the TF tree
components.role: One global, distributed, time-indexed tree of coordinate frames. Any node can publish edges on /tf (dynamic) or /tf_static (fixed). Any node can create a tf2_ros::Buffer + TransformListener and ask 'where was frame A relative to frame B at time t', and tf2 walks the tree and interpolates between the two nearest samples.
components.whyItExists: So that no node ever has to know the full kinematic chain. Your policy node wants the end-effector pose; it does not want to parse the URDF, chain five matrices, and re-derive it every time the mechanical team moves a bracket. The tree is per-EDGE distributed but must be globally a TREE — exactly one parent per frame, no cycles, no orphans. Things that make it fail: two publishers claiming the same child frame (the tree oscillates, and `ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames` is how you see it); a missing joint in /joint_states (RSP skips the edge, the chain breaks silently); requesting a timestamp older than the 10 s default buffer, or newer than the newest sample (use rclpy.time.Time() — meaning 'latest' — rather than a stale message stamp while you are learning); and a late-joining subscriber missing /tf_static because it declared VOLATILE durability. Also: the tree is in a single namespace by default, so two robots need either frame_prefix or separate /tf topics.

components.name: MECHANISM — lifecycle (managed) nodes and controllers
components.role: A four-state machine: unconfigured -> (configure) -> inactive -> (activate) -> active, plus finalized, with transition callbacks on_configure / on_activate / on_deactivate / on_cleanup. Every ros2_control controller AND every hardware component is managed this way.
components.whyItExists: Because allocating resources and touching hardware must be separable from running. on_configure is where you read parameters, allocate buffers and create publishers — everything that might fail, might block, might allocate — and if it fails you find out with a clean error and the system is still safe. on_activate is where you claim the command interfaces and the motor becomes live; it must be fast and allocation-free. The concrete payoff on this arm: you can load and configure arm_controller and gravity_compensation_controller simultaneously, but only one can be ACTIVE, because activation is what claims the `joint1/position` command interface and two controllers cannot own the same interface. That single rule is what makes safe controller switching possible at runtime — `switch_controller` deactivates one and activates the other in a single atomic call within one update cycle, so the arm is never commanded by two things or by nothing. It is also why this repo can comment out gravity_compensation_controller from the spawner list (omx_l_leader_ai.launch.py:128) without touching any other file: the controller is still declared and loadable, just not activated.

components.name: MECHANISM — QoS, and the silent non-connection
components.role: Every publisher OFFERS a QoS profile and every subscriber REQUESTS one. The middleware connects them only if the offer is at least as strong as the request. The axes that bite: Reliability (RELIABLE retransmits, BEST_EFFORT does not), Durability (TRANSIENT_LOCAL keeps the last N for late joiners, VOLATILE does not), History depth, and Deadline/Liveliness/Lifespan.
components.whyItExists: Robotics has two fundamentally different kinds of data and one transport. A camera frame is worthless 100 ms later, so retransmitting it wastes bandwidth and adds latency — BEST_EFFORT, shallow depth. A URDF is published once at startup and every node that ever starts needs it — RELIABLE, TRANSIENT_LOCAL, depth 1. Encoding this per-topic rather than globally is what lets both share one middleware. The cost is the worst failure mode in ROS 2: incompatibility is SILENT by design, because the spec treats an unmatched endpoint as simply not-a-peer. The rule to memorize is that the offer must dominate: a BEST_EFFORT publisher and a RELIABLE subscriber never connect; a VOLATILE publisher and a TRANSIENT_LOCAL subscriber never connect. The reverse directions are both fine. Jazzy does emit a 'New publisher discovered offering incompatible QoS' warning, but it goes to the node's log, which in a launch file with output='both' scrolls past in a wall of other text. Conventional assignments on this system: /joint_states RELIABLE VOLATILE depth 10 (SystemDefaultsQoS); /tf RELIABLE depth 100; /tf_static and /robot_description and /robot_description_semantic RELIABLE TRANSIENT_LOCAL; camera image topics BEST_EFFORT depth 5 (SensorDataQoS); action goal/result services RELIABLE, action feedback and status best-effort-ish with a transient_local status.

components.name: MECHANISM — executors, callback groups, and composition
components.role: An executor is the thread pool that pulls ready callbacks (timers, subscriptions, services, action handlers) off the waitset and runs them. rclcpp::spin() gives you a SingleThreadedExecutor: one thread, every callback serialized. A callback group is the unit of mutual exclusion — MutuallyExclusive (the default; every callback in a node shares one group and never runs concurrently) or Reentrant (may run concurrently with itself and others in the group).
components.whyItExists: Because with the default single-threaded executor, ONE slow callback starves everything else in that node. If your policy node's image callback does 40 ms of preprocessing on the same executor as your 100 Hz control timer, the timer fires at whatever rate is left over, and it will not tell you. Two consequences you must design around. First: never do inference, disk I/O, or a blocking service call inside a callback that shares an executor with anything time-critical — use a MultiThreadedExecutor and put the slow work in its own Reentrant callback group, or move it to a separate node/process. Second, the classic deadlock: calling a service synchronously (spin_until_future_complete, or rclpy's `call()`) from inside another callback in the same MutuallyExclusive group. The response can never be processed because the only thread is blocked waiting for it, and it hangs forever with no error. This is also why ros2_control_node runs its 100 Hz loop in a dedicated thread OUTSIDE the executor — a `list_controllers` service call must never be able to jitter the control period. COMPOSITION is the other half: rclcpp_components lets you load several nodes into one process (ComposableNodeContainer in launch, or `ros2 component load`), which buys intra-process communication — with use_intra_process_comms=True a publish becomes a shared_ptr move instead of serialize -> loopback -> deserialize. For a 921 KB image at 30 Hz per subscriber that is the difference between tens of MB/s of copies and nothing. The trade is isolation: one segfault kills every node in the container. Convention: compose the camera + image_proc + any vision preprocessing; keep ros2_control, move_group and rviz2 as separate processes so a crash in one does not take the arm with it.

components.name: MECHANISM — the middleware layer: rmw, DDS, ROS_DOMAIN_ID, discovery
components.role: rclcpp/rclpy sit on rcl, which sits on rmw, which is a swappable plugin: rmw_fastrtps_cpp (Jazzy's default), rmw_cyclonedds_cpp, or rmw_zenoh_cpp. The rmw is what actually discovers peers and moves bytes. Selected at RUNTIME by the RMW_IMPLEMENTATION environment variable.
components.whyItExists: Discovery is a thing that can break because ROS 2 has no name server. There is no roscore. With DDS, every participant multicasts an announcement and listens for others; the multicast group is 239.255.0.1 and the ports are computed from ROS_DOMAIN_ID (discovery port = 7400 + 250*domain). Everything that breaks multicast breaks ROS 2 silently: Docker bridge networks (which is why docker-compose.yml:16-17 sets network_mode: host and ipc: host — without them the container's participants are in a separate network namespace and see nobody), Wi-Fi client isolation, VPN adapters, and containers whose /dev/shm is not shared (mounted at :23, because Fast DDS prefers shared memory on localhost and falls back badly if it cannot). ROS_DOMAIN_ID is the only isolation you get, and with network_mode: host it is the ONLY thing separating two teammates' stacks on the same Jetson — the serial-port fight this team had has an exact graph-level twin, which is two people's nodes joining the same domain 30 and each other's topics. rmw_zenoh trades multicast for a broker: no discovery packets at all, every node opens a session to rmw_zenohd on tcp/7447, and the router is the graph. It is far more robust across networks and completely fragile in one new way — forget the router and you get a working-looking system with an empty graph. Also non-negotiable: every node in one graph must use the SAME rmw. A Fast DDS node and a Zenoh node on the same domain are simply two separate universes.

components.name: MECHANISM — launch, parameters, xacro, namespaces, remapping
components.role: A launch file is a Python program that returns a LaunchDescription: a list of actions (Node, ExecuteProcess, IncludeLaunchDescription, GroupAction, RegisterEventHandler) and Substitutions, which are lazy values resolved at launch time rather than at import time.
components.whyItExists: Four separate mechanisms that beginners collapse into one. (1) SUBSTITUTIONS are lazy because a launch argument's value is not known when generate_launch_description() runs. `Command([FindExecutable('xacro'), ' ', <path>, ' port_name:=', port_name])` means: at launch time, run xacro as a subprocess with those arguments and make its stdout the value of the robot_description parameter. Consequence: a xacro syntax error surfaces as an opaque launch failure, and the debugging move is always to run it by hand first — `xacro <file> port_name:=/dev/ttyACM0 use_sim:=false > /tmp/omx.urdf` — and read the output. (2) PARAMETERS come from a YAML file keyed by node name; the `/**:` wildcard at the top of every config here matches any node name in any namespace, and that is not decoration — when the leader stack is pushed into the /leader namespace its controller_manager's fully-qualified name becomes /leader/controller_manager, and a file keyed on plain `controller_manager:` would not match at all and every parameter would silently take its default. (3) NAMESPACES (PushRosNamespace) prefix every relative topic, service and node name in the group. (4) REMAPPING rewrites one specific name; applied to a Node it affects every entity in that process, which is how one line at the follower's control_node redirects the trajectory subscription of a controller that does not exist yet. Namespaces and frame_prefix are different axes: the first moves topics, the second moves TF frames, and a second robot needs both.

orderOfOperations: 0. BEFORE any ROS command in a new terminal: confirm the environment triple. `echo $ROS_DISTRO $ROS_DOMAIN_ID $RMW_IMPLEMENTATION` must print jazzy 30 rmw_zenoh_cpp, and `ros2 pkg prefix open_manipulator_bringup` must resolve. Sourcing order is underlay then overlay: /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash, THEN ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash. Reversed, the overlay's package paths get shadowed and you run yesterday's binary while editing today's source. This is step zero because every later symptom — empty node list, stale behavior, package not found — looks like a robotics problem and is this.

1. Start the middleware. `ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd` in its own terminal (or as a service), then verify with `ss -ltnp | grep 7447`. This comes first and is not in any launch file, because launch has no concept of middleware readiness — every node will start happily into a void. With classic DDS the equivalent step is verifying multicast works, which is why network_mode: host and the /dev/shm mount are in docker-compose.yml.

2. Generate and READ the URDF before launching anything. `xacro $(ros2 pkg prefix open_manipulator_description)/share/open_manipulator_description/urdf/omx_f/omx_f.urdf.xacro port_name:=/dev/ttyACM0 use_sim:=false > /tmp/omx.urdf`, then `check_urdf /tmp/omx.urdf`. This order is deliberate: the URDF is the single input to four different consumers (ros2_control_node, robot_state_publisher, move_group, rviz2), and a mistake in it produces four different unrelated-looking errors. Reading the generated file also settles the joint-limit question, because you can see exactly which <limit> values the xacro emitted versus what the <gpio> Min/Max Position Limit registers say.

3. Bring up simulated or mock hardware FIRST, then real. `ros2 launch open_manipulator_bringup omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py use_mock_hardware:=true` swaps the DynamixelHardware plugin for mock_components/GenericSystem (omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:12-16), which mirrors commands into states with zero hardware. Everything above the hardware interface — controllers, TF, topics, your policy node — is bit-identical. The reason this order is non-negotiable is that mock hardware cannot break, cannot fight over a serial port, and cannot hurt anyone, so any failure you see at this stage is unambiguously a software failure. Beginners skip this and then cannot tell a QoS bug from a servo bug.

4. Bring up real hardware with the arm in a safe pose and power ready to cut. `ros2 launch open_manipulator_bringup omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py port_name:=/dev/ttyACM0`. Internal sequence, which you should be able to narrate: ros2_control_node starts -> loads the DynamixelHardware plugin -> on_init parses the six joints and six gpios -> on_configure opens /dev/ttyACM0 at 1000000 baud and pings IDs 11..16 -> on_activate writes Operating Mode, Drive Mode, PID gains and Position Limits into each control table (this is where power-cycle-reset registers get restored) -> the 100 Hz loop starts. Independently, the spawner waits for /controller_manager services, then load -> configure -> one atomic switch_controller activating joint_state_broadcaster and arm_controller together.

5. Verify the graph before verifying motion, in this exact order, because each check depends on the previous one. `ros2 control list_hardware_components` (expect active). `ros2 control list_controllers` (expect both active, not inactive, not unconfigured). `ros2 topic hz /joint_states` (expect ~100). `ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo link0 end_effector_link` (expect a pose that changes when you backdrive the arm). Only then `ros2 action list | grep follow_joint_trajectory`. If /joint_states is silent, nothing downstream can possibly work and debugging RViz or MoveIt is wasted time.

6. Home the arm through the ACTION before streaming anything. `init_position:=true` runs joint_trajectory_executor, which sends a FollowJointTrajectory goal and blocks until every joint is within epsilon 0.15. This precedes teleop and policy execution because gravity compensation and every learned policy assume a known starting configuration, and because it is a full end-to-end proof of the command path using the interface that actually reports success.

7. First real-hardware command must be a HOLD, not a motion. Command exactly the pose the arm is already in and confirm nothing twitches. If it moves, your joint ORDERING or your frame convention is wrong, and you have just learned that at 0 velocity instead of at full speed. The team's own chunk_executor_node.py:178-194 already implements this, with the comment explaining why. Never let the first command be a computed target.

8. Only now add the perception and policy nodes, one at a time, each verified against the live graph. Camera first (`ros2 topic hz /camera1/image_raw/compressed`), then the policy node in dry-run printing targets without publishing, then finally publishing to /arm_controller/joint_trajectory. Adding them together means a failure has N possible causes.

9. Record before you train, and verify the recording before you trust it. `ros2 bag record -o ep_0001 /joint_states /leader/joint_trajectory /camera1/image_raw/compressed`, then `ros2 bag info` and check that the message COUNT matches duration x rate for every topic. Dropped frames from a best-effort image topic under load are invisible at record time and fatal at train time.

10. Reproduce the whole thing from a cold container before you believe any of it. `docker compose down && docker compose up -d` then repeat steps 1-7. The reason this is a step rather than an afterthought: every convention above (pinned image tag robotis/open-manipulator:5.1.1, rosdep install from src, colcon build in the image, udev rules for the serial device, env vars in .bashrc AND re-exported in the s6 service script) exists to make this repetition produce an identical system. If it does not, you have an undocumented manual step, and that step is what will fail on demo day.
keyFacts: The entire real-time control system is ONE process. controller_manager, the DynamixelHardware plugin, joint_state_broadcaster and arm_controller all live inside a single `ros2_control_node`. Controllers talk to hardware through raw `double*` pointers into shared arrays — no topics, no serialization, no middleware. Everything you see in `ros2 topic list` from ros2_control is output, not the control path.

update_rate is 100 Hz (open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml:4). That is a 10 ms budget for a sync-read of six servos, controller update, and a sync-write, over one half-duplex bus at 1 Mbaud through a USB CDC-ACM device. This is why Return Delay Time is set to 0 on all six servos and why the <ros2_control> tag carries is_async="true" (omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:4) — serial I/O runs in its own thread so an overrun degrades to a stale sample instead of blowing the control period.

Joint limits genuinely live in THREE places and only one of them can stop the motor. URDF <limit> tags (enforced in software by joint_limits interfaces and by MoveIt), open_manipulator_moveit_config/config/omx_f/joint_limits.yaml (planning only, ignored by ros2_control), and the DYNAMIXEL Min/Max Position Limit registers in raw 0-4095 ticks (omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:99-100 gives dxl12 830-3129, :116-117 gives dxl13 1024-3140, :133-134 gives dxl14 the full 0-4095). Only the last is enforced by firmware. When three sources disagree, the servo wins.

Drive Mode is 4 on every servo (omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:81, :96, :113, :130, :147, :164). Bit 2 set means TIME-based profile, not velocity-based, which silently changes the units of Profile Velocity and Profile Acceleration from rpm and rev/min^2 to MILLISECONDS. So `Profile Velocity: 50` means 50 ms, not 50 rpm. Reading it as rpm will make every timing calculation wrong.

The gripper servo dxl16 runs Operating Mode 5 (current-based position) with Current Limit and Goal Current both 600 (omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:165, :172-173). That is force-limited gripping done in firmware, which is why the AI config can get away with treating the gripper as an ordinary trajectory joint instead of needing GripperActionController.

The AI/imitation-learning config deliberately folds the gripper into arm_controller as a 6th joint (config/omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml:15-21) and drops gripper_controller entirely, while the standard config splits them (config/omx_f/hardware_controller_manager.yaml:9-13). A learned policy emits one 6-vector per timestep; splitting it would force you to resynchronize two independently-timed command streams.

The complete teleop path uses NO action, NO application node and NO MoveIt. The leader's joint_trajectory_command_broadcaster publishes /leader/joint_trajectory at 100 Hz; the follower's ros2_control_node remaps its /arm_controller/joint_trajectory subscription to that exact topic (omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py:144). Two ros2_control stacks wired directly together through JTC's topic interface.

A second robot needs TWO separate mechanisms, and they are not the same thing. PushRosNamespace('leader') moves TOPICS (omx_l_leader_ai.launch.py:168); frame_prefix='leader_' moves TF FRAMES (:141). TF is a single global tree, so without the frame prefix two robots both publishing 'link0' merge into a nonsense graph while every topic name looks perfectly correct.

The `/**:` wildcard at the top of every controller YAML (config/omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml:1, :12) is load-bearing, not boilerplate. Parameter files match on fully-qualified node name; once the leader stack is pushed into /leader its controller_manager becomes /leader/controller_manager, and a file keyed on plain `controller_manager:` would match nothing and every parameter would silently take its default — including update_rate.

ROS_DOMAIN_ID=30 and RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp are set in ~/.bashrc (docker/Dockerfile:82-83), which means they do NOT apply to anything that does not source .bashrc. The s6 service wrapper works around this twice: it re-exports ROS_DOMAIN_ID at docker/s6-services/common/ros2_service_run.sh:22, and it launches with `exec bash -i -c` at :56 purely to force .bashrc to load. Any process you start that misses this is on a different domain or a different middleware and will see an empty graph.

rmw_zenoh has NO multicast discovery. Every node opens a Zenoh session to the `rmw_zenohd` router on tcp/7447, and nothing in any launch file starts it. Forget it and nodes launch cleanly, log nothing unusual, and `ros2 node list` returns empty. With classic DDS the analogous failure is multicast to 239.255.0.1 on port 7400+250*domain being blocked, which is exactly why docker-compose.yml:16-17 sets network_mode: host and ipc: host and :23 mounts /dev/shm.

The spawner is a process that EXITS, and that exit is the launch system's only reliable 'controllers are active' signal — used twice at omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py:183-194. But it exits on failure too, so OnProcessExit fires either way and RViz will happily start over a dead arm. Verify with `ros2 control list_controllers`, not with the launch log.

QoS incompatibility is silent by design, and the rule is that the publisher's offer must dominate: BEST_EFFORT publisher + RELIABLE subscriber never connect; VOLATILE publisher + TRANSIENT_LOCAL subscriber never connect. /tf_static, /robot_description and /robot_description_semantic are TRANSIENT_LOCAL precisely so late joiners get them; camera images are BEST_EFFORT so stale frames are dropped rather than retransmitted. `ros2 topic info /joint_states --verbose` prints the profile of every endpoint.

rosbag2 records what it RECEIVES and replays TRANSIENT_LOCAL topics as VOLATILE unless you pass --qos-profile-overrides-path. So a best-effort camera topic under CPU load loses frames invisibly at record time, and a replayed bag shows a robot with no static transforms. For an IL dataset both are silent data corruption.

docker-compose.yml grants cap_add: SYS_NICE and ulimits rtprio: 99 (:10-14). Without those the ros2_control_node cannot obtain real-time scheduling inside the container, and your 100 Hz loop jitters under load with no error message anywhere.

The RViz-window-that-never-renders failure is documented in this repo at docker/docker-compose.override.yml:1-15: the container gets /dev/dxg from the /dev mount but not /usr/lib/wsl/lib, so Mesa's d3d12 driver finds a GPU, fails to load libd3d12core.so, and paints nothing. LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 fixes it, and a 5-DOF arm is a trivial enough scene that llvmpipe is plenty.

In this repo, every node is a separate OS process — nothing is composed. That is the correct default at 100 Hz with six joints. It stops being correct when images enter the graph: a 640x480 RGB8 frame is 921 KB, so at 30 Hz with two subscribers you are serializing and copying ~55 MB/s through loopback that composition with use_intra_process_comms would reduce to a pointer move.
beginnerMistakes: Publishing JointTrajectory on /arm_controller/joint_trajectory and then wondering why you cannot tell whether the motion finished. The topic interface has no feedback, no result and no cancel — JTC silently replaces the active trajectory and tells you nothing. The habit: use the ACTION (/arm_controller/follow_joint_trajectory) for any discrete 'go there and tell me when you arrive' motion, and the topic ONLY for a streaming loop where each message supersedes the last and you genuinely never wait. This repo does both correctly — action at joint_trajectory_executor.py:44, topic for teleop at omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py:144 — and the distinction is the reason both interfaces exist.

Writing your own node that publishes /joint_states while joint_state_broadcaster is also publishing. robot_state_publisher consumes them interleaved and the TF tree jitters between two poses. Two publishers on /joint_states is always a bug; the only sanctioned merger is joint_state_publisher itself. Same mistake in a different costume: leaving joint_state_publisher_gui running against live hardware.

Treating 'no transform from link0 to end_effector_link' as a TF bug. It is almost never TF. Check in this order: is /joint_states actually publishing (`ros2 topic hz`), does it contain EVERY joint in the chain (one missing joint breaks the chain silently), does the frame name have a prefix you forgot (leader_link0 vs link0), did your subscriber join after /tf_static was published while declaring VOLATILE durability, and is your lookup timestamp inside the 10 s buffer — while learning, pass rclpy.time.Time() meaning 'latest' rather than a message stamp. `ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames` renders the actual tree and settles it in seconds.

Debugging a topic with `ros2 topic echo`, seeing data, and concluding the subscriber should work. The CLI subscribes with a permissive profile; your node or an RViz display may not. When data flows to echo but not to your node, run `ros2 topic info <topic> --verbose` and compare Reliability and Durability on both endpoints before touching any code. The habit: QoS mismatch is the FIRST hypothesis for 'the publisher is publishing and the subscriber never fires', not the last.

Calling a service synchronously from inside a subscription or timer callback with the default single-threaded executor. The response can never be processed because the one thread is blocked waiting for it. It hangs forever with no error. The habit: inside a callback, use async calls and handle the future in another callback, or move the caller to a MultiThreadedExecutor with a separate Reentrant callback group.

Doing heavy work — inference, image preprocessing, file I/O — in a callback that shares an executor with a control timer. The timer silently runs at whatever rate is left over and nothing warns you. The habit: measure your loop's actual period (`ros2 topic hz` on your own output, or log the delta yourself) rather than trusting the rate you asked for, and isolate slow work in its own executor, callback group or process.

Setting joint limits in one place and assuming it took effect. URDF limits are software, MoveIt's joint_limits.yaml is planning-only, and the DYNAMIXEL Min/Max Position Limit registers in raw ticks are the only ones the motor obeys. The habit: when limits disagree, read the generated URDF and the servo registers (`ros2 service call /dynamixel_hardware_interface/get_dxl_data ...`) rather than the file you last edited.

Fixing a reset servo register by writing it with a standalone DynamixelSDK script. That script opens /dev/ttyACM0 as a second owner of a half-duplex bus and corrupts framing for ros2_control. The correct fix is structural: put the value in the <gpio> block of the ros2_control xacro so the plugin writes it on every on_activate, and get diagnostics through the plugin's services instead of a second serial client. One process owns the bus, always.

Starting rviz2 before robot_state_publisher and concluding RViz is broken when the robot does not appear. RViz gets robot_description over a TRANSIENT_LOCAL topic; if nothing has published it, RobotModel stays empty and the only complaint is small red text inside a collapsed panel.

Reading an empty `ros2 node list` as 'ROS is broken'. It means DISCOVERY is broken, which is a different and much shorter debugging path: is rmw_zenohd running (`ss -ltnp | grep 7447`), does every terminal have the same RMW_IMPLEMENTATION and the same ROS_DOMAIN_ID, and did this shell source .bashrc at all.

Building with colcon and then testing without re-sourcing install/setup.bash, or sourcing the overlay before the underlay. You then debug yesterday's binary while reading today's source, and every conclusion you draw is wrong. The habit: underlay then overlay, every new terminal, no exceptions; `ros2 pkg prefix <pkg>` when in doubt.

Skipping `use_mock_hardware:=true` and going straight to the real arm. Mock hardware exercises the entire stack above the hardware interface — controllers, TF, every topic, your policy node — with nothing that can fight over a port or swing into a table. Any failure there is unambiguously software. Skipping it means every later bug has twice as many candidate causes.

Making the first real command a computed target rather than the current pose. Command exactly where the arm already is; if it twitches, your joint ordering or frame convention is wrong and you have learned that at zero velocity. chunk_executor_node.py:178-194 already implements this test and explains why in a comment.

Assuming that because ros2_control runs at 100 Hz, publishing joint targets at 100 Hz is required or even helpful. JTC interpolates — you send waypoints with time_from_start and it fills in every tick. Publishing a single-point trajectory every 10 ms fights the interpolator and produces exactly the jerky motion you were trying to avoid. Send segments with real durations and let the controller do its job.

Treating docker-compose.yml's `privileged: true` and `/dev:/dev` mount as the solution to device access. It works and it hides the real problem, which is a missing udev rule. This repo ships open_manipulator_bringup/open-manipulator-cdc.rules and a generator script (om_create_udev_rules.py) precisely so the device gets a stable symlink instead of a ttyACM number that changes when you unplug something else.
communityDifferences: ros2_control adoption is nearly universal in vendor and industrial stacks (ROBOTIS, UR, Franka, ABB via ROS-Industrial) and close to absent in the imitation-learning world. LeRobot, the original UMI stack, ACT and Diffusion Policy reference implementations talk to DYNAMIXEL or Feetech servos over pyserial directly at 30-50 Hz, store episodes as HDF5 or parquet, and have no URDF, no TF, no controllers and no middleware. When that crowd does use ROS it is as a thin transport: one subscription to /joint_states, one publisher of JointTrajectory, and a plain Python loop in between — which is exactly the shape of this team's chunk_executor_node.py. Neither approach is wrong; the ROS version buys you RViz, bag recording with real timestamps, and the ability to swap in MoveIt later, at the cost of a stack you must actually understand.

MoveIt's place differs sharply. Research labs run move_group for everything because free-space collision-aware planning is the interesting problem. Industrial integrators usually do NOT run MoveIt in production — paths are taught or offline-programmed, the vendor controller owns motion, and ROS is supervisory. The IL crowd skips planning entirely because the policy IS the planner. Note that this repo takes the industrial-adjacent position for the AI path: omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py contains no move_group at all, and MoveIt lives in a separate launch file you run only when you want planned motion.

Lifecycle discipline. Research code typically ignores managed nodes outside of ros2_control, where it is unavoidable. Industrial deployments make almost everything lifecycle-managed with a supervising state machine, because 'bring the cell to a known safe state and report why you cannot' is a hard requirement. If you are writing application nodes for a capstone, ros2_control's controllers give you the pattern for free and you do not need to lifecycle-manage your own policy node.

Control rates diverge by an order of magnitude and this is the single most important difference for this team. ros2_control at 100 Hz here, 1 kHz on torque-controlled arms (Franka, UR with RTDE). Learned policies infer at 5-15 Hz and emit action chunks executed at 30-50 Hz. Nobody in the IL literature runs a policy at 100 Hz. The chunk executor that bridges those rates is not incidental plumbing — it is a real control component with a hard deadline, and it is where essentially every bug in an IL deployment lives.

Real-time seriousness. Industrial: PREEMPT_RT kernel, isolated CPUs, locked memory, and a separately certified safety channel (dual-channel STO, safety PLC) that ROS is architecturally forbidden from influencing. Research and IL: stock kernel, best effort, and 'safety' means a person near the e-stop. This repo sits in between — docker-compose.yml:10-15 requests SYS_NICE and rtprio 99, so it is at least asking for real-time scheduling, and open_manipulator_collision is an interlock, not a safety system. Be honest with yourselves about which one you have.

Reproducibility conventions. Research labs: a README and a shared workspace on one machine. Industrial: pinned apt snapshots, deterministic Debian package builds, no Docker on the robot controller. This repo takes the middle path that most modern robotics teams now use — a pinned image tag (robotis/open-manipulator:5.1.1), rosdep install from src inside the build, colcon build baked into the image, and s6-overlay as an init system so ROS launches become supervised services with logs. That last part is a genuinely industrial touch you rarely see in lab code, and it is why docker/s6-services/ exists.

Composition. The image-pipeline community (image_proc, RealSense, Nav2) composes aggressively because intra-process zero-copy is the difference between working and not. Manipulation stacks, including this one, usually do not compose anything, because at six joints and 100 Hz the copies are free and process isolation is worth more than throughput. Expect to change sides the moment two cameras enter your graph.

Middleware choice is currently in flux and this matters for what advice you find online. Jazzy's default is Fast DDS; Cyclone is the common swap for multi-machine reliability; rmw_zenoh is new, is what this container uses, and changes the failure modes enough that most tutorials you read will describe symptoms you will never see and omit the one you will (the missing router). When you search for a discovery problem, filter by which rmw the answer assumes.

components.name: Layer 0 — DYNAMIXEL firmware position limits (EEPROM Min/Max Position Limit, addr 52/48)
components.role: The servo itself clamps Goal Position into [Min, Max] and returns a Data Range Error for a write outside it. The motor never attempts the pose. This is the only layer that still functions when every line of host code is wrong.
components.whyItExists: It catches the class of error where the host commands a physically impossible pose: an IK branch flip, a sign error, a NaN, a degrees-vs-radians unit error, or a garbage action chunk from an untrained policy. No host-side check survives a host-side bug — this one lives on the far side of the serial link, in a different processor, so it fails independently. That independence is the whole argument for defence in depth: one good check is one machine that can be wrong.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_description/ros2_control/omx_f.ros2_control.xacro — dxl12 Min 830 / Max 3129, dxl13 Min 1024 / Max 3140, dxl14 and dxl15 set 0..4095 (i.e. no limit at all), and dxl11 has NO Min/Max params and `Operating Mode 4` (Extended Position), where the e-manual states these registers are not used. So joint1 is entirely unprotected at the firmware layer, and joints 4/5 nominally so.
components.interface: 4-byte EEPROM registers 48 and 52, in ticks 0..4095 with 2048 = 0 rad. Written once by the hardware interface at init; enforced continuously by servo firmware.
components.rate: written once at init; enforced every firmware control cycle

components.name: Layer 0b — DYNAMIXEL firmware rate limits (Profile Velocity 112, Profile Acceleration 108, Velocity Limit 44)
components.role: Caps how fast the servo will slew toward any Goal Position, regardless of what the host asked for or whether the host is still running. This is the actual speed governor on your arm.
components.whyItExists: A single bad Goal Position write is executed in full by the servo whether or not the host process is alive. Without a motion profile the motor slams to the new goal at full PWM. With one, 'teleport' becomes 'bounded slew' — which converts a bug into something a human can see coming and stop.
components.evidence: omx_f.ros2_control.xacro sets `Profile Velocity 50` and `Profile Acceleration 25` on every gpio block. 50 x 0.229 rev/min = 1.20 rad/s ~= 69 deg/s; 25 x 214.577 rev/min^2 = 9.36 rad/s^2. That is FAR below the 180 deg/s guard in open_manipulator/docker/workspace/dummy_exec/chunk_executor_node.py (MAX_JOINT_VEL), so your software check can never fire first — the firmware wins silently, by lagging the commanded trajectory, and nothing in the stack reports that lag.
components.interface: RAM registers. They reset to 0 on power cycle unless rewritten at init — this is exactly the 'servo RAM registers silently resetting' problem you already hit.
components.rate: written at init; applied per goal-position write (every 10 ms at 100 Hz)

components.name: Layer 0c — Torque ceiling and compliance (Current Limit 38, Goal Current 102, PWM Limit 36, Operating Mode 5)
components.role: Poor-man's force limiting. Current-based position mode drives toward a position but saturates at a commanded current, so the joint stalls against an obstacle at a bounded force instead of crushing it.
components.whyItExists: Pure position control has infinite commanded stiffness: it will bend a gripper finger, crush the object, or stall the motor at full current until the overload shutdown trips. Bounding current bounds the contact force. It is the cheapest substitute a lab has for a force/torque sensor.
components.evidence: dxl16 (gripper) runs `Operating Mode 5` with `Current Limit 600` and `Goal Current 600` against the XL330-M288's 0..1750 (~1 mA/unit) range, i.e. ~34%. Critically: joints 1-3 are XL430-W250, which has NO Current Limit register at all. Their only output cap is PWM Limit(36), default 885 at 0.113%/unit. You cannot make this arm's shoulder or elbow compliant — you can only slow them down. That is a hardware fact, not a configuration choice, and it is why the speed limits in Layer 0b matter more here than on a torque-controlled arm.
components.interface: Current Limit is EEPROM (persists); Goal Current is RAM (resets).

components.name: Layer 0d — Servo self-protection (Hardware Error Status 70, Shutdown 63)
components.role: Autonomous, host-independent. When a monitored condition trips (over-temperature, overload, electrical shock, input voltage), the servo sets the error bit and — if that bit is enabled in Shutdown(63) — clears Torque Enable(64) by itself.
components.whyItExists: It protects the motor from burning out. Be clear about what it is NOT: it protects the hardware, not the human, and it produces the worst possible failure mode for an arm — the joint goes limp instantly, under load, and the arm falls. An overheated joint2 holding an extended arm is precisely the configuration in which this will fire.
components.evidence: X-series bit layout: 0x01 input voltage, 0x04 overheating, 0x08 motor encoder, 0x10 electrical shock, 0x20 overload. XL430-W250 default Shutdown = 52; XL330-M288 default = 53. The vendor sets `<param name="Shutdown">21</param>` on dxl16 = 0b010101 = input voltage + overheating + electrical shock, deliberately REMOVING overload (0x20) — because a gripper in current-based position mode stalls on the object by design and would otherwise trip constantly. Temperature Limit(31) default is 72 C (XL430) / 70 C (XL330). Recovery: a REBOOT is the only way to set Torque Enable back to 1 — service `dynamixel_hardware_interface/reboot_dxl`.
components.rate: evaluated continuously in firmware; status readable per read cycle

components.name: Layer 0e — Bus Watchdog (addr 98): the only true hardware deadman on this arm
components.role: While Torque Enable = 1, if no instruction packet arrives within N x 20 ms (N = 1..127, max 2.54 s), the servo stops, zeroes Profile Acceleration/Velocity, latches Bus Watchdog to -1, and makes every Goal register read-only until a 0 is written.
components.whyItExists: This is the literal answer to 'what happens when the control process dies mid-motion, or the USB cable is pulled, or the container is SIGKILLed'. Without it, a position-mode DYNAMIXEL holds its last Goal Position forever and completes any profile already in flight. Your arm does not go limp and does not stop — it finishes the last bad command and then pushes against whatever it reached.
components.evidence: Not set anywhere in the vendor repo — the register default is 0 (deactivated). Adding `<param name="Bus Watchdog">5</param>` (100 ms) to each gpio block in omx_f.ros2_control.xacro gives 10x margin over the 10 ms write period implied by `update_rate: 100` in open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml. Caveat that costs you an afternoon: the -1 latch is sticky, the vendor hardware interface does not know to clear it, so recovery needs `dynamixel_hardware_interface/set_dxl_data` or a reboot. Test it by unplugging USB while the arm creeps at a safe pose — not by reasoning about it.
components.rate: N x 20 ms, N settable 1..127

components.name: Layer 1 — Hardware interface (dynamixel_hardware_interface plugin)
components.role: Owns /dev/ttyACM0, performs the sync read/write, converts ticks to radians, and is where bus faults become ros2_control faults. `error_timeout_ms=500` is its comms tolerance; `disable_torque_at_init=true` means the arm is LIMP from container start until controllers spawn.
components.whyItExists: It is the single-writer boundary on the serial port. Every 'teammate's process fighting mine over /dev/ttyACM0' incident is a violation of this boundary, not a mysterious bug. It is also the layer that must translate a comms failure into something the framework can act on: if read() or write() returns hardware_interface::return_type::ERROR, controller_manager stops every controller using that hardware and calls on_error(); if the component reaches FINALIZED it cannot be recovered without reloading the plugin (there is no Controller Manager service for that).
components.evidence: omx_f.ros2_control.xacro params block. Note `is_async="true"` on the <ros2_control> tag: the hardware runs in its own thread so serial latency cannot stall the 100 Hz loop — the price is that the state you read may be one cycle stale, which matters when you diff commanded against actual.
components.interface: read()/write() per control cycle; services set_dxl_torque, reboot_dxl, get_dxl_data, set_dxl_data; topic dynamixel_hardware_interface/dxl_state
components.rate: 100 Hz for omx_f (the omy arms in the same repo run 400 Hz)

components.name: Layer 2 — ros2_control command limiting (enforce_command_limits, URDF <limits> and <safety_controller>)
components.role: The framework's saturation and soft limiter. It runs after the controller has written and before the hardware write, clamping position, velocity, acceleration, deceleration, jerk and effort. With soft limits configured (soft_lower_limit, soft_upper_limit, k_position, k_velocity), the permitted velocity is ramped down as you approach the hard limit, so you decelerate into the stop rather than arrive at speed.
components.whyItExists: It catches a controller doing something legal-looking but out of range: a JTC handed a goal outside limits, a chained controller summing into an over-range command, a teleop axis scaled wrong. It is the checkpoint between 'your code' and 'the motor', and unlike Layer 0 it can decelerate smoothly instead of hard-clamping.
components.evidence: On this repo it does nothing at all. open_manipulator/open_manipulator_description/urdf/omx_f/omx_f_arm.urdf.xacro gives every joint `<limit velocity="4.8" effort="1000" lower="-2*pi" upper="2*pi"/>` (lines 37, 72, 107, 142, 177, 212) — placeholders. grep finds no <safety_controller>, no soft_lower_limit, no k_position anywhere in the repo, and `enforce_command_limits` is set in no hardware_controller_manager.yaml. Putting real numbers here is the single highest-value configuration change available to you.

components.name: Layer 3 — Controller guards (JointTrajectoryController constraints and cmd_timeout)
components.role: JTC can abort a goal when actual strays from desired by more than `constraints.<joint>.trajectory`, or misses the endpoint by `constraints.<joint>.goal` within `constraints.goal_time`; `cmd_timeout` marks the command stale after the trajectory ends.
components.whyItExists: This is how you detect 'the arm is not doing what I asked' — stalled against the table, jammed gripper, a servo that hit its own firmware limit, a load it cannot lift. Without it the controller reports success while the arm sits still. It catches a different class from Layer 2: Layer 2 catches bad commands, Layer 3 catches good commands that reality refused.
components.evidence: Absent from open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml, which sets only joints, interface_name, command/state interfaces, and allow_partial_joints_goal: true. Given Layer 0b caps you at ~69 deg/s, your arm is routinely lagging its commanded trajectory right now and nothing says so. Note the gotcha: cmd_timeout is measured from the END of the trajectory and is ignored unless it is greater than constraints.goal_time; default 0 disables it.
components.rate: evaluated every controller update (100 Hz)

components.name: Layer 4 — Geometric collision checking (MoveIt PlanningScene, or the vendor self_collision_node)
components.role: Checks the robot's collision geometry against itself and against a modelled world (table, camera rig, bins) at every sampled state ALONG a plan, with an Allowed Collision Matrix for pairs that are always in contact.
components.whyItExists: Analytic IK answers 'what joint angles put the tool there'. It says nothing about whether the arm passes through the table, through itself, through the camera mast, or through a hand on the way. Collision is a different question from kinematics and no amount of IK correctness substitutes for it. This is the layer a UMI-style open-loop IK pipeline most conspicuously lacks.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_collision/src/self_collision_node.cpp wraps each link in an FCL capsule built from the URDF <collision> cylinder, runs KDL FK, and checks 13 hard-coded pairs (link6 vs link0/1/2/3; end_effector_flange_link vs link1-4; link5 vs link1-3; link4 vs link1; link3 vs link1), publishing std_msgs/Bool on /collision_flag. Two limitations to know: it subscribes to /leader/joint_states (it was written to guard the leader arm during teleop), and it models nothing outside the URDF — no table, no fixture, no human.
components.interface: in: sensor_msgs/JointState; out: std_msgs/Bool on /collision_flag, visualization_msgs/MarkerArray on /collision_marker

components.name: Layer 5 — Application-level sanity checks (your own gate, before you publish)
components.role: The cheapest and most specific layer: reject a command you already know is wrong, in the units and the coordinate frame the application actually thinks in, with a human-readable reason.
components.whyItExists: It is the only layer that knows intent — that this chunk is a pick, that the gripper should already be closed, that a 40 cm jump between consecutive anchor poses means the policy lost the frame. Every lower layer sees only numbers and can only clamp; this layer can say WHY and refuse the whole segment.
components.evidence: You already have the right shape of this. chunk_executor_node.py build_segment() rejects an entire segment if any step exceeds MAX_JOINT_VEL = 180 deg/s and holds position rather than publishing something unsafe; omx_kinematics.py has within_limits()/limit_report(); and `--hold` commands exactly the measured pose as a first-contact test so nothing should move. What is missing and costs an afternoon: a table z-floor check (reject any commanded TCP below the table plane), a reach check against MAX_REACH = 0.4032 m, an explicit NaN/inf check, and a staleness check on /joint_states (if the last JointState is older than ~100 ms, stop publishing — right now `self.q` simply keeps its last value forever).

components.name: Emergency stop — hardware, IEC 60204-1 Category 0
components.role: A latching mushroom-head switch wired in series with the DC feed to the servo power hub, so pressing it removes motor power with zero software in the path.
components.whyItExists: Every software stop requires the software to be alive, the network up, the topic subscribed, the executor scheduled and the CPU not pegged. Those are exactly the conditions that fail when you need the stop. ISO 13850 permits only Category 0 (immediate power removal) and Category 1 (controlled stop, then power removal) for an emergency stop; Category 2 (software stop, power retained) is explicitly excluded from being called an e-stop. A `ros2 lifecycle` call, a deactivate service, a Ctrl-C and an /emergency_stop topic are all Category 2 at best.
components.evidence: Cost: a latching NC mushroom switch rated for your supply current, spliced into the barrel-jack line, ~$10-20 and one hour. Two traps: (a) do NOT put it in the USB line — killing comms leaves torque ON and the servos hold their last goal forever, which is a stuck robot, not a stopped one; (b) on a 560 g arm with no brakes, cutting power to an extended arm means the arm falls. That is still the correct trade, and it is precisely why the arm should never be extended over anything you care about. For a capstone this is mandatory; dual-channel ISO 13849 PLd Cat-3 safety relays are industrial practice and overkill here.

components.name: Gravity and torque sequencing — startup, shutdown, holding vs braking
components.role: Defines what the motors are doing at every transition. The OMX has no brakes: torque off means free fall, torque on means the servo snaps to whatever Goal Position it holds.
components.whyItExists: This is the most common way a student arm damages itself, and it happens at bring-up and shutdown, not during the interesting part. Torque-enable with a stale goal makes the arm jump at Profile Velocity from wherever it physically is to wherever the register says. Torque-disable drops 335 g of linkage.
components.evidence: Masses in omx_f_arm.urdf.xacro sum to 0.559 kg total (matching the 560 g figure), of which 0.335 kg sits above joint2 and falls. Holding that horizontally is roughly 0.6-0.7 N-m at joint2, ~40% of an XL430-W250's stall torque — a continuous load that heats the joint toward the 72 C Temperature Limit, at which point Shutdown(63) cuts torque and the arm falls anyway. Meanwhile `disable_torque_at_init=true` in omx_f.ros2_control.xacro means the arm is limp for the whole window between container start and controller spawn. The rule: torque-cycle ONLY in a folded/parked pose where every link is supported or near-vertical, and never park an extended pose for minutes. Startup: support by hand or in a cradle, start the stack, read back Present Position and confirm it matches the fold, run `--hold` and confirm nothing moves, only then move. Shutdown is the exact reverse: drive to park, WAIT for arrival, stop the controller, torque off, cut power.

components.name: Process lifecycle and shutdown sequencing (s6, launch, container)
components.role: Converts 'someone pressed Ctrl-C' or 'the container restarted' into a defined motor state rather than an accident.
components.whyItExists: SIGKILL leaves the servos exactly as they were: torque on, holding the last goal, mid-reach. SIGINT with enough grace period lets ros2_control deactivate controllers and the hardware interface run on_deactivate. The gap between those two outcomes is where you either park safely or freeze the arm over the table.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/docker/s6-services/open_manipulator_bringup/down-signal = SIGINT; docker/s6-services/common/ros2_service_finish.sh writes the process-group id to /run/<service>.pgid, sends SIGTERM to the whole group, waits up to 30 s, then SIGKILL. That is a competently built sequence — copy the pattern. But docker/docker-compose.yml sets `restart: always`, which means a crashed stack comes back up and re-enables torque with no human present; for an arm that is the most dangerous line in the file. The same file uses `privileged: true`, `/dev:/dev` and `network_mode: host`, so the container will happily contend with any host process for /dev/ttyACM0 — the serial-port fight you already had is structural, not bad luck.

components.name: Post-mortem instrumentation (rosbag2 + run stamping)
components.role: Records enough that you can answer 'what was the arm doing 200 ms before it hit the table' without having to reproduce the incident.
components.whyItExists: Hardware incidents are expensive and frequently not reproducible. What you need afterwards is the command stream, the state stream, and an exact record of what code and what servo configuration were running. Two of those three are not in git: RAM registers reset on power cycle, so the servo's actual configuration is only recoverable if you dumped it.
components.evidence: `ros2 bag record -o run_$(date +%F_%H%M%S) /joint_states /leader/joint_trajectory /dynamixel_hardware_interface/dxl_state /collision_flag /tf /rosout` costs a few MB per minute at 100 Hz for six joints — leave it on permanently. Replay with `ros2 bag play --clock` and `use_sim_time:=true` on every consumer, including RViz, or your timestamps come from the wall clock and nothing lines up. Stamp each run with `git rev-parse HEAD` for both the vendor repo and your own workspace, the image tag (`robotis/open-manipulator:5.1.1` per docker-compose.yml), and a full control-table dump from docker/workspace/dummy_exec/omx_probe.py.

components.name: Human factors — the first-motion-of-the-day ritual
components.role: The procedural layer that the technical layers assume exists.
components.whyItExists: Most near-misses in a student lab are not software faults. They are a person leaning into the workspace while a teammate runs a script from another terminal. No amount of joint limits addresses that; a named operator and a cleared table do.
components.evidence: Concrete version for your arm: clear a 0.5 m radius (MAX_REACH = 0.4032 m in omx_kinematics.py, plus gripper and payload); exactly one person is the operator and has a hand on the e-stop or the power switch; announce out loud before any run; the first run of the day is `--hold` (nothing should move), then a real run at `--time-scale 8` before dropping toward the TIME_SCALE = 2.0 default. And the discipline that pays for itself fastest: never change two things at once. One variable per run, written down, with the bag filename next to it.

orderOfOperations: 1. Read the truth off the hardware before you write anything anywhere. Stop the ros2_control stack (only one process may hold /dev/ttyACM0) and run docker/workspace/dummy_exec/omx_probe.py, extended to also dump Model Number(0), Shutdown(63), Hardware Error Status(70) and Temperature Limit(31). Cost: zero. It goes first because every number in every later layer must be derived from what is actually enforced, and because you cannot settle a limits argument with a datasheet — you settle it with a register read.

2. Collapse the limits to one authoritative source and generate the rest from it. Today four numbers disagree per joint (URDF +/-2pi and velocity 4.8; MoveIt joint_limits.yaml max_velocity 5.0; firmware Velocity Limit(44) default 6.35 rad/s; actual Profile Velocity 1.20 rad/s). Pick the servo EEPROM as truth, emit the URDF <limits> and your Python JOINT_LIMITS from that one table, and demote the datasheet to documentation. Cost: an afternoon. It goes second because the three-sources-disagree problem is a structural defect, not a puzzle to solve once — left in place it will re-bite you every time someone edits a file.

3. Install the hardware e-stop in the DC feed. ~$15 and one hour. It goes before any autonomous motion because it is the only layer that works when everything else is broken, and it is by a wide margin the cheapest risk removed per hour spent. Test it by pressing it while the arm moves slowly in a folded pose, so you see the fall you are choosing to accept.

4. Make the arm only ever torque-cycle in the fold. Build or buy a physical cradle; write a park-then-stop shutdown path; remove or gate `restart: always` in docker/docker-compose.yml so a crash cannot silently re-energise the arm. Cost: a day. It comes here because you will do this transition dozens of times a day — it is the highest-frequency risk you own, and frequency beats severity in expected cost.

5. Turn on rosbag recording for every run and write a three-line run-stamp script (git SHAs, image tag, servo control-table dump). Cost: one hour. Do it before tuning anything, because from this point every incident becomes analyzable and the value compounds; done later, the expensive failures you already had stay unrecoverable.

6. Add the application-level gates your pipeline is missing: table z-floor, reach vs MAX_REACH, NaN/inf, and /joint_states staleness. Cost: an afternoon. It comes before framework-level clamping because it is the cheapest code to write, it catches the errors your specific pipeline actually makes, and it fails loudly with a readable reason instead of silently saturating.

7. Fill in the URDF <limits> with real numbers, add <safety_controller> soft limits, and enable `enforce_command_limits` on ros2_control_node. Cost: a day including testing. After step 6 deliberately: a framework clamp silently modifies your command, so you want your own gate to fire first and tell you why.

8. Set Bus Watchdog(98) on every servo — 5 (100 ms) is a sane start against a 10 ms write period — and verify it by physically pulling the USB cable while the arm creeps in a safe pose. Cost: an hour to set, half a day to handle the sticky -1 latch and write a clear-and-recover path. It comes after steps 3 and 4 because testing a deadman is itself a motion test and needs the e-stop and the safe pose to already exist.

9. Add JTC `constraints` (per-joint trajectory and goal tolerances, goal_time) and `cmd_timeout`. Cost: a day of tuning. After steps 2 and 7, because tolerances only mean something once you know the achievable rates — set them tight while Profile Velocity caps you at 69 deg/s and every goal aborts, and you will disable them in frustration.

10. Add a geometric collision layer. Either adopt MoveIt's PlanningScene with the table and fixtures modelled (roughly a week, and it changes your architecture — MoveIt plans, it does not stream), or extend open_manipulator_collision/src/self_collision_node.cpp with a table half-space and re-point it at /joint_states (roughly a day, keeps your streaming architecture, gives you a /collision_flag your executor can latch on). It is last of the technical items because it is the most work and, for a table-top pick, the z-floor check from step 6 already buys most of the practical benefit.

11. Write the operating procedure as a one-page checklist and put it on the wall next to the arm. Cost: one hour. It is last because it should describe what the system actually does, and it only becomes true once steps 1-10 exist. A checklist that describes aspirations trains people to ignore checklists.
keyFacts: Your arm's real speed cap is firmware, not software: Profile Velocity 50 x 0.229 rev/min = 1.20 rad/s = 69 deg/s, and Profile Acceleration 25 x 214.577 rev/min^2 = 9.36 rad/s^2. Your app-level guard is 180 deg/s and therefore can never fire first.

Four sources give four different velocity limits for the same joint: URDF 4.8 rad/s, MoveIt joint_limits.yaml 5.0 rad/s, firmware Velocity Limit(44) default 265 = 6.35 rad/s, actual enforced 1.20 rad/s. Only the last one is real.

Position limits are enforced by firmware only in Operating Mode 3. joint1 (dxl11) runs Operating Mode 4 (Extended Position), where the e-manual states Min/Max Position Limit are not used — and the xacro sets none anyway. joint1 has zero firmware protection and can wind up multiple turns.
joint2 is clamped to ticks 830..3129 and joint3 to 1024..3140 in omx_f.ros2_control.xacro. joints 4 and 5 are set to 0..4095, which is the full range, i.e. no limit.

URDF masses sum to 0.559 kg total, with 0.335 kg above joint2. That 335 g is what falls when torque is disabled, and holding it horizontally is ~0.6-0.7 N-m at joint2 — about 40% of an XL430-W250's stall torque, a continuous thermal load.

Temperature Limit(31) defaults to 72 C (XL430-W250) and 70 C (XL330-M288). On trip the servo clears Torque Enable itself, and a REBOOT is the only way to re-enable torque. So over-temperature manifests as the arm going limp, not as a warning.

Shutdown(63) X-series bits: 0x01 input voltage, 0x04 overheating, 0x08 motor encoder, 0x10 electrical shock, 0x20 overload. XL430 default 52, XL330 default 53. The vendor sets 21 on the gripper — deliberately removing overload, because a gripper in current-based position mode stalls on the object by design.

XL430-W250 has no Current Limit register at all. Joints 1-3 cannot be current-limited or made compliant; their only output ceiling is PWM Limit(36), default 885 at 0.113%/unit. Compliance on this arm exists only on the XL330 joints (4, 5, gripper).

Bus Watchdog(98) is the one real hardware deadman available: 1..127 in units of 20 ms, max 2.54 s. It is currently 0 (off) throughout the repo. On trip it stops the servo, zeroes the profile, latches to -1 and makes all Goal registers read-only until a 0 is written.

controller_manager `update_rate` is 100 Hz for omx_f and 400 Hz for the omy arms in the same repo — so a DYNAMIXEL write goes out every 10 ms on your arm. `error_timeout_ms` is 500, and `is_async="true"` puts the hardware in its own thread, meaning read() state can be one cycle stale.

ISO 13850 and IEC 60204-1 permit only stop Category 0 (immediate power removal) and Category 1 (controlled stop then power removal) as emergency stops. Category 2 — software stop with power retained — is explicitly excluded. Every ROS-level stop you can write is Category 2.

In ros2_control, a read()/write() returning hardware_interface::return_type::ERROR causes controller_manager to stop every controller using that hardware and call on_error(). If the component ends in FINALIZED it cannot be recovered without reloading the plugin, and there is no Controller Manager service to do that.

JTC `cmd_timeout` is measured from the END of the trajectory, is ignored unless greater than `constraints.goal_time`, and defaults to 0 (disabled). It is not a heartbeat on the publisher — if you want 'the policy process died', you must implement that yourself.

EEPROM registers (Operating Mode 11, Current Limit 38, Min/Max Position Limit 48/52, Shutdown 63) survive power cycles. RAM registers (Position P/I/D Gain 80/82/84, Profile Acceleration 108, Profile Velocity 112, Goal Current 102, Bus Watchdog 98) do not. That asymmetry is the 'registers silently resetting' behaviour you already hit, and it is why a run stamp must include a control-table dump.

MoveIt's `default_velocity_scaling_factor` and `default_acceleration_scaling_factor` are both 0.1 in open_manipulator_moveit_config/config/omx_f/joint_limits.yaml — but that file also declares NO position limits, and none of it applies to you anyway, because chunk_executor_node.py publishes JointTrajectory directly and bypasses MoveIt entirely.

The s6 shutdown path in docker/s6-services/common/ros2_service_finish.sh is SIGINT, then SIGTERM to the recorded process group, then a 30 s wait, then SIGKILL — a good pattern to copy. But docker-compose.yml sets `restart: always`, which will re-energise a crashed arm with nobody watching.
beginnerMistakes: Believing a software stop is an e-stop. A topic, a service, a lifecycle transition and a Ctrl-C all require the software to be alive, scheduled and connected — the exact conditions that fail when you need to stop. A real e-stop removes motor power in hardware; everything else is a 'stop request'.

Putting the kill switch in the USB line. Cutting comms on a position-mode DYNAMIXEL leaves torque ON and the servo holding its last goal forever. You get a stuck robot straining against an obstacle, not a stopped one. The switch belongs in the DC power feed.

Treating the URDF as the limit authority. In this repo every joint reads lower=-2pi upper=2pi effort=1000 — placeholders that would let you command anything. The URDF is a description of geometry for FK and visualisation; it enforces nothing unless ros2_control's limiter is explicitly enabled with real numbers.

Torque-disabling an extended arm to 'reset it' or 'move it by hand'. There are no brakes. Fold it first, or hold it, every time — including when you are just restarting the container, which with disable_torque_at_init=true means the arm is limp the whole time the stack is coming up.

Testing at full speed because slow 'is not a real test'. Almost every failure mode you care about — wrong sign, wrong frame, IK branch flip, joint-order mismatch — appears identically at 10% speed and costs nothing there. Your TIME_SCALE knob exists for this; use 8 before you use 2.

Assuming a position-controlled servo stops when the host dies. It does not. It holds the last Goal Position indefinitely and completes any in-flight motion profile. Only Bus Watchdog(98) changes that, and it is off by default.

Assuming analytic IK protects you from anything geometric. IK answers 'what angles put the tool here'. It is silent on whether the path passes through the table, through the arm itself, or through a hand. Those are separate checks and you currently have neither.

Checking only the endpoint pose instead of the path. A chunk decoder that validates the final target and not the intermediate steps will happily swing through the table between two legal poses. Your build_segment() already validates per-step — extend that discipline to z-floor and reach, not just velocity.

Changing two things at once. The single most expensive habit in robot bring-up: after a run that behaves differently you cannot attribute the change, so you burn a day re-deriving what you already knew. One variable per run, written down, with the bag filename beside it.
Not recording anything, so the one genuinely interesting crash is gone forever. Rosbag on /joint_states plus your command topic is a few MB per minute. Turn it on and leave it on.

Reading 'the controller reported success' as 'the arm got there'. With no `constraints` configured, JTC will report a successful goal while the arm sits stalled against an obstacle or lagging far behind because firmware capped it at 69 deg/s.
Leaving `restart: always` on a robot container. It is correct for a web service and dangerous for an arm: a crash loop re-enables torque repeatedly with nobody present.

Writing RAM registers once and assuming they persist. Profile Velocity, PID gains, Goal Current and Bus Watchdog all reset on power cycle. If your bring-up does not rewrite them every time, your arm's behaviour silently depends on whether someone unplugged it.

Trusting one good check instead of layers. Every check runs on some machine that can itself be wrong — the same process that computes the bad command also runs the validator that should reject it. Defence in depth is not redundancy for its own sake; it is placing checks on hardware that fails independently (servo firmware, hardware interface, controller, planner, application).

Mistaking overload/overheat shutdown for a safety feature that protects people. It protects the motor. From the arm's point of view it is an uncommanded, instantaneous torque-off under load — i.e. it makes the arm fall at the worst possible moment.

Skipping the `--hold` step on the first run after any change. Commanding exactly the measured pose is a complete end-to-end test of joint ordering, units, frames, remapping and the controller chain, and it is the only test where the correct outcome is visibly 'nothing happens'.
communityDifferences: Industrial practice builds safety in an independent hardware channel: dual-channel e-stop loops with safety relays, ISO 13849 PLd / Category 3 architectures, a safety-rated controller that monitors the motion controller, fail-safe brakes on every axis that engage on power loss, and — for collaborative operation — ISO/TS 15066 power-and-force limits validated with an actual force gauge, then certified by a third party. None of that is available or proportionate on a 560 g hobby-class arm. What transfers, and transfers cheaply, is the principle: the protective channel must be independent of the channel it protects, and stopping means removing power, not asking politely.

Research labs typically run exactly one hardware e-stop, lean on ros2_control and MoveIt for limits, and rely heavily on culture — first run at 10% speed, hand on the button. Per-project safety code is written ad hoc and rarely reviewed. A notable split within labs: teams on torque-controlled arms (Franka, UR, Kinova) get mechanical compliance for free and therefore under-invest in command sanity checking, and their habits transfer badly to a position-controlled DYNAMIXEL arm where an out-of-range command is executed with full stiffness. You are in the second category; do not copy the first category's casualness about command validation.

The imitation-learning community (UMI, ALOHA, Diffusion Policy, LeRobot) mostly relies on: a small weak arm, low position gains, a current-limited gripper, and a human standing there — plus an action space defined relative to the current pose, which bounds per-step motion by construction. They bypass MoveIt entirely and stream joint targets at 10-50 Hz, so planner-level collision checking simply does not exist in that pipeline. That is a defensible engineering choice at their scale, and it is essentially your situation.
