But be explicit about the consequence: your application-level gate and the DYNAMIXEL profile limits are carrying the entire safety load, and nothing in ROS is quietly protecting you.

On instrumentation the communities want different things and you can have both from the same recording. Industrial practice logs for traceability and repeatability — every cycle, retained for audit. The IL community logs episodes for training data and usually throws away control-loop internals. A rosbag of /joint_states plus your command topic plus /dynamixel_hardware_interface/dxl_state serves both: it is training data and it is the flight recorder.

On limits, MoveIt-centric teams put the authoritative numbers in the URDF and joint_limits.yaml and expect the planner to respect them; firmware-centric teams (the DYNAMIXEL and hobby-servo world) put them in EEPROM and treat the host as untrusted. The second is stricter and is the right default for you, because the enforcing processor is not the one running your policy. The cost is that limits then live outside git, which is why the control-table dump has to be part of your run stamp.

components.name: Demonstration rig A — leader/follower teleop (what you have)
components.role: A kinematically similar 'leader' arm is backdriven by a human while the 'follower' mirrors it. The leader's joint vector is recorded as the action label; the follower's joint vector is recorded as the state. On OMX this is two ros2_control stacks: the leader runs gravity_compensation_controller on the effort interface plus joint_trajectory_command_broadcaster; the follower runs a plain JointTrajectoryController whose input topic is remapped so the leader drives it directly.
components.whyItExists: The action label must live in exactly the space the policy will command at runtime. If you label in Cartesian and command joints (or label at 30 Hz and command at 100 Hz), the network has to absorb a representation gap that nothing in the data explains. Leader/follower makes label ≡ command by construction — the recorded action IS the message the robot will later receive. Gravity compensation exists because a human physically cannot hold a 5-DOF arm steady across 200 episodes; without it your demonstrations are contaminated by operator fatigue, and fatigue is a temporally-correlated confounder the policy will happily learn.
components.interface: Leader: effort command interface, 5 joints, kinetic_friction_scalars [0.0005, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15], torque_scaling_factors [200, 350, 300, 300, 300]. Out: trajectory_msgs/JointTrajectory on /leader/joint_trajectory with joints [joint1..joint5, gripper_joint_1]. Follower in: same topic, because ros2_control_node is launched with remappings=[('/arm_controller/joint_trajectory', '/leader/joint_trajectory')].
components.rate: ros2_control update_rate: 100 Hz on both leader and follower; recording sampled at dataset fps (typically 30).
components.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_l_leader_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml; .../config/omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml; .../launch/omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py line 144 (the remapping). Note the AI follower config folds gripper_joint_1 into arm_controller's joint list, while the non-AI config .../config/omx_f/hardware_controller_manager.yaml splits it into a separate GripperActionController — the AI variant exists precisely so one 6-vector action can be sent as one message. ALOHA is the same pattern in ROS 1: master/puppet, DT = 0.02 (50 Hz), in aloha_scripts/constants.py.

components.name: Demonstration rig B — UMI handheld gripper (no robot in the loop)
components.role: A 3D-printed handheld gripper carrying a GoPro Hero 9 with a 155° fisheye and the camera's built-in IMU. Trajectory is recovered offline by a modified ORB-SLAM3 (inertial-monocular, with map-based and marker-enhanced initialization); finger width is read continuously from fiducial markers on the fingers. No arm, no teleop, no ROS, no lab.
components.whyItExists: Leader/follower binds your dataset to one robot in one room with one lighting condition. UMI's entire reason for existing is that data collection throughput is the binding constraint in imitation learning, and a robot in the loop caps that throughput. UMI collected 1400 demonstrations across 30 physical locations in 12 person-hours. The cost is that you now owe the system an offline SLAM pipeline and a latency-matching story, because the human's 'gripper' has essentially zero actuation latency and your robot does not.
components.interface: mp4 (video + embedded IMU) → run_slam_pipeline.py → scripts_slam_pipeline/07_generate_replay_buffer.py → zarr replay buffer. Action = relative SE(3) transform of EE pose at t w.r.t. pose at t0, plus absolute gripper width.
components.rate: Capture 60 fps, policy executed at 10 Hz (20 Hz for dynamic tossing).
components.evidence: real-stanford/universal_manipulation_interface, README and scripts_slam_pipeline/. RSS 2024 paper p045 (arXiv 2402.10329): mean ATE 6.1 mm position / 3.5° rotation; 80 mm finger stroke, 780 g, $73 BoM; images fed to the policy as raw fisheye without undistortion at 224×224.

components.name: Recorder / episode writer
components.role: A process that, each tick, pulls the latest camera frames and joint states, pairs them with the current action, and appends one row to a dataset. It also owns episode boundaries (start/stop/re-record/discard) and the natural-language task string.
components.whyItExists: rosbag is the obvious thing to reach for and it is the wrong tool here. A bag is a log of messages with per-message receive timestamps and no notion of a training row; converting bags to training tensors later means re-deriving the (obs_t, action_t) pairing offline, and that is exactly where silent off-by-one errors in the action label live. Writing the training row at collection time forces you to decide the pairing once, on the robot, where you can still see whether the arm moved the way the label says. It also makes the discard button meaningful: a bad episode should never enter the dataset, not be filtered later.
components.interface: In: sensor_msgs/CompressedImage per camera, sensor_msgs/JointState (follower), trajectory_msgs/JointTrajectory (leader = action). Out: parquet rows + mp4 shards + meta/*.json.
components.rate: Fixed dataset fps, enforced by a cycle timer; LeRobot's record loop times each section ('observe', 'teleop', 'write') and sleeps the remainder.
components.evidence: ROBOTIS physical_ai_tools: physical_ai_server/config/omx_f_config.yaml specifies observation_list: [camera1, state], camera_topic_list: [camera1:/camera1/image_raw/compressed], joint_topic_list: [follower:/joint_states, leader:/leader/joint_trajectory]. LeRobot: src/lerobot/scripts/lerobot_record.py, order per tick is get_observation → processor → teleop.get_action → send_action → dataset.add_frame.

components.name: Dataset format (LeRobotDataset v3)
components.role: The on-disk contract between collection and training. Tabular low-dimensional signals (state, action, timestamp, episode_index, frame_index, task_index) in Apache Parquet; camera frames concatenated and encoded into MP4 shards; JSON/Parquet metadata in meta/ carrying feature schema, fps, normalization stats, task strings, and per-episode byte/frame offsets.
components.whyItExists: Three separate failures. (1) One file per episode blows up the filesystem at scale, so v3 packs many episodes per shard and reconstructs episode views from metadata rather than filenames. (2) Storing images as raw arrays is 50–100× the bytes of H.264, and you will collect hundreds of gigabytes. (3) meta/stats.json exists because normalization constants must be frozen with the dataset — if train and deploy compute normalization differently, the policy outputs garbage and nothing in the stack will tell you why. Freezing fps in meta/info.json is the same argument for time: the model learned a fixed Δt between steps, and that number has to travel with the weights.
components.interface: dataset[i] → {'observation.state': tensor, 'observation.images.<name>': [C,H,W] uint8, 'action': tensor, 'timestamp': float, ...}. delta_timestamps={'observation.images.front': [-0.2, -0.1, 0.0]} returns a stacked [T,C,H,W] window.
components.rate: fps is a field of meta/info.json, not a runtime choice.
components.evidence: huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/en/lerobot-dataset-v3. Contrast: ALOHA/ACT uses one HDF5 per episode with /observations/images/<cam> and /action (aloha_scripts/constants.py, 4 cameras: cam_high, cam_low, cam_left_wrist, cam_right_wrist, 480×640). UMI uses a single zarr ReplayBuffer.

components.name: Observation assembler / time alignment
components.role: Turns N asynchronous streams (each camera, proprioception, gripper) into one observation dict whose entries all refer to the same instant. Two designs exist: 'latest message per topic' (cheap, what ROBOTIS does) or 'pick a reference clock and interpolate everything onto it' (correct, what UMI does).
components.whyItExists: This is the single largest source of silent failure in an IL stack and the one beginners never see. A USB webcam, a Dynamixel bus and a policy timer are three free-running clocks. If the image is 80 ms stale relative to the joint state, the policy is trained on a state-image pair that never physically co-existed, and it learns to compensate for a phase offset that will be different at deployment. It still 'works' — just worse, in a way that looks like 'the model needs more data'. UMI selects a reference camera by minimizing pairwise sync error across cameras, then aligns everything backward from that camera's latest timestamp using nearest-neighbour for images and interpolation for robot/gripper state.
components.interface: UMI get_obs() returns camera{i}_rgb, robot{i}_eef_pos, robot{i}_eef_rot_axis_angle, robot{i}_gripper_width, timestamp — all on a common evenly-spaced grid last_timestamp - arange(horizon)*down_sample_steps/frequency.
components.rate: Alignment grid = policy frequency (UMI default frequency=20, camera_obs_horizon=2, robot_obs_horizon=2).
components.evidence: umi/real_world/bimanual_umi_env.py get_obs() ~lines 262–356; constructor lines 23–56. Counter-example worth knowing: ROBOTIS' physical_ai_server/communication/communicator.py (651 lines) does NOT use message_filters.ApproximateTimeSynchronizer — each topic callback just overwrites a dict entry and get_latest_data() returns whatever is newest. That is a pragmatic choice, not a correct one, and it is the first thing to instrument if your trained policy underperforms your teleop.

components.name: Training job (strictly off-robot, strictly offline)
components.role: Reads the frozen dataset, trains weights, emits a checkpoint plus its config and normalization stats. Runs on a workstation GPU or in the cloud, not on the Jetson.
components.whyItExists: The architectural point is that this is an OFFLINE batch job with no connection to the robot — which is precisely the opposite of a classical stack, where the 'intelligence' (planner, IK solver) is online and stateless. It means the robot is idle during the most compute-expensive phase, it means you can retrain without touching hardware, and it means the feedback loop from 'the arm did something dumb' to 'the arm stops doing that' is hours long, not seconds. That latency in the engineering loop is the defining fact of IL project management.
components.interface: In: dataset + config. Out: checkpoint (weights), config.json, normalization stats.
components.rate: Hours to days. UMI trained on 4×A10g or 8×A100 depending on task.
components.evidence: lerobot-train --dataset.repo_id=...; UMI: python train.py --config-name=train_diffusion_unet_timm_umi_workspace, accelerate-wrapped for multi-GPU. ACT: 50 demos per task (100 for Thread Velcro) was enough for its tasks.

components.name: Policy inference process
components.role: Loads the checkpoint, takes an observation dict, returns an action chunk of shape [H, action_dim]. It is a pure function of the observation window; it holds no plan, no goal, no map, no state machine.
components.whyItExists: This is THE architectural difference. A planner is queried once per goal and produces a trajectory that remains valid until the world changes; a policy is queried continuously and produces a short, disposable trajectory that is invalid the moment the next observation arrives. Everything downstream — chunking, receding horizon, temporal ensembling, latency compensation — exists to bridge that gap. Also: a planner can say 'infeasible'. A policy cannot. It will always return floats.
components.interface: predict(images: dict[str, np.ndarray], state: np.ndarray, task_instruction: str) -> np.ndarray[H, D]. LeRobot wraps this as select_action() draining an internal chunk queue.
components.rate: Called at the replan rate, not the control rate: 10 Hz typical (UMI, Diffusion Policy), or 50 Hz if using ACT with temporal ensembling.
components.evidence: physical_ai_server.py (1043 lines) line ~605: action = self.inference_manager.predict(images=camera_data, state=follower_data, task_instruction=...). LeRobot ACTConfig defaults: chunk_size=100, n_action_steps=100, n_obs_steps=1, temporal_ensemble_coeff=None, vision_backbone='resnet18', dim_model=512.

components.name: Action representation + decoder
components.role: The code that turns the network's output vector into something a controller can accept. This is where absolute-vs-relative, joint-vs-Cartesian, and rotation parameterization are decided — and it must match the training-time encoder exactly.
components.whyItExists: The training-time action representation constrains the runtime controller, and this is a one-way constraint people discover backwards. If you train on relative EE poses (UMI), you need FK at runtime to get the anchor, IK to get back to joints, and you inherit every IK branch flip as a potential discontinuity. If you train on absolute joint positions (ALOHA/LeRobot/ROBOTIS), you need no kinematics at all at runtime and the whole IK/FK problem disappears — but you can never deploy those weights on a different arm, and the policy must relearn the arm's geometry from data. Rotation parameterization is a real trap: quaternions have a double cover, Euler angles have gimbal lock and 2π wraparound, so the field settled on the continuous 6D representation (Zhou et al. 2019) which the decoder Gram-Schmidts back to SO(3).
components.interface: Your own code: 10 floats per step = [0:3] Δposition (m, relative to anchor), [3:9] Δrotation 6D (relative), [9] gripper width normalized 0..1 (ABSOLUTE, because width means object size and a relative encoding is meaningless). Mixed frames in one vector is the easiest place in the whole pipeline to make a silent mistake.
components.rate: Microseconds; negligible in the latency budget.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/docker/workspace/dummy_exec/action_format.py (ACTION_DIM = 10, rot_from_6d Gram-Schmidt). UMI paper Section III-B PD2.1: 'sequence of SE(3) transforms denoting desired pose at t relative to initial EE pose at t0'. ALOHA/ACT and LeRobot's omx_follower instead use absolute joint positions, so no decoder exists at all — action_features is literally {f'{motor}.pos': float}.

components.name: Receding-horizon chunk executor
components.role: Accepts a chunk of H future actions, publishes a prefix of them as a timed trajectory, but only allows E < H steps to elapse before discarding the rest and replanning from a fresh observation. Publishing further ahead than you execute is deliberate.
components.whyItExists: Three distinct problems collapse into one mechanism. (1) Latency: inference takes 15–150 ms; if you only committed to the single next action, the arm would stall between calls. The chunk is the buffer that covers inference time. (2) Compounding error: predicting k steps at once means the policy commits to k steps of intent, so small per-step errors do not accumulate into drift. (3) Non-Markovian demonstrations: human pauses and multi-modal choices are impossible for a single-step Markovian policy to model, and a chunk absorbs them. The horizon trade-off is real and measurable: longer execution horizon = smoother, more latency-tolerant, less reactive to disturbance; shorter = twitchier at chunk boundaries but faster to respond. Diffusion Policy found Ta=8 optimal across most tasks.
components.interface: Publishes trajectory_msgs/JointTrajectory with PUBLISH_STEPS points but replans after EXECUTE_STEPS. Crucial ROS 2 detail you have already hit: JointTrajectoryController falls back to LINEAR interpolation when a point carries no velocity (velocity step at every waypoint), and rejects a trajectory whose final point has non-zero velocity unless allow_nonzero_velocity_at_trajectory_end is set. Publishing past the replan point keeps the arm permanently in the smooth middle of the spline and never reaching the zero-velocity tail.
components.rate: Your executor: EXECUTE_STEPS=3, PUBLISH_STEPS=8, DT=0.04, time_scale=2.0 → replan every 0.24 s (4.2 Hz). UMI: steps_per_inference=6 at 10 Hz → replan every 0.6 s. ACT without ensembling: query_frequency = chunk_size = 100 at 50 Hz → replan every 2 s.
components.evidence: open_manipulator/docker/workspace/dummy_exec/chunk_executor_node.py. UMI scripts_real/eval_real_umi.py (~550 lines), 'Over budget' branch: is_new = action_timestamps > (curr_time + action_exec_latency); if np.sum(is_new)==0 it keeps only the last action and reschedules it. Diffusion Policy IJRR: 'the action horizon of 8 steps to be optimal for most tasks that we tested'.

components.name: Temporal ensembler (ACT's alternative to receding horizon)
components.role: Instead of executing E steps of one chunk, query the policy at EVERY control step and, for each timestep t, average all the predictions that earlier queries made about t, with exponential weights. Buffer is all_time_actions[max_timesteps, max_timesteps+num_queries, state_dim].
components.whyItExists: Naive chunking produces a visible discontinuity at every chunk boundary — the arm jerks when the new chunk disagrees with the old one. Ensembling removes that by construction: consecutive commands differ only by one new prediction folded into an average. The price is that inference must run at the full control rate, which is 50 Hz on ALOHA. That is affordable only because ACT is small — 52 M parameters, ~0.01 s inference on an RTX 2080 Ti. It is NOT affordable for a diffusion policy or a VLA, which is exactly why UMI and Diffusion Policy chose receding horizon instead.
components.interface: exp_weights = np.exp(-k * np.arange(len(actions_for_curr_step))) with k=0.01, normalized, then weighted sum. Note the index order: element 0 is the OLDEST prediction, so the oldest gets the highest weight — the paper says so explicitly ('wi=exp(−m∗i), where w0 is the weight for the oldest action'), and smaller m means faster incorporation of new observations. This surprises everyone who reads the code first.
components.rate: Inference at full control rate (50 Hz on ALOHA).
components.evidence: tonyzhaozh/act imitate_episodes.py ~lines 218–226 (~380 lines total). LeRobot enforces the coupling: ACTConfig.__post_init__ raises NotImplementedError if temporal_ensemble_coeff is not None and n_action_steps > 1.

components.name: Latency-matched action scheduler (the part almost nobody builds)
components.role: Rather than 'execute this action now', schedule each action to be reached at an absolute wall-clock time, computed from the observation's timestamp, and subtract each actuator's measured latency from that target time. UMI's env calls robot.schedule_waypoint(pose, target_time - robot_action_latency) and gripper.schedule_waypoint(pos, target_time - gripper_action_latency).
components.whyItExists: A policy trained on human demonstrations learned the timing of a system with one set of latencies. Deploying it on a system with different latencies is a domain shift in the time axis, and it manifests as the policy overshooting or oscillating — behaviour that looks like a training problem and is not. Latency matching is what makes one set of weights deployable across a UR5 and a Franka. It requires you to MEASURE four separate latencies, each with its own method: camera latency by filming a QR code showing its own display timestamp; proprioception latency from robot timestamps (Franka) or ½ ICMP round-trip (UR5); gripper execution latency by commanding a sinusoid and cross-correlating; robot execution latency by optimal alignment of desired vs. actual EE pose.
components.interface: exec_actions(actions, timestamps) → per-robot schedule_waypoint(pose, t - latency). Actions whose target time is already past are dropped.
components.rate: UMI eval config: camera_obs_latency=0.17 s, robot_obs_latency=0.0001 s, gripper_obs_latency=0.01 s, robot_action_latency=0.18 s, gripper_action_latency=0.1 s.
components.evidence: umi/real_world/bimanual_umi_env.py exec_actions() ~lines 358–396; scripts_real/eval_real_umi.py lines ~155–166 for the latency constants; UMI paper appendix A.0-A1..A4 for the four measurement procedures. Your chunk_executor_node.py currently anchors on the arm's PRESENT q with no latency term — that is the gap.

components.name: Safety wrapper / action gate
components.role: The mandatory code between the policy's floats and the motor command. Minimum viable set: (1) per-joint velocity limit = |Δq| / dt against a real number, not a per-step angle; (2) IK feasibility — reject, do not clamp; (3) workspace bounds, especially a floor; (4) discontinuity / branch-flip rejection across chunk boundaries; (5) a watchdog that holds position if no chunk arrives within N periods; (6) a deadman the operator must actively hold; (7) an effort/current limit so a stall does not cook a servo.
components.whyItExists: A planner that fails returns 'no solution'. A policy that fails returns a confident, well-formed, physically insane number — an EE pose 40 cm inside the table, or a wrist flip of 170° in one 40 ms step. There is no in-band signal that it failed. Every bit of the sanity that ros2_control, MoveIt and joint_limits give a classical stack for free must be reconstructed here. Two subtleties worth internalizing: a fixed per-step angle threshold is the WRONG quantity, because the same 6° is gentle at time_scale 8 and violent at 0.5 — you must gate on velocity, since the step's duration is DT × time_scale. And IK branch flips are the failure this catches most often: they jump far more than any legitimate motion, so a generous velocity cap (e.g. 180 deg/s against a URDF rating of 4.8 rad/s = 275 deg/s) still catches them while never rejecting a correct fast reach. On rejection, HOLD POSITION — never publish a partial or clamped trajectory, because a clamped action is a new action the policy never chose and its consequences are unmodelled.
components.interface: chunk [H,10] → (points, reason). reason is None or a human-readable string naming the step and the number that failed.
components.rate: Runs on every chunk, before publication. Cost is negligible.
components.evidence: Your build_segment() in chunk_executor_node.py already does (1), (2) and returns rather than clamps — that is correct and ahead of most student projects. UMI's equivalents are cruder: target_pose[2] = np.maximum(target_pose[2], 0.055) (a hard floor), np.clip on gripper width to [0, 0.09], max_pos_speed=2.0 m/s, max_rot_speed=6.0 rad/s, and a keyboard 'S' to stop. LeRobot's is one function: ensure_safe_goal_position() in src/lerobot/robots/utils.py lines 59–92, driven by OmxFollowerConfig.max_relative_target — a per-joint cap on |goal − present|, defaulting to None (i.e. OFF).

components.name: Low-level trajectory / servo controller
components.role: Takes sparse, low-rate waypoints from the policy layer and produces a dense, smooth command stream at the hardware rate. In ROS 2 this is joint_trajectory_controller inside ros2_control; in UMI it is a PoseTrajectoryInterpolator inside a dedicated process calling ur_rtde servoL.
components.whyItExists: A policy emits 10–25 commands per second. A servo bus wants 100–500. Something must fill the gap, and it must do so with bounded velocity and continuous position, or the arm rings. This layer is also where real-time discipline lives: UMI's controller is its own multiprocessing.Process explicitly 'due to python GIL', regulated by precise_wait() on a monotonic clock, polling at most one command per cycle with get_k(1) so a command backlog can never accumulate. That last detail is the kind of thing that only shows up after a week of mysterious lag.
components.interface: ROS 2: trajectory_msgs/JointTrajectory in, position command interface out at controller_manager update_rate. UMI: rtde_c.servoL(pose, vel, acc, dt, lookahead_time, gain) with lookahead_time ∈ [0.03, 0.2] s and gain ∈ [100, 2000].
components.rate: OMX: 100 Hz. UR5 via RTDE: 125 Hz (CB2) to 500 Hz (UR3e). Franka: 200 Hz. WSG gripper: ~30 Hz.
components.evidence: umi/real_world/rtde_interpolation_controller.py (~208 lines): class extends multiprocessing.Process, main loop ~150–186, servoL at line 167, SharedMemoryQueue.get_k(1) at line 175. OMX: controller_manager ros__parameters update_rate: 100.

components.name: Motor bus / hardware interface
components.role: The single owner of /dev/ttyACM0. Performs one sync-read of Present_Position and one sync-write of Goal_Position per control cycle across all six servos on the half-duplex bus, Protocol 2.0.
components.whyItExists: Half-duplex means exactly one transaction can be in flight; two processes on the same port do not interleave, they corrupt each other's status packets. This is why the port must be owned by exactly one process and why every stack in this space has a hard rule about it. It is also why 'just open the port from my Python script while the driver is running' is never a shortcut. The sync-read/sync-write group instructions exist because addressing six servos individually would triple the bus time.
components.interface: LeRobot: DynamixelMotorsBus, PROTOCOL_VERSION = 2.0, DEFAULT_BAUDRATE = 1_000_000, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS = 1000, GroupSyncRead/GroupSyncWrite (the 'Fast Sync Read/Write' variants are still a TODO in that file). Control table: Torque_Enable (64,1), Operating_Mode (11,1), Goal_Position (116,4), Present_Position (132,4). ROS 2: dynamixel_hardware_interface as a ros2_control SystemInterface with read()/write() called by the controller manager.
components.rate: 100 Hz on OMX. Bus budget at 1 Mbps (my calculation, not measured — verify it): sync-write of 6×4 bytes ≈ 46 bytes ≈ 0.46 ms; sync-read ≈ 14-byte instruction + 6 status packets of ~15 bytes ≈ 1.0 ms of wire time, PLUS Return_Delay_Time (address 9, factory default 250 = 500 µs) charged once per status packet = 3 ms. So ~4.5 ms/cycle of the 10 ms budget goes to the bus, and setting Return_Delay_Time to 0 recovers most of it. Raising the baudrate to 3 or 4 Mbps helps the wire time but not the return delay.
components.evidence: LeRobot src/lerobot/motors/dynamixel/dynamixel.py (345 lines, DEFAULT_BAUDRATE at line 45) and tables.py (AVAILABLE_BAUDRATES up to 4_000_000). LeRobot upstream already ships YOUR arm: src/lerobot/robots/omx_follower/omx_follower.py (287 lines) declares shoulder_pan=Motor(11,'xl430-w250'), shoulder_lift=Motor(12,'xl430-w250'), elbow_flex=Motor(13,'xl430-w250'), wrist_flex=Motor(14,'xl330-m288'), wrist_roll=Motor(15,'xl330-m288'), gripper=Motor(16,'xl330-m288'). Separately: Return_Delay_Time and Operating_Mode live in servo RAM/EEPROM and reset behaviour differs by address — that is the 'registers silently resetting on power cycle' you hit.

components.name: Camera process(es)
components.role: One OS process (not thread) per camera, capturing continuously into a shared buffer at the camera's native rate, decoupled from the policy's rate. The consumer reads the most recent frame whenever it wants.
components.whyItExists: Python's GIL makes threads useless for this — a decode in one thread stalls the control loop in another. Separate processes plus shared memory is the standard answer outside ROS; inside ROS it is separate nodes plus intra-process or zero-copy transport. The decoupling matters for a second reason: the policy must never block on a camera. If get_obs() waits for a fresh frame, a single dropped USB frame becomes a control-loop stall, and a control-loop stall on a chunked policy means the arm runs off the end of its trajectory.
components.interface: UMI: SingleRealsense / UvcCamera process → SharedMemoryRingBuffer (described as a 'lock-free FILO data structure ... to utilize multiple CPU cores while avoiding pickle serialization and locking overhead'). ROS 2: usb_cam or realsense2_camera node → sensor_msgs/CompressedImage. ROBOTIS requires the topic name to end in /compressed.
components.rate: UMI handles mixed rates transparently (4K@30 and 1080p@60 in the same rig). ALOHA: 4× Logitech C922x at 480×640. Typical UVC webcam: 30 fps → 33.3 ms frame period.
components.evidence: diffusion_policy/real_world/ (SingleRealsense, SharedMemoryRingBuffer); umi/real_world/multi_uvc_camera.py, uvc_camera.py, video_recorder.py. Jetson-specific: the 8 GB Orin paper used GStreamer with NVIDIA NVMM buffers (v4l2src, max-buffers=2, drop=true) so decoded frames stay in GPU-accessible memory — peak single-core utilization fell from 98.0% to 77.0%.

components.name: IPC substrate: shared-memory ring buffer vs DDS/zenoh
components.role: How processes exchange observations and commands. The IL research community overwhelmingly uses Python multiprocessing plus a hand-written SharedMemoryRingBuffer / SharedMemoryQueue. ROS-based stacks use the RMW (CycloneDDS, FastDDS, or rmw_zenoh_cpp).
components.whyItExists: The research-lab choice is not ideology. A ring buffer gives you the raw sensor timestamp with no serialization hop, no QoS negotiation and no discovery, in ~50 lines of numpy over multiprocessing.shared_memory — and time alignment is the thing these systems care about most. The RMW gives you language interop, network transparency, introspection (ros2 topic echo/hz), recording, and a discovery mechanism, at the cost of a serialization round trip and an extra clock. rmw_zenoh specifically REQUIRES a router process: UDP multicast scouting is disabled by default (deliberately, to avoid misconfigured networks and containers, and to stop robots on one LAN from silently talking to each other), so peers discover each other by gossip through rmw_zenohd. Nothing discovers anything until that router exists — which is exactly the failure you hit.
components.interface: SharedMemoryRingBuffer.get() / .get_last_k(); SharedMemoryQueue.get_k(1). Versus rclpy publisher/subscription with a QoS profile.
components.rate: Ring buffer read: microseconds. DDS loopback for a small message: order 0.1–1 ms; a CompressedImage adds JPEG encode+decode.
components.evidence: ros2/rmw_zenoh docs/design.md (jazzy branch) on the router requirement and ZENOH_ROUTER_CHECK_ATTEMPTS; your Dockerfile bakes in export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp, export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=30 and alias zenohd='ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd'. Diffusion Policy README states plainly that it does not use ROS.

components.name: Async inference client/server (the modern compromise)
components.role: Split the policy off the robot process entirely: the robot runs a thin client that streams observations and drains an action queue; the policy runs on a server (possibly a different machine) and returns chunks over gRPC. The client requests a new chunk when its queue drops below a fraction of a chunk, and merges overlapping chunks with an aggregation function.
components.whyItExists: Synchronous inference means the robot is stationary while the GPU thinks. On a Jetson with a 100 ms policy that is 100 ms of dead time per cycle, and it shows up as visible stuttering and lower task throughput. Decoupling lets the arm keep executing chunk N while chunk N+1 is computed. It also lets you keep the heavy CUDA/torch stack off the robot computer entirely — which solves a dependency problem as much as a latency one.
components.interface: gRPC: Ready(), SendPolicyInstructions(), SendObservations() (streamed in chunks), GetActions(). Two daemon threads behind a barrier: an action-receiver and the control loop. Request trigger: action_queue.qsize() / action_chunk_size <= chunk_size_threshold.
components.rate: Control loop paced by environment_dt = 1/fps. Measured effect on SO-100: cycle time 13.75 s (sync) → 9.70 s (async); throughput 1.8 → 3.8 objects per 60 s.
components.evidence: lerobot/src/lerobot/async_inference/robot_client.py (573 lines; gRPC channel at lines 94–96, _ready_to_send_observation at line 453, _aggregate_action_queues at 323–372) and policy_server.py. LeRobot paper Table 5.

components.name: Container split: robot container vs learning container
components.role: Two separate Docker containers on the same machine sharing host IPC and the host network. One holds ROS 2 + ros2_control + the Dynamixel driver + RealSense; the other holds torch/CUDA + LeRobot + the policy. They talk over the RMW, not over a Python import.
components.whyItExists: ROS 2 Jazzy pins python3.12 and a specific numpy; torch pins its own CUDA and often a different numpy; librealsense needs a udev-rule-and-kernel-adjacent build. Putting them in one image means every torch upgrade risks breaking the robot driver, and the robot driver is the thing you cannot afford to break. Splitting them also makes the serial-port ownership rule enforceable: exactly ONE container mounts and drives /dev/ttyACM0. The failure this prevents is precisely the one you hit — but note where it actually came from in your setup: the open_manipulator image ships s6-overlay services (open_manipulator_bringup, leader_bringup) with restart: always in docker-compose.yml, so the container can be auto-starting a bringup that grabs the port before you type anything. Check /run/robot_type and the s6 service state before blaming your own launch file.
components.interface: docker-compose.yml: network_mode: host, ipc: host, privileged: true, volumes /dev:/dev and /dev/shm:/dev/shm, cap_add SYS_NICE, ulimits rtprio: 99 (so the controller can request real-time priority), memlock 8428281856. components.name: Evaluation harness / episode manager
components.role: Runs N trials, resets the scene between them, logs success/failure and the reason, and records video of every rollout. Owns the start/stop/abort keys and the policy-engaged state.
components.whyItExists: A learned policy has no correctness proof and no unit test. Its only specification is a success rate on a distribution of scenes, which means the ONLY way you know whether a change helped is to run 20 trials before and 20 after. Teams that skip building this end up arguing from anecdote ('it felt better'), and with a stochastic policy anecdote is worthless — a 50% policy produces a clean run of 3 successes about 1 time in 8. Video of failures is what tells you whether the failure is perception (never saw the object), representation (reached the wrong frame), or control (commanded correctly, servo could not track).
components.interface: Operator keys: UMI uses SpaceMouse to jog, 'C' to hand control to the policy, 'S' to take it back. Your --hold flag is the same instinct: command exactly where the arm already is, and if it twitches, your joint ordering or frame is wrong — learn that before it swings.
components.rate: Per episode.
components.evidence: UMI scripts_real/eval_real_umi.py; ACT reports 50 demos/task and success as X/20 trials; UMI reports 18/20 = 90% on the Franka FR2. Your chunk_executor_node.py --hold and --dry-run are the right two pre-flight gates and most teams have neither.

orderOfOperations: 1. Fix the action representation BEFORE collecting a single episode. Decide: absolute joint positions, or relative EE poses? This is the most expensive decision to reverse, because it invalidates the entire dataset. Absolute joints (ALOHA / LeRobot / ROBOTIS) needs no kinematics at runtime, cannot transfer to another arm, and is what your vendor stack already supports end to end. Relative EE poses (UMI) needs FK+IK at runtime and inherits every IK branch flip, but is hardware-agnostic. For a 5-DOF arm with a capstone deadline: joints, unless the whole point of the project is UMI-style cross-embodiment.

2. Prove the command path with the policy replaced by a constant. Publish the arm's CURRENT position as a JointTrajectory and confirm nothing moves. This exercises joint ordering, frame conventions, message construction, controller acceptance, and topic remapping in one test — and every one of those can be wrong in a way that looks identical at the message level. Do it before anything can swing.

3. Measure your latencies, all four of them, with the actual methods. Camera: film a screen displaying its own timestamp and subtract. Proprioception: timestamp in the driver, not in the subscriber. Actuation: command a sinusoid and cross-correlate commanded against measured. Do this before collecting data, because the numbers determine your fps and your chunk size, and because after training you will not be able to tell a latency problem from a data problem.

4. Choose fps and freeze it into the dataset metadata. It must satisfy: fps ≤ camera rate, 1/fps > (measured inference time + execution path), and fps fast enough that the task's fastest motion is not aliased. 30 Hz recording with 10 Hz policy execution is the common answer. Write it into meta/info.json; never let it be a command-line flag at deploy time.

5. Build the time-alignment layer now, not later. Even if you start with 'latest message per topic', log all three timestamps (camera capture, joint state, action) into the dataset so you can measure the skew afterwards. A dataset that does not record when each stream was sampled cannot be debugged, only re-collected.

6. Collect a deliberately small dataset first — 20 to 30 episodes — and train on it. The goal is not a working policy; it is to discover that your normalization is wrong, or your images are BGR at collection and RGB at training, or your action column is off by one frame. Every one of those is invisible until you train, and each costs a full re-collection if you find it at episode 300.

7. Then collect the real dataset, and vary what you want the policy to generalize over. Object position, lighting, distractors, starting pose. Everything you hold fixed, the policy is permitted to memorize. ACT got away with 50 demos per task; UMI needed 300–1400 for in-the-wild generalization. If the arm always starts folded, the policy will only ever work from folded.
8. Train off-robot. Save the checkpoint WITH its config and normalization stats as one unit. A checkpoint without its stats is not a policy.

9. Build the safety gate before the first policy rollout, not after the first crash. Velocity limit, IK feasibility, workspace floor, watchdog, deadman. Reject and hold; never clamp. The reason this comes before the first rollout rather than after is that the first rollout of a freshly trained policy is the single most likely moment for it to emit nonsense, because you have not yet seen its failure modes.

10. Run the policy with the execution horizon set very short and the time scale set very slow. Your time_scale=2.0 is the right instinct. Slow is not just safer; it is diagnostically clearer, because you can see which phase of the motion is wrong.
11. Establish a baseline success rate over ≥20 trials with a fixed reset protocol. Everything after this is measured against that number. Without it you cannot tell whether your next change helped.

12. Only now optimize latency, and optimize the dominant term. Profile before converting anything to TensorRT — if your camera pipeline is 80 ms and your inference is 15 ms, quantizing the model buys you nothing and costs you a week.

13. When it fails, diagnose in this order: (a) watch the recorded rollout video — did the camera see the object at all? (b) replay the logged observation through the policy offline — does it produce the same action? If yes, it is a data/training problem; if no, it is a preprocessing mismatch between collection and deployment. (c) compare the commanded joint trajectory against the measured one — if they diverge, the problem is below the policy and the policy is innocent. Most teams skip straight to 'collect more data', which is the most expensive hypothesis and usually not the right one.
keyFacts: LeRobot upstream already ships YOUR arm. src/lerobot/robots/omx_follower/omx_follower.py (287 lines) declares Motor(11,'xl430-w250'), Motor(12,'xl430-w250'), Motor(13,'xl430-w250'), Motor(14,'xl330-m288'), Motor(15,'xl330-m288'), Motor(16,'xl330-m288') on one DynamixelMotorsBus. Before writing anything, read that file and config_omx_follower.py — they are the vendor-blessed answer to 'what is the interface between policy and motors' for this exact hardware.

ROBOTIS' physical_ai_tools vendors LeRobot as a git submodule and bridges it into ROS 2. The inference node publishes trajectory_msgs/JointTrajectory to /leader/joint_trajectory — i.e. the policy literally takes the leader arm's place, using the same topic the human's leader arm used during collection. The follower's ros2_control_node is launched with remappings=[('/arm_controller/joint_trajectory', '/leader/joint_trajectory')] (omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py:144). This is why the same follower stack works for teleop and for policy without modification, and it is an elegant design worth copying.

The AI follower config folds the gripper into the arm controller. .../config/omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml lists joints [joint1..joint5, gripper_joint_1] under a single JointTrajectoryController, while the non-AI .../config/omx_f/ splits gripper_joint_1 into a separate GripperActionController. That difference exists purely because a policy emits one 6-vector and you want it to arrive as one atomic message.

controller_manager update_rate is 100 Hz on both the OMX leader and follower. That is your hardware control rate. Your policy replan rate (chunk_executor: EXECUTE_STEPS=3 × DT=0.04 × time_scale=2.0 = 0.24 s → 4.2 Hz) is 24× slower. The gap between those two numbers is exactly what JointTrajectoryController's spline interpolation is filling in.

Measured ACT inference on a Jetson Orin Nano Super (8 GB): 114.02 ms mean / 144.73 ms p95 in FP32 PyTorch; 17.93 ms / 21.92 ms in FP16 TensorRT; 12.65 ms / 16.27 ms in INT8 TensorRT — a 6.4× and 9.0× reduction with task success preserved at all three precisions. At 10 Hz the control period is 100 ms, so unconverted FP32 PyTorch does not fit. (arXiv 2608.03938)

Policy inference latency by model class, same GPU (RTX 4090, LeRobot paper Table 3): ACT 5.01 ms ± 0.061 (52 M params, 211 MB); SmolVLA 99.24 ms ± 1.195 (450 M params, 1.75 GB); π₀ 209.38 ms ± 2.762. On CPU: ACT 182.31 ms, SmolVLA 2028.46 ms. On a Jetson AGX Orin, SmolVLA first-action P50 was 1202 ms. The model class you choose is a 40× latency decision.

Diffusion Policy real-world: 'predicts robot commands at 10 Hz and these commands then linearly interpolated to 125 Hz for robot execution', with 'DDIM with 100 training iterations and 10 inference iterations enables 0.1s inference latency on a Nvidia 3080 GPU'. Action horizon of 8 steps was found optimal for most tasks.

ALOHA/ACT runs at DT = 0.02 → 50 Hz teleop, recording and control, with chunk_size k = 100 (2 seconds of lookahead), inference ~0.01 s on an RTX 2080 Ti, 4× Logitech C922x at 480×640, 50 demos per task. LeRobot's ACTConfig defaults match: chunk_size=100, n_action_steps=100, n_obs_steps=1, temporal_ensemble_coeff=None.

ACT's temporal ensembling weights the OLDEST prediction most: 'wi=exp(−m∗i), where w0 is the weight for the oldest action', implemented as exp_weights = np.exp(-k * np.arange(len(actions_for_curr_step))) with k=0.01 in imitate_episodes.py. Smaller m means faster incorporation of new observations. It requires inference every control step, which is why LeRobot raises NotImplementedError if temporal_ensemble_coeff is set with n_action_steps > 1.

UMI's deployed latency constants (scripts_real/eval_real_umi.py ~lines 155–166): camera_obs_latency=0.17 s, robot_obs_latency=0.0001 s, gripper_obs_latency=0.01 s, robot_action_latency=0.18 s, gripper_action_latency=0.1 s. The camera and the actuator each cost ~175 ms and the proprioception costs nothing — that asymmetry is the whole reason latency matching exists.

UMI's over-budget handling is three lines and worth memorizing: is_new = action_timestamps > (curr_time + action_exec_latency); if np.sum(is_new) == 0, keep only the LAST action of the chunk and reschedule it to the next feasible step, printing 'Over budget'. It never skips a cycle and never publishes a stale action.

None of UMI, Diffusion Policy, ALOHA-ACT or core LeRobot uses ROS 2. Diffusion Policy and UMI use Python multiprocessing plus a hand-written lock-free SharedMemoryRingBuffer 'to utilize multiple CPU cores while avoiding pickle serialization and locking overhead'. ALOHA uses ROS 1 Noetic purely as a device-driver bus (interbotix_xs_modules) — no MoveIt, no planning, and its README tells you to delete the forward-kinematics call from interbotix arm.py because it 'delays teleoperation'. LeRobot deliberately exposes a plain Python ABC instead: connect / get_observation / send_action / disconnect (src/lerobot/robots/robot.py, 251 lines).

LeRobot's entire built-in safety layer is one function: ensure_safe_goal_position() in src/lerobot/robots/utils.py lines 59–92, which caps |goal − present| per joint. It is driven by OmxFollowerConfig.max_relative_target, which defaults to None — i.e. OFF. If you use LeRobot's omx_follower as-is, you have no safety layer until you set that.

rmw_zenoh_cpp requires the rmw_zenohd router process because UDP multicast scouting is disabled by default — a deliberate choice to avoid misconfigured networks and containers and to stop robots on the same LAN from silently discovering each other. ZENOH_ROUTER_CHECK_ATTEMPTS controls the retry. Your Dockerfile sets RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp and ROS_DOMAIN_ID=30 in .bashrc and aliases zenohd, which is why nodes see nothing until you start it.

Your open_manipulator container ships s6-overlay services (docker/s6-services/open_manipulator_bringup/run and leader_bringup/run) that launch omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py / omx_l_leader_ai.launch.py based on /run/robot_type and /run/leader_type, under restart: always. The container can therefore be holding /dev/ttyACM0 before any human types a command. Check the s6 service state first when the port is busy.

DYNAMIXEL bus budget at 1 Mbps for 6 servos (my calculation from the Protocol 2.0 packet format — verify before relying on it): sync-write of 6×4 bytes ≈ 46 bytes ≈ 0.46 ms wire time; sync-read ≈ 1.0 ms wire time PLUS Return_Delay_Time charged once per status packet. Factory default Return_Delay_Time (address 9) is 250 = 500 µs, so 6 servos cost 3 ms of pure waiting per read cycle. Setting it to 0 is the single highest-value register change on a 100 Hz bus.

LeRobotDataset v3 separates storage from API: many episodes per Parquet and per MP4 shard, with episode boundaries resolved through meta/episodes/ offsets rather than filenames. meta/info.json carries fps and the feature schema; meta/stats.json carries normalization statistics. You must call dataset.finalize() before push_to_hub() or the Parquet footers are never written and the files are corrupt.

UMI's dataset scale for generalization: 1400 demonstrations across 30 diverse physical locations collected in 12 person-hours, versus 305 episodes for the narrow single-location version of the same task. SLAM accuracy: mean ATE 6.1 mm position / 3.5° rotation. That is the price of hardware-agnostic in-the-wild data.
beginnerMistakes: Treating the policy like a planner and asking it for a goal. A policy has no goal, no plan, and no termination condition. It emits the next H actions and nothing else. If you want 'did it succeed?', that is a separate detector you have to build; the policy will happily keep grasping at empty air forever.

Clamping an out-of-range action instead of rejecting it. A clamped action is a DIFFERENT action that the policy never chose, executed in a state the policy has never seen, which is the definition of distribution shift. The correct response to an unsafe chunk is to hold position and log why. (Your build_segment() already returns a reason rather than clamping — keep that.)

Gating on per-step angle instead of velocity. The same 6° step is gentle at time_scale 8 and violent at 0.5, because the step's duration is DT × time_scale. A fixed per-step threshold rejects legitimate motion (a real pick from the folded pose needs ~6.8° in one step) while saying nothing about actual speed. Gate on |Δq|/dt against a real rad/s number derived from the URDF rating.

Assuming the camera frame and the joint state refer to the same instant. They do not, and the offset is typically 50–200 ms dominated by the camera. If you train on a mismatched pair and deploy with a different mismatch, the policy learned a phase offset that no longer holds — and it will look exactly like 'needs more data'.

Recording with rosbag and deriving training rows offline. The (observation, action) pairing is the single most error-prone decision in the pipeline and it belongs at collection time, on the robot, where you can still watch the arm and check the label. Off-by-one in the action column is invisible in a bag and fatal in training.

Changing fps, image resolution, color order or normalization between collection and deployment. All four are silent. The policy does not crash; it just becomes bad. Ship normalization stats with the checkpoint (meta/stats.json) and treat fps as part of the model, not a runtime flag.

Believing the first successful rollout. A stochastic policy with a 50% success rate produces a clean run of three successes roughly one time in eight. Until you have ≥20 trials with a fixed reset protocol, you do not have a number, you have an anecdote.

Optimizing inference before profiling. Converting to TensorRT is a satisfying week of work that buys nothing if your camera pipeline is 80 ms and your model is 15 ms. Measure each stage first; on a Jetson the answer flips depending on whether you are still on FP32 PyTorch.

Opening the serial port from a second process 'just to check something'. The DYNAMIXEL bus is half-duplex: two writers do not interleave, they corrupt each other's status packets, and the symptom is intermittent, not a clean error. Exactly one process owns /dev/ttyACM0, always — and on this stack that process may already have been started by s6 inside the container.

Writing your own kinematics when the action representation does not need them. If you train on absolute joint positions, there is no FK, no IK, no frames, and no branch flips at runtime — the whole class of bugs disappears. Analytic 5-DOF kinematics is genuinely valuable learning and genuinely optional for a joint-space policy. Know which one you are paying for.

Setting the execution horizon equal to the chunk length. Executing all 100 steps of an ACT chunk means 2 seconds of open-loop motion at 50 Hz, during which the policy is blind. The horizon is the knob that trades smoothness and latency-tolerance against reactivity; Diffusion Policy measured 8 steps as the sweet spot for most tasks.

Forgetting that the final point of a ROS 2 JointTrajectory must have zero velocity. JointTrajectoryController rejects the whole message otherwise (allow_nonzero_velocity_at_trajectory_end defaults to false), and if you omit velocities entirely it silently falls back to LINEAR interpolation, putting a velocity step at every waypoint. Publish further ahead than you execute so the zero-velocity tail always lands beyond the replan point.

Skipping the hold test. Command exactly the pose the arm is already in, and confirm nothing moves. If it twitches, your joint ordering or frame convention is wrong, and you want to find that out at zero velocity rather than at full reach.

Collecting demonstrations that vary in nothing. Whatever is constant across your dataset — object position, lighting, start pose, which hand holds the leader — the policy is licensed to memorize. If the arm always starts folded, the policy only works from folded, and no amount of additional episodes from the folded pose will fix it.
communityDifferences: Research labs (Stanford/Columbia: UMI, Diffusion Policy) do not use ROS at all, and it is a considered choice, not ignorance. They run Python multiprocessing with hand-written lock-free shared-memory ring buffers, talk to the arm through the vendor's own real-time interface (ur_rtde servoL, libfranka), and own every timestamp in the system end to end. What they gain is exact control of time alignment and latency measurement, which is the thing their research is actually about. What they lose: no TF (so every frame transform is hand-composed and every frame bug is yours), no RViz (so you debug geometry by printing numbers), no rosbag (so introspection is print statements and saved videos), no MoveIt (so no collision checking, no planning around obstacles, no reachability analysis), no ros2_control (so no joint limit enforcement, no controller lifecycle, no hardware abstraction, and no standard place to put a safety layer). Every one of those is reimplemented badly or not at all. Their codebases are small — umi/real_world/rtde_interpolation_controller.py is ~208 lines total — because the scope is deliberately narrow.

ALOHA (Stanford/Trossen) occupies a middle position that is easy to misread. It runs ROS 1 Noetic and interbotix_xs_modules, but uses ROS purely as a device-driver bus: no MoveIt, no planners, no TF-based reasoning, and the README explicitly instructs you to disable the forward-kinematics call in interbotix's arm.py because it delays teleoperation. That is a lab treating ROS as an inconvenient but working motor driver. If you read ALOHA expecting ROS architecture, you will find none.

HuggingFace LeRobot is deliberately, aggressively ROS-free and its abstraction is a plain Python ABC — Robot.connect / get_observation / send_action / disconnect, 251 lines. What that buys is enormous: pip install, one process, no colcon, no workspace overlays, no RMW, no discovery, direct integration with the Hub, dataset streaming, and a policy zoo. What it costs is the same list as the research labs plus one more: there is no standard place for a safety layer, so the entire built-in protection is a single clamp function (ensure_safe_goal_position) that is disabled by default. The ROS 2 bridges that exist (ycheng517/lerobot-ros, sacovo/lerobot_ros, astroyat/lerobot-ros) are all community wrappers, not upstream.

Industrial practice inverts the priority. The learned policy is demoted to a setpoint generator running on a non-safety computer, and everything between it and the motors — velocity limiting, workspace monitoring, collision detection, e-stop — lives in certified hardware or a safety-rated controller that the policy cannot influence. ros2_control on a PREEMPT_RT kernel, deterministic cycle times, watchdogs on every link. The policy is untrusted by construction. This is the opposite of the research posture, where the policy output goes almost directly to servoL.

ROBOTIS' physical_ai_tools is the hybrid, and it is the one your project actually inhabits. ROS 2 Jazzy + ros2_control + a Dynamixel SystemInterface for the robot; LeRobot vendored as a git submodule for the learning; and a bridge node (physical_ai_server.py, 1043 lines) that converts ROS topics to LeRobot observation dicts and publishes the policy's output back as JointTrajectory. You keep RViz, rosbag, TF, MoveIt and the lifecycle machinery for the robot, and you get LeRobot's datasets and policies for the learning. The seam shows, though: the bridge's Communicator (651 lines) does not use message_filters.ApproximateTimeSynchronizer — it just stores the latest message per topic — so the time-alignment rigor that UMI treats as the core of the system is simply absent. That is the concrete price of the hybrid, and knowing where the price is paid is more useful than knowing which camp is right.

On the data-collection rig the split is philosophical, not technical. Leader-follower teleop (ALOHA, LeRobot SO-100/101 and Koch, ROBOTIS OMX-L) gives labels that are trivially in the robot's own action space and costs you a second arm plus one operator per session. Handheld rigs (UMI and its descendants) decouple data from the robot entirely and buy 100× throughput and real environmental diversity, at the cost of an offline SLAM pipeline, a latency-matching subsystem, and a gripper-geometry constraint that ties your robot's end effector to the handheld one. Neither community thinks the other is wrong; they are optimizing different constraints — one optimizes fidelity to the deployment hardware, the other optimizes data volume and diversity.
